Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to write unit tests for classes with only private methods and properties?
Answer: Your class is always going to have at least one public method, its constructor. In some languages there are testing frameworks that can bypass the visibility of a method for testing purposes and so would let you individually test methods even though they are private. So on the face of the question, yes, but i don’t think it’s a great idea, you should test a class at its effective boundaries, and if there are “orphan” methods ie they are private but never called from another methods so effectively unreachable, then you probably shouldn’t test it - either make it public or delete it.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Are there any front-end frameworks that could overtake React in the future?
Answer: React today is not the dominant framework, it never has been and never will be. The vast majority of the web doesn’t use React, Angular etc. but it either generated by a backend or uses some kind of CMS system like wordpress. Most of the super high traffic web properties, like amazon dotcom, any of the google 1b+ users products etc. don’t use an oss web framework. I don’t think that there’s going to be any framework in the foreseeable future that will replace React as the de facto choice for anyone who wants to use a web framework, that said in the last 5+ years there have been 4 robust choices - React, Angular, Vue and Svelte, which all power major web apps in production. There’s another batch of frameworks like Alpine and Solid which are arguably production ready and which just don’t have the traction of the main 4. React is not necessarily the best web framework and there are governance concerns but it definitely has the most developers compared to its direct competitors now. But in the grand scheme of things I don’t see things changing significantly over the next few years, if anything I imagine that completely AI is going to grow in competency and that entire web apps generated by AI will eat into the market share of web frameworks.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: As a frontend dev, do you ever get the feeling that Angular is the last reliable framework these days? React's basically hooked on Next.js & Vercel now, and all these other frameworks keep re-discovering themselves every year.
Answer: I don’t think so. I feel that Angular, React, Svelte and Vue are all reliable, and large companies have strategic web apps in production based on one of these. Also, most of the web still doesn’t use a “framework” (CMS platform, static HTML, entirely generated on the backend, etc.) A lot of the discourse around web technology focuses on new features. For instance there are new web standards becoming generally available on all browsers every month, Vercel that you mention cuts a new major release of next.js every year or so, etc. But the reality of web development is that no solution is written instantly from scratch using latest technologies. Most of the web using frameworks is going to be a few major version late, and using various technologies which may no longer be the state of the art, but which were future proof enough to not need being replaced anytime soon.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you give some examples of when Google has rejected a candidate after a referral?
Answer: Won’t get into too much detail out of privacy but none of the candidates I referred to Google were hired and most didn’t make it to the interview stage, even though they were all highly qualified in my professional opinion. Being referred is definitely not a guarantee of getting an offer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Trump use a phony AI post of Swifties for Trump?
Answer: In May 2015, the any pundit would have predicted that the GOP nomination would go to either Jeb Bush, Scott Walker or Marco Rubio. All three were well known and had strong backing. But then rumors started that Trump would join the primary, which is did in mid June with an incendiary speech about Mexican migrants. Every media outlet talked about that speech, and following that about every outrageous thing that Trump did or say. This is earned reach - while typically candidates spend on ad campaigns to have their names in front of voters, sometimes this happens for free. Walker dropped out of the primary in September - Trump had become the favorite by then. And even though Bush raised much more than him he had to exit the race unceremoniously as well. All the heavy hitters, Ted Cruz, Chris Christie, Huckabee, Santorum - lost because they couldn’t compete with the enormous amount of earned reach - essentially free advertisement - that came with Trump. Fast forward to 2024. Trump creates outrageous images and montages that energize his base but which are also being generously re-shared by his critics. For instance, when the sub-reddit “facepalm” makes “fun” of these images, which it’s done several times, it’s being shared with its 10 million members, over and over again, and it’s just one of many avenues by which it’s reshared. Whenever he’s going to create another image, and why wouldn’t he do that every few days, it’s going to be “criticized”, “ridiculed” etc. by the usual suspects but really what happens is that unwilling accomplices are going to say “Trump” multiple times to tens of millions of people. there is little chance of a blowback here. Some commentators assumed that Taylor Swift would sue, but why would she? She’s seen first hand how long and difficult it is to see the former president convicted, and how much publicity it will give him. All publicity is good publicity. We’ve known this since the 19th century.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Are unit tests good for testing video games?
Answer: Unit tests are seldom a bad idea, but they are not enough for videogames. When you think about testing strategy the question you are trying to answer is, how can i be sure that my system is working as expected? Let’s suppose all the methods of your game are unit tested - great. But that itself doesn’t mean that players will have a good experience. Those problems typically happen because the player goes through a very specific sequence of events. As modern games give more freedom to players, there is a near infinite amount of situations and automated tests are very bad at covering that. (this also goes for larger scaled tests, like integration or end-to-end tests. we can verify that the code works and that various parts of the system work together, but not that what happens is what the player expects, that the player isn’t stuck, etc. this is why games still have to rely on manual QA, ie having humans play the game and report problems.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it true that no one has ever been rejected from a job interview at Google?
Answer: yes. When they call you for interview, and you actually show up, they give you a computer, a badge and a handshake and just show you to your desk.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is being good at games a requirement for working as a video game tester?
Answer: No. When people talk about video game tester they usually mean quality assurance teams. These folks are given a scenario and need to execute it and report things not working as expected. I’ve never met a tester that wasn’t at least decent at videogames because the recruitment is kind of self-selective, people who are willing to play the same half-baked videogame level over and over all day and who are excited to receive a new half-baked videogame level are interested in gaming and they are good at it. But in the game development process the design team may want to do user research and they may want to hear from highly skilled players, like competitive players. i.e. if I’m building a team-based battle royale shooting game, a market which is both very though to crack and very lucrative to lead, then I very much care about the experience of very experienced and highly skilled players of competing, existing games. But “testing” / “QA” refer specifically to addressing bugs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason behind companies like Google asking difficult technical questions in their interviews?
Answer: The problem that Google faces is that they receive millions of applications per year but only have thousands of open jobs. So, they need to devise a process such that the best applicants be hired. If in order to get hired, a candidate only has to answer easy questions, then being hired is essentially a test of luck. Conversely if the questions are selective, luck is still involved but there is a stronger guarantee that the candidate has the required skill to take on the job. So, this is much more advantageous for Google or any desirable tech company to ask hard questions.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can someone without coding experience pass Google's coding interviews?
Answer: To pass the interview, you need to have great feedback on your interview, which is not exactly the same as doing great at the interview. So, theoretically, if the interviewer, who is the one writing the feedback, is in on it, they could sing the praises of the candidate regardless of their performance. This comes with several caveats. First, there are several interviewers, and if the feedback of one is very different from others this calls for additional scrutiny. So several / all interviewers would need to be involved. The coding interviews are logged so what the candidate types needs to be consistent with the feedback, though it’s possible that if all coding interview feedback are strong yesses no one will look at the logs. Helping a candidate cheat is very risky and if caught the interviewer(s) will face very unpleasant consequences, and it does leave a trail of evidence. Without cheating - there is not a chance that someone who doesn’t know how to code can pass. Not by a long shot. This is not a “monkeys with an infinite amount of time” situation. In order to pass, a candidate must: a) solve the problem at hand b) be familiar enough with the programming language to implement this within the time limit. Coding experience is required for both. In addition candidates are evaluated on their coding style, proper use of algorithms etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it accurate to say that most professional programmers are not skilled at coding?
Answer: No. Of course that depends on what you call “professional programmers”. But - given that the vast majority of software engineers in tech companies have less than 3 years tenure, given that they all needed to pass several demanding coding tests to be considered for hiring, given that virtually all tech companies have some form of best practices / code style / code standards that all code must adhere to, processes around code reviewing, deployment, incidents etc. which involve constant peer reviewing, given that on top of that, software engineer performance is constantly monitored and tied to their compensation, and largely depends on the code they write, and given that there are companies out there which are spending a lot of money for their coding output, then it’s more the opposite. Tech companies software engineers are very skilled at coding, the same way that professional chefs are very skilled at cooking, professional athletes are very skilled at their sport, etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What's your take on Imane Khelif, a biologically proven male boxer, taking part in the Women's Boxing event at the Paris Olympics 2024?
Answer: Beyond her individual case I have issues with the phrase, a “biologically proven male”, and statements such as: Back in my days, there were men and there were women. Or: There are two sexes, male and female. It’s that simple. It’s science actually. At birth, a medical professional attempts to make a determination of the “biological sex” of the baby - basically checking the presence of a penis. Except it’s not always possible: ambiguous genitalia is when this determination is not even possible. That happens roughly 1/5000 times. But that’s far from the only cases where people’s body deviate from the idea we have of a “male” or a “female” body: We surveyed the medical literature from 1955 to the present for studies of the frequency of deviation from the ideal male or female. We conclude that this frequency may be as high as 2% of live births.[1] So you have up to 2% - one out of 50. several in any highschool - people who maybe don’t have XX or XY chromosomes, or who don’t have the chromosomes that align with their genitalia, etc. and most often are not aware of it. So I don’t believe in biologically proven male. What I believe in is: I’m actually not sure that a male in the same weight category would even have an advantage on a woman to begin with, but again that’s irrelevant because Ms Khelif is a woman and has been deemed apt to participate by the IOC.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to get hired at Apple or other tech companies with self-taught experience and a strong portfolio of projects?
Answer: Yes, it’s possible, and it’s harder. The most selective part of being hired is being invited to interview. It’s always possible to be considered for a position by being referred. There was a time when being referred was an almost certain guarantee to interview, not any more. But at least a recruiter would look at the candidate resume and may schedule a call. Some companies have hard conditions to be met to be referred (like relevant degrees) but this is not the norm. It’s also technically possible to be contacted by a sourcer or an employee just because they see your work. This is unlikely. It is not completely impossible, but just putting projects out there doesn’t mean that you’re going to get a job offer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is there any way Trump won't win re-election in 2024?
Answer: It’s incredibly difficult to predict the 2024 election results based on the data that the general public has access to. The main numbers we get are what percentage of respondents would vote for Trump or the dem nominee. But the 2 last elections are proof these are not great predictors of the election outcome. Clinton was beating Trump like a drum and got most of the popular vote by a large margin. And yet she lost. Likewise, Biden had a comfortable lead on Trump and won the popular vote by millions, and while he did win it was a narrow and contested victory. In order to be elected, a nominee has to get the vote of electors. The electors will in turn be determined by voters in their respective states. In order to be able to do so, any citizen must: be eligible to vote, be registered to vote, be willing to vote, be physically able to vote and have their vote taken into account. A lot of variables and events are going to affect all of these steps. This is why it’s extremely difficult to model what is going to happen in November. Trump is unique in the history of modern candidates in that he has a huge “earned” reach. Traditionally the candidates campaign rely on “paid” reach (ie ads) so they have to spend money to get their message across. Everything he says or does is scrutinized and commented on both social or national media. That’s a huge advantage. But he’s also been a very unpopular president when in charge, he’s a convicted felon, a sex offender who lost in appeal, and he can’t use the #1 argument of populists worldwide - you’ve tried everything but me and look where it got you - not anymore. So he’s definitely not unbeatable. But neither the Republicans, nor the Democrats have really executed their strategy to secure victory, so it’s very early to tell what can happen.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump?
Answer: In the weeks leading to November 7, 2016, there is not a single news article I read or anyone that I interacted in that entertained the possibility of Hillary Clinton being defeated. Pundits agreed she had come on top in all three debates, she was way ahead in the polls, she was considered one of the most qualified candidates of all times and she was running against someone that had never held a political office. And yet, the strategy of the Trump campaign worked. They lost the popular vote, but they crafted a message that resonated with the white working class voter, and carried states where that demographic is well-represented like Pennsylvania, Michican and Wisconsin that the Democrats thought were unlosable. On July 20th, Joe Biden is still the candidate. A few weeks ago, his performance at the debate was abyssmal. In contrast, Trump has just triumphed at the RNC. He survived an assassination attempt. He’s surging in the polls. He is way ahead the democrats in terms of fund raising. His VP pick is expanding his reach. But is a Trump victory unavoidable? He was a deeply unpopular and divisive president, conservatives are lost every vote when abortion is an issue, he’s now a convicted felon, he’s lost a civil case around nothing less than a rape, then lost again in appeal. Most importantly, the Biden campaign still hadn’t executed their strategy. They still hadn’t showed their hand. There are very smart, very rich, and very influential people who support a liberal agenda and these hadn’t really come into play yet. And on July 21st - Biden announces he’s dropping out and quickly endorses Kamala Harris. Less than 48 hours later, she has enough delegates to be nominated, and got the full endorsement of many of the most influential dem leaders. She’s also raised a record amount of money, while all of the Trump campaign money spent attacking the person of Joe Biden is now pointless. This was a scenario that was anticipated by the Republicans but still requires a massive pivot of their communication and messaging, so this is highly disrupting. So as of today on July 24th - nobody knows what will happen on November 5th. A Harris victory is definitely possible, just as a Biden victory was.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the potential disadvantages of being a full-stack web developer compared to specializing in either frontend or backend development?
Answer: Nobody knows everything there is to know on software development. But no matter how you slice and dice the things what someone needs to know to be considered a “full-stack developer” they will always need to be competent in front-end development. Ergo, a full-stack developer and a front-end developer are essentially the same thing, as every developer knows things outside of their area of expertise. I am not a fan of the full-stack label as I find it disingenuous and misleading. There are two ways to think about that. Once is to consider that a software developer is a software developer (or engineer) and that their scope doesn’t have fixed limits. That’s empirically true, anyone who has some experience in a C-like language can ramp up in another. The other is to assume that someone who has domain knowledge on a specialty will be more productive in their domain of expertise and shouldn’t be encouraged to branch out. Also largely true, and not incompatible with the above. The idea that it’s somehow better to know a little bit on many domains, as opposed to have stronger expertise on just one, is just as wrong in software development as it is in say law or medicine. The contexts where it’s actually better to be a jack-of-all-trades are very situational, but include being a founding engineer or an early stage developer which is what explains the allure.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the advantages and disadvantages of working for a large tech company like Google or Microsoft compared to a smaller company like Facebook or Uber?
Answer: I’ve worked in all companies mentioned in this question except Microsoft. I don’t think Uber, which has the smallest engineering force of the 4, would remotely qualify as a small company. While the work experience there may be different compared to the other 3, it is even more different from the experience of working at a startup.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What factors may influence an engineer or developer working at a big tech company (such as Google, Facebook, or Apple) to leave the Bay Area or California?
Answer: Different people have different approaches to working in person. Anecdotally I find that recent hires are more likely to prefer working from the office, where they can get help when needed, than more tenured employees who are already operational and who can achieve as much with fewer hours. I’m not sure this can be generalized. But there is definitely a large number of big tech employees that do prefer working remotely. The Bay Area has notoriously high cost of living. If your compensation stay the same wherever you live, then living in the Bay Area is definitely not where your money is going to go the furthest. Even when compensation is adjusted, the cost of living outside of the Bay Area can make this advantageous from a purely monetary point of view. During my tenure at Google, we were all offered the possibility to relocate, subject to approval but this was a formality, but with the caveat that compensation may be impacted - it could decrease by up to 25% for most of the country. But living remotely with 75% of a Google engineer salary in most of the country is much more advantageous than living in the Bay Area with 100% of it - again, from a purely monetary point of view. For the record, I do live in the Bay Area, even if my current company will pay my full compensation anywhere in the country.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you agree with a major Silicon Valley founder who said “Every Democrat outside the Beltway knows [Biden]'ll lose”? Why or why not?
Answer: All the pundits expected a Hillary victory in 2016. Countless people had written Trump off. Turns out predicting the future is harder than it seems. In 2022/2023, dozens of tech CEOs justified rounds of layoffs with the same excuse: unpredictable macroeconomic headwinds - when this is literally their job to adjust to conjoncture. So while I don’t take predictions from anyone for absolute truth, I would trust the confidence of a “silicon valley founder” least of all.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do all ex-Googlers want to return to work at Google?
Answer: From the answers it is clear that there is at least one ex Googler who doesn’t want to return to work at Google. I would love to relive the feeling of my first few weeks at Facebook in March 2013. Just 4000 employees. Instagram team is 12 people or so, it doesn’t seem it will be mainstream any time soon. The entire design team can fit in a room and does so every Monday morning. I feel our work is making what has become a daily habit of more than a billion people somewhat more positive and interesting. Also we are super well treated - excellent food, treats, gym, there’s even my favorite pinball machine on site (and it is free). However this era is gone forever. What is true for Facebook is true for Google which I never knew at that size. Google could get away with being a different company at that size and, truth be told, it was able to keep being Google as it crossed the 1000, 10000 and 100000 employees mark. But less and less well. Google will just never be the magical place it once was. When I left it had over 10,000 teams. Nobody can reason with 10,000 teams. Nobody can understand what should be prioritized or not. I’m sure many ex Googlers would love to go back to 2005 or 2010 (but so would a lot of people in tech). Unfortunately (or fortunately, for you glass half-full people) that world is long gone.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: The internet shuts down in 1 hour. It will never be back again. How will you spend this hour?
Answer: there’s 2 parts in the premise. if the internet were to stop in one hour, yes there would be major panic but there’s no technical problem we can’t solve, and worst case scenario, there are people who know everything one needs to know to the create the internet from scratch. what worries me is the “it will never work again” part. does physics no longer work the way it used to? did we kill all the scientists? Whatever caused the “never work again part”, this is definitely a bigger worry than me not having notification for the next hour.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reasoning behind companies hiring only front-end or back-end developers instead of full stack developers? What are the advantages of this approach?
Answer: A software engineer is not either “front-end” or “back-end”. There are many specialties. Unless your system is very small, there is not going to be one person who has operational knowledge of everything that’s required to make it work, and who can write mobile code one morning, responds to a security incident over lunch, sets up a web server in the afternoon and optimizes data pipelines at night (or again there may be if all of these systems are very simple). The reality is that software engineers work on projects for long periods of time - months, quarters - during which their technological environment is fairly stable. There are two school of thoughts. One who argues that an engineer is an engineer and can learn anything. One good representative of that approach is Google. Then again, to be operational at Google, one must first learn how to write code at Google and how to use the internal tools. Once that’s done, writing Google code is designed to be easy for all “Googlers”, so it’s arguably easier for someone who worked 3 years at Google as a data engineer to write front-end code than for a front-end engineer on their first week. There are quite a few other companies who value versatility and the capacity for engineers to switch from one technology to the other. The other philosophy is that since engineers are going to work on one sub domain at a time, it’s beneficial to have specialists who can be more productive on what they will work on, even if that means they are somewhat pigeonholed. This is the dominant approach. There is so much to know about CSS and web frameworks, on how to write modern C++, on data modelling etc. that you can’t be just as good if you get to work on this every 2 years - and if you do you’ll be penalized by having to spend several weeks re-learning the technology. it doesn’t mean that “front-end” or “back-end” engineers can’t reason about anything outside the code they write - with the possible exception of the most junior developers. But to recenter on your question, the rationale is that specialists can be more productive at the tasks for which they are hired, and this is generally what companies are interested in.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: In your opinion, why is "Can I trust you?" not included in the typical interview process?
Answer: Would you trust somebody you have never met, regardless of what they say to you? if so i may have a bridge to sell you. Besides that, a question such as “can I trust you” begs insincere answers. So all in all this would be a waste of interview time, when actual skills can be assessed.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you provide examples of questions asked in Google interviews for software engineers, particularly on data structures and algorithms?
Answer: Here’s one example of question that was asked at Google and which I know for a fact is banned, but is also fairly typical of DS&I questions - “sleeping lions”. Imagine a 2d matrix of dimensions mxn. Every cell of this matrix has x,y coordinates (0 <= x < m, 0 <= y, n). The matrix represents a lion-infested savannah. There’s a person somewhere in the matrix at coordinates X0, Y0. They want to reach their car at coordinates X1, Y1. But there are also a number of sleeping lions at coordinates xi, yi. There’s also a distance D whereby if somebody gets within a D radius of a sleeping lion, they would wake up the lion. Given all of these coordinates and the distance D, return the the fastest route between the person and their car that doesn’t wake a lion, or null if there is no such path.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What should I say or not in an exit interview when I have been fired?
Answer: Exit interviews are a complete waste of time for all involved in general, but I really cannot see the justification for holding one in case of an involuntary termination. Really say whatever you want.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you determine if someone is the best software engineer on your team? Is there a way to identify the top performer?
Answer: typically engineers in a team are not going to be at the same level. The expectations are not the same for somebody fresh out of college and a more senior contributor. Tech companies usually have formalized the expectations for various levels in a document called competencies, ladder or something similar. Then, there is a regular process to evaluate how everyone in the team is performing compared to what can be expected of them - unsurprisingly called performance evaluation or perf. In order to make that determination, there are several sources: self evaluation of the individual, peer feedback as well as manager feedback, each time using the expectations for the level of the person as a guide. That document would describe what can be expected of a professional according to several criteria level by level, expectations being higher with each level. So if for a given category a junior engineer performs as the level above, that is very very good, but if a senior engineer has the same output this will not be not meeting expectations. So performance is always relative to a level.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you demonstrate your coding skills in an interview to show that you are above average as a software engineer?
Answer: I remember when the phrase exceeds expectations became fashionable in business lingo around the turn of the 21st century, you had so many businesses and individuals who took pride in “not only meeting but always exceeding expectations” - but it’s impossible to always exceed expectations especially if you advertise it - because then expectations are raised, up to the point you just meet them, or even not meet them. As a coding interview candidate, you should focus on performing the task which is asked of you. This is important, so I’m going to bold it: you should not try to impress your interviewer by going above and beyond. Maybe counter-intuitively what will impress them is you doing the job cleanly, quickly, legibly etc which may sound boring, and what will definitely NOT impress them is you trying to write a clever one-liner that you can’t actually troubleshoot, using the latest syntax of the language that you’ve actually never used and that you don’t master, or starting to code all guns blazing in order to save some precious seconds without asking the disambiguating question that will prevent you from completely misunderstanding the exercise. Modern coding interviews are not trick questions (if your coding interview is a trick question, this may not be a great place to work anyway). Take the time to understand the question, don’t hesitate to ask question, and get to work. show you can do the job for which they want to hire you.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do candidates typically answer questions about their potential weaknesses or missing information during job interviews?
Answer: Insincerely, which begs the question of why these are being asked in interviews in 2024. When I was in business school in the 90s, we were being coached for the interview style of the time. Interviewers were trying to trip us so we had to “think on our feet”, and if there ever was a box, we had to think outside of it. We all knew the actual reason why manholes were round, but we also had an even more clever answer just in case. Our biggest weakness was either too much attention to detail or never being able to completely turn off our “work mode”, and that was not trite yet. OK. so back of the napkin says there’s been over 30 billion job interviews for professional roles over the past 30 years. Let’s say that one out of 3 has featured a question on the candidate’s biggest weakness. that’s 10 billion. Assuming 5 minutes were spent on each, that’s 50 billion minutes, or approximately 100,000 years that have been wasted on this, and let me tell you this: not one useful bit of information has come out of this.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you determine if someone is lying during an interview, especially if they are skilled at deception?
Answer: 1) you can’t, 2) it doesn’t matter. The goal of the interview is not to tell if your candidate is telling the truth. It’s to use human judgment to evaluate if the candidate has the required skills to perform the job they are applying for. But what if they are lying? well, that’s what the background check and reference processes are for - to catch the lies which would make you reconsider extending an offer. I don’t think an untruthful answer is necessarily a bad thing. First, there are questions which call for an insincere answer, such as what is your biggest weakness or why did you leave your last job. Of course you shouldn’t ask them to begin with, but this is just to make a point that an untrue answer may not be on the candidate. Second, from the signal one gets from an answer, there’s no difference between a behavioral question (tell me about a time when you…) and a hypothetical question (imagine that tomorrow, …). I’m totally ok to have candidates treat a behavioral question as a hypothetical question and answer with an improvised fiction, as long as it demonstrates they have the skills and this is how they would solve this specific situation. Finally, I don’t think that “lying” would give the candidate a leg up. Here’s an example. A very classical behavioral question is tell me about a time you disagreed with somebody your senior. Let’s say our candidate doesn’t want to actually tell about an actual interaction, and instead invent a fable where they saved the day and everybody ended up agreeing with them. This is actually a weak answer, it doesn’t demonstrate what the candidate has done to build the alignment, it doesn’t offer surface for follow up questions such as “what would you have done differently?”, “what did you learn?” etc. so lying actually puts the candidate at a disadvantage. What a younger generation would describe as “not the flex you think it is”.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: I don't understand why our Biden Democrats want an open border when nothing good has come of it so far. Can a Democrat explain this to me?
Answer: very few people in the US advocate for open borders as in - the US should let everyone and everything in no questions asked. Biden is definitely not one of them. Has ICE been abolished? Have border patrols been defunded? In fact, the number of migrants arrested for entering the country illegally has increased[1], and while it’s difficult to find long time series that unambiguously compare the drug seizures under Trump versus under Biden, nobody is denying that there have been massive drug seizures under Biden - in fact, Republicans use these very seizures - a proof that law enforcement is doing their job - to argue that this is a “Biden border crisis”. [2] However, two statements can be true at the same time. You can be for the rule of law, and against separating families / keeping children in cages.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Microsoft build its products (e.g., Visual Studio Code) in JS rather than C#?
Answer: I’m not privy to what led to the actual decision but I am confident I can reverse engineer it. There’s 2 main reasons. 1) Today, and for a good 10 years, If you want to build an interactive user interface, the standard is to build a web app. Let’s go back to 20/30 years ago. At that time, the standard way to let users interact with your service was to to let them access and execute a binary file. You would build graphical users interface, if needed, from scratch or from some kind of development framework. And users would expect to buy CD-Roms, etc. to install their software. But the web standards are now the most precise and exhaustive system to describe a user interface. Anything that is not going to be described through the DOM is going to be less than. It doesn’t mean it’s not possible to create performant UX outside of the web, it’s just that for a project born in the late 2010s the go-to approach would be to create a web app. erg...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the difference between a test case and a unit test case?
Answer: it’s the exact same thing. one may object, oh but a unit test case is the test case of a unit test, not a general test. But a test case is really a scenario to be tested. it is not a bit of code, it is not tied to a test runtime or a testing environment. A test case could conceptually be part of several test pl...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the difference between code review and unit testing in terms of reducing risk?
Answer: It’s like asking what’s the difference between wearing seatbelts and using turn signals when driving in terms of road safety. There is no tradeoff or situation where one is better than the other, and best practices are to do both. In a tech environment, there is usually no tolerance to commit unreviewed code for normal business (that is, unless you need to solve an urgent incident etc.). If a bug is introduced, this is not the responsibility of the individual, but the entire organization that should have prevented that on a best effort basis. Having someone else approve of the code change is a cheap sanity check that prevents a code change that could be blatantly wrong to make it to the code base. Of course solo developers don’t have that luxury, but they can still write their code as if it would be reviewed - small commits, comments, tests etc. To continue on the driving metaphor, this is the equivalent of driving at the speed limit even if you know there are no radars. Unit tests are a bit more complicated, in the sense that while they are super useful in maintaining code health, they can be a huge burden to write if you come from a situation where the tests are already lacking. If you merge on a highway where the speed limit is 50 but everyone is already driving at 70, it is difficult to actually stick to 50. And yet, there’s no reason not to write unit tests for projects which are going to be maintained (throwaway code may or may not have them).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the significance of unit tests? How do they aid in identifying and resolving bugs before a product is released?
Answer: Unit tests do not catch bugs. this is a common misconception. Unit tests prevent bugs. Developers write unit tests on deterministic code. That means code that, with given inputs, produce predictable outputs. If the code is non deterministic then unit tests cause more chaos than anything else and are eventually removed. As a consequence, when unit tests are written, unless something changes in the system, the same test cases will pass just like the day they were written. Another characteristic of unit tests is that they are run automatically in some kind of pipeline, such as CI/CD jobs. When a developer wants to commit new code, unit tests would run to check if this code change doesn’t break anything. Again this isn’t part of the definition of unit tests per se but writing unit tests without running them automatically is like buying avocados and never eating them. There isn’t a law against that but it’s not the intended use. So when somebody wants to make a change in the system: Regardless - before the code change is committed, you have a body of unit tests that will always pass. After the code change is committed, you have a body of unit tests that will always pass. There are other types of tests or checks that could signal that something is not right even if code hasn’t changed. In an integration test, a component will call another component, there’s an inherent risk of failure with that, plus there can be some version skew problems (ie one component is upgraded such that it will no longer send the same request or response, and the other one doesn’t expect that), end to end tests may use live endpoints, monitoring may signal abnormal behavior… all of this can be diagnosed and investigated. but unit tests are not supposed to suddenly fail out of the blue unless the code they cover changes, the testing environment changes etc. So you can’t measure their usefulness by the number of bugs they catch. That number is going to be 0. However, when writing new code, they offer a safety net and an advanced signal if the intended code change would break existing code - before an actual bug could occur.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do programmers know what to code before they write any code?
Answer: large tech companies have code bases with billions (or higher multiples) of lines of code. This is mind boggling if you think of writing code as - start from an empty file, type statements, run the code, then iterate by adding lines and so on and so forth. Let’s say you’re a very prolific developer and you can write an average of 1000 lines of code per day, that’s 250,000 per year (bear with me). It would take you 4000 years to write 1 billion lines of code, or 200000 years to write 50 billions loc. That’s a similar effort to building the Notre Dame cathedral. So let’s forget the code editor for a second. Let’s forget typing 1000 lines of code per day or else. Let’s start instead with a problem statement. “We want to create an app that let people send messages instantly to each other”. Engineers are capable of taking that statement and disambiguate it. What are we trying to optimize? what are the constraints? who are the users? what is the volume of data? do these messages need to persist? etc. Answering these questions let them get a more complete picture of what needs to be built. Add to that product designers that can describe how users will use the service, product managers that would set priorities… From there, the requirements can be broken down into features and into more atomic tasks. So now, developers have to execute these tasks and write one or two hundreds of lines of code at a time, which are enough to implement something which is easy to describe and to understand by their peers. Like so, the work can be organized, split, tracked, and progress in the right direction.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do companies like Google use code challenges during interviews? If yes, which languages are most commonly used?
Answer: Candidates can use pretty much any language they want. Interviewers have to specify which languages they feel confident interviewing in and there are so many options including really arcane ones. You can interview in Cobol, in Pascal, in Closure - that’s a weird flex but ok.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the purpose of coding interviews for senior software engineer positions at companies like Facebook and Google? What skills or abilities are they trying to assess through this test?
Answer: Let’s forget about the coding interview specifically and let’s agree that Facebook, Google etc. want to hire the best candidates. So let’s say 100 people apply for 10 positions, ideally they want the 10 best ones, more realistically they want to be reasonably sure the 10 people they extend offers to are among the 30 best ones, and they want to be very certain that none of the worst 20 ones are hired. One way to operate this selection is through the resume. In order to apply to a senior role, a candidate’s resume has to demonstrate that they have a sporting chance to pass the interview, so they need relevant experience, which implies they have written professional code for several years. So Meta could say - I won’t consider interviewing anyone with fewer than 5 years of experience at Google, Microsoft, Apple or Amazon. But then that leaves a large number of qualified candidate without a possibility to access the company. Not great. Also, this assumes that just because a candidate has worked X amount of years as a software engineer in tech, then they are good at coding, and I have interviewed enough candidates with prestigious backgrounds to tell that it’s not true. Indeed, the coding interview(s) provide a great signal of how good a candidate is at the fundamental skill of the job, and is a good tool in determining who should receive offers.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the potential drawbacks of not refactoring old code when working on a new feature in a project with poorly written code and no unit tests?
Answer: You should look at it the opposite way and think of what is the value of refactoring old code, etc. It’s obvious that code written a long time ago, before certain features of the language emerged, new libraries appeared, good practices were widely accepted… is going to be substantially harder to maintain and evolve than a hypothetical new and pristine code base made to modern standards. But refactoring is not always the right call - like everything in engineering it is always a matter of return on investment. You can probably form an idea of how much this would cost to rewrite your codebase - even just based on the line count. But what value does that create? if there’s no further motive in this refactor then this is simply a pointless exercise. However if this part of the code base is widely used and if many systems rely on it and it causes frequent outages then you can make a case that getting this code to be me more reliable has a tangible value, that may justify the refactoring effort. But again if the value is not here, then so matter how strong the refactoring itch can get, just let it go. Having no unit tests really impacts the cost of the refactoring more than anything else. With comprehensive coding you can at least attempt to rewrite a code base such that the tests which describe the behavior we’re interested in pass. Without the unit tests, whether the refactored code is equivalent is much more difficult (and sometimes impossible) to determine.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should I approach this wild +40k lines of code in a single file of ReactJS component?
Answer: There are 2 rules which one should keep in mind when dealing with engineering problem of whatever nature. 1) it’s safer and desirable to achieve any coding tasks by changing the fewest lines of code and preserving existing logic as much as possible 2) for everything you do there is an ROI. There’s a cost which is usually easier to estimate, and there’s at least a supposed value. Here those two rules are at odds. I can completely understand how someone would want to approach this very cautiously and chip at the giant file 100 lines at a time. However, this is going to take forever, most of these changes would be impossible to code review so you’d be flying completely dark. This is an insane task, as in: a literally unbounded amount of work, extremely risky, dubious results. If I were asked to review the first code change of many to undo this file I would reject it with very strong language. There are only two reasonable approaches. first, do nothing. Treat it as a black box. It “works”, kind of - and that’s it. It won’t be maintained, touched, and it will do what it used to do until it’s no longer used. “but but” - sure, but this situation didn’t happen overnight, that thing has festered for many years to get that big. second, rewrite it entirely from scratch with modern language. It’s going to take much less time than trying to refactor it and it is going to be considerably safer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What does a good one page resume for a senior software engineer look like?
Answer: I don’t think a senior software engineer resume *has to* fit in one page. I’ve personally kept my resumes under one page through my entire career, because I believe that the information that would let a recruiter decide whether they want to interview me for a position can fit under one page. i use a 2 column, 1/4 - 3/4 layout In the leftmost column, I list my skills including the programming languages, then education, then the professional experiences that I don’t highlight in the main column - just name of organization and dates, In the main column, I put selected work experiences with a little bit of detail - title, mission, accomplishments. But especially as my experience grows, I have to be aggressively selective to keep it under one page. I think that’s fine, we don’t have to be exhaustive. But it’s definitely easier to allow oneself to go to two pages, which is definitely tolerable. The lenght of resumes starts getting problematic beyond 4 pages, because nothing really matters at that level of detail - not for the decision that people who will read the resume will take.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is the interview process at Google as stressful and competitive as portrayed in the media? Is it true that most people fail their first interview with the company? Can you share your personal experience with the interview process at Google?
Answer: A lot of engineers start their career at Google by converting an internship. That means that they first got in a great computer science college, they got an internship at Google, they met expectations during their internship which meant they got a return internship or a return offer if they were seniors. The internship interview is not as difficult as the regular software engineering interview but you see how the selection process is spread over several checks as opposed to just one. The interview process is arguably more stressful than other tech companies because it lasts longer - the time between your first interview and the hiring decisions can take months. It is selective too, it’s supposed to be, but not necessarily more or less than other tech companies. When I applied to Google I applied to other tech companies at the same time, some of which rejected me. And I think at the time (2019) it was fair to say that Google was the most desirable tech employer. The interview proper may be selective but not as much as what happens before, which is whether a candidate gets the opportunity to interview. A candidate needs to have a really strong profile to be considered for the interview.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you tell if a candidate is lying during an interview? Are there any effective methods besides asking about their greatest weakness?
Answer: Somewhat controversially, but I don’t care much if a candidate lies during their interview. What I want to know is: can we demonstrate that they have the skills that are needed for this position. In behavioral interviews this is usually established by questions of the form: can you tell me of a time when you did X / encountered Y situation. whether the story is factually correct or not doesn’t really matter. What is important is what does the candidate think is the right way to handle this situation if it were to happen now, what have they learned, how would they do it differently. Typically stories where the candidate saves the day just by being there and everybody agrees with what they say or do are not very convincing. But I feel it’s ok to take some creative liberties to retell a work story because the interviewer is more interested in how the candidate would solve it now with what they know, than in what actually happened. That said, if you want to get confirmation that what they said was true or at least consistent, ask for details. Ask what happened next. FWIW, i don’t think asking for a candidate’s greatest weaknesses (which really is a prompt for an insincere answer) is a good way to detect if they have been otherwise truthful.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it common for companies like Google and Facebook to hire individuals who have cheated during the hiring process, specifically during coding challenges?
Answer: As a parent, I’m pretty familiar with the situation when one of my kids would lie to my face and think that they are so clever and that they are going to get away with whatever they were trying to lie about. Except it’s obvious to me and to any reasonable person that they were lying to begin with. This is the same with cheating in software engineering interviews. There are so many tells. It’s really painful for the interviewer because nobody wants to write that feedback. If a candidate is suspected of cheating there is no way they will get an offer. The cheating would have to be highly sophisticated to get a chance of not being detected - but at that point, that effort could have gone through preparing for the interview. It is very likely though that it will be detected, and in that case this is a deal-breaker.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do employers prioritize hiring software engineers who can code quickly over those who take their time to write accurate and efficient programs?
Answer: Those two things are not contradictory. Professional software engineers write good clean code fast. There is no guarantee that taking more time for the sake of taking more time is going to result in better code. However, code must pass certain quality requirements in order to be committed to the code base. So these professionals are neither slow nor sloppy.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why is TypeScript not as commonly used with React as it is with Angular?
Answer: I don’t think that’s factually true, however - Angular made the decision a few years ago to write its docs with TypeScript. Many people assume that TypeScript is required to use Angular, when you really need anything that can compile to JavaScript. At Google, a significant proportion of the Angular apps use Dart instead of TypeScript. Meanwhile, React has made the decision to write their docs with JavaScript. I have to say that I find that decision confusing as React has excellent TypeScript support, to the point where the typical development experience with React is with TypeScript. The React.dev site has a button to toggle between light and dark mode, when that could be inferred from the reader’s OS’s / browser’s preferences, not no button to switch the entire doc from JS to TS. One thing that could explain that is the original investment in Flow which was a competing typing system. Facebook went all in with Flow at some point but I don’t know if this is still the same. At any rate, the React team made the decision that not knowing a type system should not be a blocker for learning React. (conversely, Google has been an early user of TypeScript, and the way JavaScript code was written pre-TypeScript was actually pretty similar).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the reasons for people switching from Angular to React, despite both having their own advantages?
Answer: The most common reason is organizational. Let’s say one company has projects in React and Angular, and they want to support just one stack going forward, and they decide to normalize to either one. That can be because they acquired a company whose product uses a different stack, because they made an architectural decision at some other level of their stack which means that one web framework is going to perform much better than another, etc. Both Angular and React are sensible modern frameworks which support large existing applications in production, and there’s no consensus that one is inherently superior to another (although individuals, of course, can have strong convictions). But rewriting a web application from one to another is a costly project, which only makes sense if there is a return on that cost.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can I work as a barista at Google HQ?
Answer: from my interactions with them, you just apply when there’s an open position. Baristas at Google possess a unique skill which has astonished me from the day I interviewed, which is they get your first name perfectly right without peeking at your badge no matter your ethnicity. Chinese, Indians, non-Anglo Europeans… we know it’s not your typical experience at, say, a Starbucks. I am not sure this is evaluated at the interview though. Latte and a cupcake at the Boston office And they spelled my name right! San Francisco office This one was for Google’s birthday. Also San Francisco Barista of Mountain View I appreciate you! They put so much heart in their work. It felt so great that during a minute of your day, somebody really cared about you.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Has anyone ever been rejected at a Google onsite interview despite receiving positive feedback from all the interviewers? What could be the reason for this?
Answer: A candidate would not know the feedback from their interviewers, let alone whether they got positive feedback from some, all or none. The recruiter can tell them things like “the feedback seems generally positive” but that’s it. The candidate would definitely not have access to their actual evaluation. As to this scenario, it can happen for a number of reasons - there are still a number of checks between the hiring committee and an offer. For instance, a candidate can get negative feedback from an internal reference. Something can come up during the background check. etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some common coding questions asked in Google interviews?
Answer: This is a little bit like the Shrödinger cat - when a Google coding question is made public, it’s banned. So if there were a common coding question at Google at a time t, discussing this question on a public forum means it won’t be asked again in interviews and therefore it won’t be a common coding question.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did the French lynch Gerard Depardieu?
Answer: The tiniest violin sings for Depardieu… after several women came forward and gave damning, graphic description of not just sexual assault but how the entire movie industry had acted to sweep this under the rug, none other than President Macron offered him public support and denounced the manhunt against “an immense actor” who “makes us proud”. Shortly after, M. Macron fired Rima Abdul-Malak, the minister of culture who had suggested removing him from the legion of honor. So the fallback of the many accusations of sexual violence has so far been negligible.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is system design asked in FAANG companies for junior engineers interviews the same as design patterns?
Answer: There is no system design question at Google for junior engineers. As it should be imo, I don’t think there is any useful information to be gained from asking system design questions to junior candidates.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason behind Google's intense hiring process with multiple rounds of programming tests compared to other companies?
Answer: Having interviewed at other silicon valley tech companies, I don’t think the hiring process of Google for software engineers is more (or less) intense. As to whether it is more selective than other workplaces for developers, probably, but the compensation (and other non-material benefits) is also much higher than outside of the tech bubble, so you have many more applicants.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you share your experience of interviewing with Google, Microsoft, Facebook, or Apple for a software engineering position?
Answer: I never interviewed for Microsoft, I never went through the full loop at Apple (I withdrew my application), but I did go onsite and was ultimately hired both by Facebook and Google, back when the onsite interview was the norm. I don’t think anything hasn’t been said about the technical aspects of the interview. There are so many books and classes on the topic. I have spent a lot of time on the other side of the interview room but my experience is still anecdotic. However, I can tell you a little bit about how it feels to come to a big tech HQ, having never been in one. It is very apparent that you are in a special place. It feels so different from another workplace, and especially from a non-tech one. To quote a popular video game: Just stepping foot inside Facebook in 2013 felt like such a privilege. Instagram was just 10 people or so. Facebook had just crossed one billion users - one of very few services in the world who had achieved that. All of this was very vibrant anywhere you were on campus, from the minute you entered. The space was both very efficient but also fun and different, a little bit arrogant but also very creative. It was a place thought by wunderkids, for wunderkids. You know that feeling when one of your friend tells you that outrageous brag, but the brag is actually true ? So you had stuff like that: All the meeting rooms had fun names that resonated with “the culture” like My interview room was “R-garita”. There was a lot of art on the campus, so much art, but also unconventional: It really felt so special. When I interviewed Facebook was between 3 and 4000 people (I was close to employee 4000) and I guess maybe 3000 people, or fewer, worked on the main campus. The idea that as a guest you were so close from people that were literally shaping the future, and that on top of Zuckerberg and Sheryl Sandberg who were mainstream famous, there were so many people who were the titans of their technical field and who were immensely respected by people who knew their name, that was very palpable. One of the rarest pictures of inside the FB campus - the door leading out of Mark Zuckerberg’s old office. Of course you wouldn’t see that when interviewing. But it’s very consistent with everything else one would see on the campus. When I interviewed at Google, this was in 2019, the company had already well over 100,000 employees, so it was a different kind of magic. I thought I was walking in a slightly cooler IBM - my dad had worked at IBM in the 70s and 80s so I had that reference point. But the San Francisco office was much nicer than I thought. Sorry that I only have that lame picture from that day: TBH google offices are slightly more boring than Facebook was especially in its heyday. That was taken when we were allowed to return on campus as the covid restrictions eased, you can still feel the Dilbert vibes. But you still are reminded, now and again, that this is f***ing google. Like, the delorean meeting room: The vibe feels a little bit more artificial and manufactured than early Facebook, but it’s still super nice: The feeling that I was walking into the future was a little bit more diffuse when I was interviewing at Google in 2019 compared to Facebook in 2013 but I could still very much feel how special that day was and all that this opportunity meant.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: At Google, what is the difference between an Engineering Manager and a Staff Engineer who has reports?
Answer: I have two contrasting answers to this, because it’s a question that i found asking myself a lot. I didn’t have reports while at Google. One of my coworkers who was at the same level but who did, and whose title was engineering manager, believed that the expectations of the staff engineer and engineering manager were exactly the same. We help ICs grow and be successful by coaching them and offering technical support, while also steering our organization in the right technical direction, writing okrs, design docs etc. This doesn’t resonate with my own experience - I was aware that not being a people’s manager meant there wasn’t an HR component to my work, I had a different role through perf, I didn’t have to have hard conversations or put people on PIP, etc. But I found this point of view interesting. The other perspective I can offer is from engineering managers who switched back to an IC role, which happened somewhat frequently in my organization during my tenure. My coworkers who were managers (in title) could see their team size fluctuate a lot, and go from 4 to 30 over a quarter and then back to 4 or 3 or 10. In my experience, one way Google is different from other most tech companies is through the belief that when you’re an engineer, you’re an engineer and you can do anything that an engineer does - you can learn any language and you don’t have to be pigeonholed in one speciality. By the same token, at least in my organization, when you’re a manager, you’re a manager and you can manage any team and any group. So because managers could get many reports suddenly, whereas TLMs’s teams stayed small and our staff engineers didn’t have formal reports, it was more difficult for EMs to have meaningful technical contributions as individuals. Sure they would still liaise with other teams, sure they would attend a lot of the same meetings as us but they had much more time taken by supporting their ICs than we did.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the differences between working as a senior and staff member at Google?
Answer: I am not sure how this works for non-engineering roles, but for software engineers, the main difference is that the staff+ person no longer gets assignments. Instead, they have to figure out what to work on. The lemma is that the senior engineer is expected to be a prolific coder. The staff engineer doesn’t have to (although code output is still a signal through which they are judged, and some staff engineers write even more code than seniors) however the staff engineer is going to figure out what needs to be done and prepare that work such that more junior engineers can run with it. They come to that realization by talking to peers in different teams or different organizations and find out where are the stumbling blocks, pain points and opportunities - and reading their weight in design docs every week. Staff engineers typically do more writing, research and experimentation.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How would a software engineering manager handle new hires who criticize bad designs after joining the team?
Answer: You know about these “design Instagram”, “design Uber” or “design Google drive” interview questions? As an alumni from Facebook, Uber and Google I have seen first-hand how these decisions being made and read the actual technical docs. Needless to say, the actual implementations are always very different from what could be assumed from the outside, and for 3 reasons, from least to most common: So, I get how somebody could join a new company and look at the codebase with their nose in the air. At the same time, an external point of view can be very precious and unlock great progress. To their managers, my advice is to tell them - 1) Hold judgement, but write down everything. You see something you think is wrong? write it down. This is valuable. Your point of view is useful and one that your peers don’t have. Just don’t necessarily act on it. 2) bring your experience, not your solutions. Putting myself in the shoes of my coworkers, it must be annoying to hear me go “at Google, we…” all the time (even though i’m pretty self-aware about that). There are lots of things that work in company X because of its specific context, practices, business etc. and won’t necessarily work at company Y. Then again, there are also times when it’s useful to coworkers to bring an external perspective.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you give some examples of how to answer questions about conflict resolution during interviews?
Answer: Sure, let’s assume the question is “give me an example of a conflict you had at work and how you solved it” (as any question about this is going to be a variation of that one). there’s 2 things to keep in mind, the scope of the example and what happened. If you’re interviewing for a VP position and your example is something trivial like where should we go for lunch, because we went to that taco place yesterday already, you see how this doesn’t project a great image. The conflict should be on something substantial and corresponding to the level of the candidate. For instance our VP may disagree with a peer on the priority of the objectives to execute this year. The harder the problem, the more impact a “right” or “wrong” decision could have, the better. Then there’s what you’ve done. Ideally when you have a situation where person A thinks we should do x and person B thinks we should do y, what should happen is either: we do z, which is better than x and y, and is informed by both strategies - so how do we reach a better solution as a group than one we would have recommended as individuals, or we can establish that x is better than y (or y is better than x), such that A and B can be confident this is the right way to go. so how can we go from an opinion to evidence-based decision. But let’s suppose you’re person A in this scenario. There are two outcomes which are not good and you don’t want to be flexing on: Typically, what goes into getting the good outcome is doing more work, including research or experimenting, getting third party involved, engaging with people who don’t agree, etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: When was the last time you used JQuery for a project and why did you choose it over other options such as AngularJS or ReactJS?
Answer: The last time I used jQuery in a project (such that actions by users would exercise some jQuery code) was in 2014.
