Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason for Google and other tech companies to ask data structure questions in interviews?
Answer: The general idea is that companies want to assess how good a candidate is at coding. Let’s say candidate A and candidate B have the same resume, but somehow you could have evidence that A is a much better programmer than B. That would inform your decision to hire A and pass on B. Ok, but how can you evaluate the coding ability of a candidate? We need a tool which is: There are several approaches to that, the data structure and algorithm is one, take home exercises another, “realistic” problems similar to what people actually do on the job is a third, and there are variations of these. IMO, and I’m not going to commit Google there, but the DS&A approach is the best for these 3 criteria. You’re a software engineer (/ data scientist, other coding type etc. ) candidate, you can learn and prepare, you can do well. It is very fair, and relatively low friction for both candidate and interviewer. Yes a candidate will need to prepare for the DS&A coding interview but it’s not completely different from spending time learning to code. The scope of the algorithms and data structure a candidate is expected to know is well-known and delimited. By contrast, the take home exercise is, again IMO, very unfair - you simply don’t know what resources a candidate will have access to to complete the exercise, it’s also biased against candidates who are caretakers (parents etc. ) and very high friction for the candidate. The “realistic” coding exercise is similar to the DS&A in all aspects except fairness - it is also deeply unfair, because “real-life” scenarios mean - similar to the context and the technical stack this company is using. It would be easier for candidates who are familiar with that context and harder for those who are not, even though they could be just as successful if hired. Here the scope of what a candidate should know is neither well-known not delimited. So I personally feel that DS&A is the superior coding exercise. I expect it’s a matter of time a conversation with an AI can offer both a better signal and a better experience than the current coding exercises but in the meantime that’s what we have. Now as to why Google uses the DS&A coding interview, it’s simple - they use it for tens of thousands of interviews per year, it gives them the signal they need, they don’t need to get a perfect crystal ball.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you think Angular will be replaced by React in the future? What is your opinion on this potential change?
Answer: I don’t think so, I actually anticipate Angular to claw back some of the mind share it’s lost to React. Angular is releasing a major new version every 6 months. 17 was last november, following 16 one year ago. 18 is around the corner. That was the case during the golden years of React when it was tightly controlled by Facebook - 0.10, 0.11, 0.12, 0.13, 0.14 and 15.0 were roughly 6 months apart between March 2014 and April 2016. Since then - 17 was released in October 2020, 18 in March 2022, so over 2 years ago. Most of the key React team has left Meta and it can really no longer been said that “what’s good for React is good for Meta and conversely”. So the governance of the project is less straightforward. The landscape is also more diverse than what it used to be, with Vue and Svelte still #3 and #4 but with more recent frameworks like Preact, Solid or Alpine getting some traction and some older frameworks like Ember still holding on.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: I got fired for poor performance. What should I say in my next job interviews?
Answer: There are two ideas which are somewhat contradictory in recruiting. On one hand, the tenet behind behavioral interviewing is that past behavior is a good predictor of future behavior. This translates into the widespread belief that past performance is a good predictor of future performance. Companies try to get employees to refer high-performers with the assumption that they will perform well if hired. But also, there is consensus that performance over one period, for one role, in one company, doesn’t define an individual. In behavioral interviews there are frequent questions about failure, with the assumptions that these stumbling blocks are a good thing and a necessary step in a growth journey. Anyone that has never experienced setbacks when asked about professional difficulties is not going to deliver a great answer. Where does that leave you - Just don’t be forward with it. Don’t mention it unless you can use it in a good answer, and even then, feel free to talk about how your performance declined and why and what have you learned from that time, but don’t say you were fired. I would go even as far as don’t admit to it if directly asked “why did you leave company X” - this is a dreaded question by people who were terminated but it doesn’t often happen. “Our goals and priorities no longer aligned and I needed a new challenge”. - technically true. But the best scenario is that nobody talks about it. You’re a candidate, there’s a job opening, you’re interviewing, and great news: you can start right away.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you describe the interview process for a senior software engineer at Google? What advice would you give to increase the chances of being hired?
Answer: you will talk to a sourcer, then to a recruiter. The recruiter will work with you to “build a loop” for the interview. The recruiter is obviously your very best source of information for the process, though they don’t know the technical aspects of the interview ie what really happens in an interview room / on a call. The typical loop for a senior engineer is a behavioral interview (“googleyness and leadership”), a design interview and 3 coding interviews. All are very classic in nature, in the sense that big tech interviews are really variation on the Google interviews, but all have google specificities. The criteria evaluated for Googleyness and Leadership are obviously unique to Google, though they are not really different across tech companies IMO. For a senior engineer candidate, the key is to convey that you have worked as a senior software engineer, even if that wasn’t your title - but that you have skills comparable to those of a senior software engineer. ie you’ve done difficult projects, you’ve navigated tricky human interactions, etc. This is not a “cultural fit” interview, there is no right and wrong answer, you are not here to “wow” your interviewer or to make them like you - but you should show that you have the technical depth and the maturity expected at that level. The 2 unique things about the Google design interview is that every interviewer has to come up with their exercise, and also, that there are typically geared towards a speciality. So you won’t have a textbook question like: build instagram. Instead, you’ll have a specific question, both more concrete and more geared towards the expertise you’re supposed to bring. For instance when I interviewed test engineer candidates, the scenario i offered was, your team operates a single-player scrabble game, and you’re developing a multi-player version, how would you go about testing it? Lastly, the unique part about the coding interview is that Google uses its own interview platform where the code doesn’t run. You won’t be able to run your code during the interview to check if it works or use partial results. but you can be handwavy and not implement helper functions, and you can have syntax errors - not that you should, but it’s not the end of the world if there’s a typo. How to maximize your chances, well really, there’s no secret - you should prepare, there’s really ample resources to do so. If not prepared, your chances are low. If not enough prepared, you can probably push the interview date, although at some point you need to face the music. If well prepared, the last thing you need is sleep well and be well-situated to interview - good connection, no interruption if doing this remotely for instance.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you respond if an interviewer asks, “Are there any questions we didn’t answer for you?
Answer: well, are there? Let’s suppose you get an offer. If you sign the offer, you’re going to spend 2000+ hours per year focused on that job. The most of every day. You’re also going to be thinking about work outside of your working hours. Do you have enough information to tell whether this is a good or a bad idea?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should one behave in a job interview if they know they will not be hired?
Answer: There are really many different contexts in which that could happen. If as a candidate you have reached the conclusion that whatever happens, you do not want to work at that company, now or ever, you can simply leave. About 10 years ago when interviewing for tech roles for tech companies, they would typically fly you to the silicon valley and put you up in hotels while you interview. So leaving the interview room was a bit dramatic, and made for an awkward conversation around expenses. Now a more typical experience is interviewing over a video call, so it’s as simple as hanging up. I’ve done this once in 2014. This was the most miserable interview experience I ever had. I felt that if I stayed a minute longer in that circus, I would be a clown too. Fortunately no plane tickets or hotel nights were involved. However if as a candidate you feel that you’ve bombed badly, but you’re still interested in the role, just take a deep breath after your last interview and go back at it. You don’t know how poorly you’ve done according to the criteria they’re interested in. And this is still a learning experience.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How hard is it for a new Quora user to get 1,000 upvotes on an answer in 2024?
Answer: It’s pretty difficult. Looking at my content stats over my last 500 questions - My average upvote to views ratio is around 0.007. In other words i need about 130 views to get 1 upvote. Over my last 500, the maximum value for that ratio was around 5% (ie 20 views per upvote) but I think 1/130 is not bad, I write on the things I have expertise on so I am pretty confident my answers are valued. So this is mostly about getting enough views - to get 1000 upvotes, i should get 130k views. Over my last 500 answers I have had 10 which got over 130k views - this happens. But! the upvote to views ratio tapers. None of the answers I wrote in 2024 had over 1000 upvotes, even though 2 had over 130k views. Looking all my answers over times, I had approx 20 which had more than 1000 upvotes. I have been using Quora for a long time, writing regularly for the past ~9 years. Again the best way to get upvotes is to get views, but the ratio is not consistent. For instance, in 2023 I wrote an answer which got 6.5M views and got 1856 upvotes, that’s 0.02% - much lower than my regular 0.7% - but that’s still a great answer which is still picking up views and comments. My 2nd most seen answer of 2023 had 1.5M views but only 153 upvotes - 0.01%! that answer was pretty controversial (but no less true), so I guess it got downvoted too. As authors, we only see the “net” upvotes, not the total upvotes and downvotes. Conversely I had an answer in 2019 which got 5000+ upvotes for about 100000ish views. So, let’s talk about getting views, and how being a new Quora user impacts this. And the answer is quite a lot. Answers get views because they are picked up by spaces or because they are interacted with by people that have an audience. This is what gets the answers on people’s feeds. It’s difficult for an answer, even very good, to get traction by its own merits. It’s possible, but the lack of an audience definitely slows down that process, and 1000 upvotes is a high bar. You may wonder why answers with many views get proportionally fewer upvotes: shouldn’t great answers pick up both views and upvotes? maybe so, but answers that have traction will appear in a lot of people’s feeds, this will mechanically increase the number of views, however people who get an answer in their feed will not necessarily read it thoroughly and are less likely to upvote it. Conversely, answers which are found through direct search or which are very close to the person’s interests are more likely to be read with more interest and generate an upvote. In other words, the initial views are more likely to yield upvotes. When you get the notification - “10,000,000+ people have been sent your answer in the Quora Digest”, this will generate a lot of views but not a lot of upvotes. I just checked out an answer I wrote that triggered that notification, as of today it got 1.3M views, 3856 upvotes, so about 0.2%. this answer was great at the time I wrote it, it’s one of those I was very well positioned to give a high-quality answer. It’s no longer really relevant now.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it acceptable for developers to skip testing when writing code?
Answer: When my sister was a young adult she dated that guy who felt that speed limits shouldn’t apply to him because his car was high-end (and for the record - it wasn’t). By saying this, he implies that he doesn’t think that speed limits are useful (either to him or to the community). And people who share that opinion are exactly the reason why we have speed limits. Likewise, somebody who feels they should be able to commit code without the agreed-upon level of testing think that tests are not useful to them or to the codebase. These developers are exactly the reason why there are coverage requirements. There can be exceptions, just like there can be some valid reasons to drive over the speed limit. But these are few and far between. Doing this as a rule (just like driving 20 mph over the speed limit as a habit) is dangerous for all involved and a terrible practice.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How much practice did it take for you to receive an offer from Google, Apple, or Facebook for an SDE position? Were you asked any design questions during the interview process?
Answer: For Google I had my first email from the sourcer on 7/1/2019, and my first email from the recruiter on 7/17/2019 which is the one which contained interview instructions. Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you explain the importance of QA testing and its different types?
Answer: QA and testing are not exactly the same thing, but QA (quality assurance) is born out of the belief that it is more advantageous to prevent bugs, incidents and outages than to fix them after the fact. In software, automated testing should be the main way to provide quality insurance. Given the same inputs, code should give the same, predictable outputs. So, developers can come up with scenarios, or test cases, exercise their code according to these scenarios and be able to make the same observations (or assertions) on the output each time. It follows that developers should write their code such that it can be testable, meaning that whenever possible, “the same inputs give the same predictable outputs” is true. In technical terms that means making the code pure and deterministic, and isolating the parts that can’t be, and in the name of practicality, because it’s typically easier and faster to only exercise a little chunk of the code at each time, the codebase should be separated in well-delimited components, that have a clear interface with one another. Making your code base testable is really the great benefit of automated tests, because if a codebase has these characteristics, even if out of constraint, it is also much more robust and maintainable as if these attributes were not true. Not everything can be tested automatically, at least not for every project. So sometimes manual testing is still required, in which people go through checklists and verify what happens. There’s also evaluations, as opposed to “correctness testing”, where human raters check if the output of a program is good or not even if the program doesn’t crash or show an error. Tests cannot prevent every bug and outage though, and so the next line of defense is monitoring and alerting. Even though the code is assumed to be good at some point, you still want to periodically check that certain signals emitted by your system, for instance the content of its logs or its memory usage. If these become anomalous, you would then trigger an alert such that a person would investigate if everything is actually ok. The final line of defense is an actual bug report system, when users find anomalous behavior despite everything done upstream. Somebody will triage the bugs, and teams organize support rotations so that somebody can handle the occasional problems.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is being rejected by Google an indication of a poor resume or simply due to not being needed by the company?
Answer: To paraphrase your question, being interviewed by Google is an indication of a strong resume. Beyond that, I believe you can’t get an offer without the skillset, but the opposite is not true. You can definitely have great skills and not get an offer because of tons of reasons outside of your control. Google is well aware that’s how it works, and is fine with passing on potentially great candidates. Beyond that, for the past 2 years it’s no longer on a hiring spree, as opposed to the previous 20 or so years.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some lesser-known tricks that can make a programmer appear more skilled during interviews (not related to coding)?
Answer: For a coding interview one aspect which is not related to coding that will increase success is to plan your answer. Instead of starting to type right away (as most interviews are now done with computers vs a white board, where what i’m describing is more natural), a candidate could doodle how a solution may work, then implement it. Doing this actually does help solving the problem - it’s not just for show. But simply going through that ritual also projects a better image. Conversely, when the candidate starts coding heads on, that they didn’t ask clarifying questions or that they didn’t explain their thought process is usually part of the feedback.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the toughest technical interview process among Google, Microsoft and Facebook? Why? What's your experience like if you've been through it before?
Answer: In big tech all interviewing pipelines are comparatively selective and all the interviews are comparatively difficult. The difficulty of an interview exercise, by the way, is irrelevant - whether you ask a hard question to 100 people and want to keep the 10 best, or you ask an easy question and still want to keep the 10 best, being able to complete the exercise or do well doesn’t matter, it’s whether a candidate can demonstrate they have the skillset and that they are objectively better than the bar at which the company is comfortable hiring - bar which is comparable across big tech company. Where you’re going to have more differences is in the ratio between applications and offers, not necessarily between these 3 which are comparable, but between large public tech company who receive millions of applications a year and have to select very few people to interview, using criteria which are not necessarily objective by the way, and smaller tech companies.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason behind Google's lengthy and challenging technical interviews and comparatively lower salaries compared to other tech companies such as Facebook or Microsoft?
Answer: I’ve never worked at or interviewed for Microsoft but I did work at Facebook and I think the interview experience and compensation are comparable. The actual make of the interview, ie exercises, logistics etc. fluctuates, and the compensation is very influenced by the stock. If you look at recent years, in 1/1/2020–1./1/2022 Google stock has grown much faster than Facebook or Microsoft, in 1/1/2023–1/1/2024 Meta stock has almost tripled and grown much faster than the other 2, but overall 1/1/2020–1/1/2024 Microsoft has increased the most.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is code quality important to Google interviewers?
Answer: At Google the coding interview is administered by an engineer, who needs to interact with the candidate during the entire time of the interview, making sure the candidate is always unstuck and can show their best work. Then the interviewing engineer has to write detailed feedback and grade the candidate according to 8 criteria, substantiating their grade with evidence from the interview. Then, a hiring committee is going to interpret that feedback to make a hiring recommendation. With that in mind, would that be fair to candidates to not take code quality into account? Between 2 candidates that solve the same problem and finish at the same time and are equivalent on all the other criteria, should one that writes clean and maintainable code have the same evaluation as one that doesn’t?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What did you learn when you worked at Google?
Answer: Google has much more processes than where I was before (Uber) and in general is very opinionated on many technical aspects. On one hand, some of the most important computer science advances this century happened at Google, and it also operates several 1 billion+ users products. It’s also been around for decades and has around 100,000 engineers, so the cumulative technical wisdom at Google is mind-boggling. On the other, a lot (most?) of these technical decisions are the results of survivor bias. The Google way of doing X is not necessary superior, but is how Google chooses to do a specific task, which has worked not too bad historically, and it’s arguably not a completely terrible way to think about that task. But again it’s not necessarily the right way, and it doesn’t necessarily work well outside of Google. Google, like many big tech companies, boasts of taking data-driven decisions. That is a mischaracterization. When I was at Facebook, there were posters from engineering teams that claimed: “code wins arguments”. Then data scientists one-upped them and put posters that said “data wins arguments”. But we all knew that it was Zuckerberg who won arguments, so - product, business intuition. The same goes at Google. The processes are not rational. They are presented as rational and logic but they were decided at some point by a person, who was able to make a case for that and get an organization to follow (which is no small feat). Likewise, the business strategy of Google is not rational or logic or data-driven. The OKR process (which is a good combination of what is a “process” and what is “strategy”) is a fine example of that. You’re going to have very smart people who think very hard as to what problems need solving and how to prioritize that and how to connect the work of their team with the goals of a larger organization and eventually that of the company. And yet the OKRs for my organization were just not useful. At the end of the day so much energy and resources were put into something that had arguably a net-negative value. So, with the caveat that the Google way is not the only way or the always right way, it’s been super interesting to learn the Google approach to: write code, think about infrastructure, quality, testing, interfacing with different organizations, etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What criteria do you use to evaluate an entry-level software engineer during an interview, especially if they have limited experience?
Answer: There are typically 3 exercises in the software engineering interview, coding, system design and behavioral interview. System design for an entry-level engineer is a complete waste of time. Most companies don’t do it, those who do are not going to be able to differentiate great, good and bad candidates from it. The behavioral interview doesn’t yield a lot of signal for entry level candidates. For a more experienced candidate the behavioral interview is a levelling opportunity (i.e. can this person demonstrate they acted as a senior software engineer?) For an entry level engineer, this is unfortunately more subjective, because a lot of the questions are geared around their experience, but it can still produce interesting signals: it can expose red flags - some super problematic attitudes or beliefs that this candidate’s first employer may not want to spend time correcting, and it’s also an occasion for candidates to give reasons to their interviewers to go to bat for them. So, really, for entry level candidates, the most important part is the coding exercises, there are probably going to be several and they should just do their best on those.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why would you attempt to answer a question on Quora using the comments section of another answer to do so?
Answer: Answers get views largely based on who writes that answer - not on their own merit. If a person who doesn’t have an audience on Quora wants reach for what they write, it’s much easier to get it through comments on a popular answer than through writing an answer that will not be picked by feeds.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you provide some real examples of dumb interview questions asked by recruiters or HR personnel from top companies like Google and Facebook?
Answer: I can’t, because even though I was interviewed and hired by Google and Facebook, I can’t in good faith characterize any question I heard from their recruiters or their HR as dumb. In my experience, in the tech industry, HR and recruiters are pretty hands off. Their job is to get candidates in the pipeline and make sure they have a good experience. The questions are going to be mostly asked by technical interviewers.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it worth pursuing a career as a video game designer/developer, despite the uncertainty of financial success and public recognition?
Answer: If your goal is public recognition this is extremely unlikely. Some back of the napkin math says there’s about 1 million people working in the videogame industry. As of today I don’t think most people can name one single person working in games. (by opposition to say the movie industry, which employs more people, generates less revenue but of which can be said that most people can name several people on top of their head). But just like with any industry, contributors can be recognized within their company and within the trade and sometimes in the outside world. No one is going to stop you from writing articles / being interviewed or speaking at conferences for instance. Some games made by solo developers get significant critical recognition - then again it’s more the exception than the rule. I have worked in the videogame industry for a few years. I had absolutely no delusion that I would become rich or famous. My motivation was anchored on two aspects. 1) this was really doing what I wanted. For some time, my job responsibilities included opining on whether my company should acquire publishing or distribution rights for certain games. Of course these deals were mostly about the business and the technology, but now and again I was asked to play unreleased games to give recommendations as a gamer as to whether we should go ahead, and I would play them with “development kits”, which are souped-up versions of the consoles available to the general public, that I had on my desk in my work office. That was my job that I was paid for! 2) there are very advanced technical problems in gaming. Back in my days even the most mundane of game project was going to do something that had never been achieved before. This is probably not true anymore of all projects but many games are really on the cutting edge of technology especially in terms of graphics, animation and AI. If it weren’t for gaming, PCs wouldn’t all have GPUs from the late 90s, and without GPUs + without all the technological advances that happened because there were applications in gaming. There are very bright, creative problem solvers in the gaming industry, and great solutions to known problems raise the bar to how this would be addressed in other games. That also applies to game or level design, art direction, writing, music etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How would you react as an interviewer if a candidate asks dozens of questions at the end of the interview?
Answer: Unless these questions are very short they probably won’t get answers to all of them. But in general, more power to them. That’s a great time to get honest information that may affect taking a life-changing decision.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it common for developers to fail interviews and get rejected? What can they do to improve their performance during interviews?
Answer: Candidates don’t really get “rejected”, they don’t get an offer. A candidate who is invited to interview is already selected and already looks good enough on paper. The mental model where developers base their worth on their track record on interviews is simply wrong, as the outcome of an interview depends on many factors, most of which beyond the candidate’s influence. That said, it is obviously not only possible, but definitely recommended to come prepared to a software engineer interview. There are many resources available, though companies tend to come up with unique ways to evaluate interviews and even a unique way to run interviews. In my last “campaign” of application, no company I interviewed with did the “classic” coding + design interview + behavioral interview loop, they all threw in a unique exercise to the mix. But because these interviews are not all alike, and also because of external factors mentioned above, for instance - a reorganization, projects being cancelled, internal transfers etc. even people who are very qualified and very well prepared do not get offers all the time.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What might motivate someone to leave a large company like Google or Facebook to work for a smaller company like Microsoft or Twitter?
Answer: to give you a certain order of magnitude of what’s a large or a small company, Microsoft has roughly 220,000 employees Google has roughly 180,000 Meta has around 60,000 X corp has less than 2,000. As someone who’s worked at both Google and (then) Facebook I feel that these companies have a pretty similar culture. Google and Facebook/Meta are unique and have their particularities, but for somebody who would leave Google to go anywhere else, Meta is where they would see the least jarring differences. Microsoft is also pretty similar afaik, and so was Twitter 10 years ago, even though it was much smaller. Microsoft, Google and Facebook had a few thousand employees for quite some time before getting very large, and they were still distinctively large tech companies. A lot of folks went from Google or Facebook to Twitter in the mid 2010s, because Twitter was headquartered in San Francisco and San Franciso based tech employees resent having to commute one hour and a half both ways everyday. A lot of people working at Google and Meta are liberals and the workplace is run with a liberal mindset, for instance there are efforts put behind DEI programs and these companies try to prevent harassment, discrimination etc. However, politically the CEOs stay hands off. Zuckerberg had to do a lot of efforts to court conservatives and convince them that his platform wasn’t discriminating against them. All tech companies give money to conservative PACs that otherwise advance their interests in DC. Twitter/X, though, is different, with Musk having bought it for clearly ideological reasons. So IMO for somebody to go from Google or Meta to X they would have at least to be comfortable with this very different culture.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Where do pro-choicers come from? I'm pro-life personally and don't understand the other side's views. Could someone explain them to me?
Answer: Sure. “I’m pro-life personally”. Let’s start by this. You identify as “pro-life”, you see people labelled as “pro-choice” as disagreeing with you. So you may assume: we are pro-life, we respect and value the sanctity of life, the others are therefore anti-life and do not care or value human life. That’s a fallacy. Everybody cares about and values life (except for the occasional homicidal maniac). So if you’re wondering, how could all these people not respect life, that’s the first part of your answer. They do, no less than you do. So, pro-choice. What does this mean? They believe that a woman should have the right to abort her pregnancy. There are a lot of nuances here, most people who identify as pro-choice don’t believe that the right to an abortion should be absolute and unlimited. But they all believe that there are some cases when this should be a possibility offered to a woman, and that is very different from thinking that no woman should ever be allowed to abort her pregnancy and that every pregnant woman should carry her pregnancy to its natural outcome. OK, so you have on one hand people who think abortions should never be possible, and people who challenge that, and both claim to have morals that back their position. The people who believe that women can have the choice to abort a pregnancy in certain cases base that belief on the notion that like any other person, they have a right to their bodily autonomy. Specifically, nobody should be able to make decisions on their body on their behalf. There’s a long tradition of texts both specific to US law and international texts that affirm that notion. So, whether at the end of the day you think that there should never be abortions or that abortio...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the characteristics and elements of a well-written test case in software testing?
Answer: It really boils down to two, but these have far reaching consequences. 1) If this test case passes, I am confident that the code it covers works as intended. 2) for any of the assertions in this test case, should they fail, I know where to look fix the problem. 1) means that there’s no softball assertions, the goal of a test is not to pass, the goal is to exercise all the different ways a piece of code can be used and verify they all work as expected. A lemme of 2) is that if when a test fail, we do not take action (or we simply disable the test) then that test is not useful, actually it is a net negative because it had a cost to write and to run, but we’re not able to benefit from it.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do liberals think a baby deserves to be killed just because its mother is 10 years old?
Answer: In 2022, a 10-years old girl who was a victim of child rape had to leave her state of Ohio to receive an abortion. This story received a lot of coverage as it happened in the weeks following the overturning of Roe v. Wade, with some people feeling justified that either: So two irreconcilable opinions. Where are the facts though? 1) Abortions among 10-years-olds are extremely rare. Yes, despite articles like “Ohio 10-year-old's abortion isn't a rare exception[1]”. These abortions are so rare there is no official statistics about them. The latest numbers say that abortions when the mother is younger than 15 represent 0.2% of the total of abortions.[2] This doesn’t mean they never happen. But it’s not like 10 years old were lining at abortion clinics under Roe, and that now, they can start happy families. Further numbers: the birth rate to girls 14 and younger in the US was 0.2 per 1000 girls in 2021. And that’s for the whole age group. Fewer than 10% of all girls start menstruating before 11, so pregnancies at 10 are even more rare than that, and abortions are obviously rarer than pregnancies. 2) abortions is not killing babies. embryos, fetuses, babies, three different things, only one of which is born, and that’s the one which is not concerned with abortions. 80.8%[3] of all abortions happen before an embryo reaches fetal development, and 93.5% performed before 13 weeks. I’m not insisting on this because pro-life folks are pushing for different definitions of what’s a human being than the ones we’ve used in the anglo-saxon legal systems for centuries. 3) nobody can force a woman whatever her age to have an abortion. There are states where parents need to be notified or to give consent for an abortion of a minor to proceed, but the explicit consent of the mother - even if she’s a minor, especially if she’s a minor - is always necessary. So, no one is advocating to force 10 years old to have abortions and no one is advocating for killing babies, liberal or not.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What factors contribute to good Unit Test coverage? Are there any industry standards or recommended criteria for measuring it?
Answer: Automated unit test coverage measurement is a proxy answer to the question: Can I be confident that my codebase is working as intended ? The way this works under the hood is that a test runner can instrument how many times a function or a method is called, and which part of a code branch (ie if statements) is being exercised. As a result it is able to count of all the possible branches, which are being covered by tests. From there, it is also possible to derive the number of lines covered. Whether 80% is good or bad depending on the method used is arbitrary. However if you have 100% line coverage you will have 100% branch coverage too and you can claim all of your code is exercised. You could have 100% file coverage without having either of the above but file coverage is not a very high bar. If your code coverage is low, and low is still going to be arbitrary but let’s say lower than 50%, then the answer to the underlying question (again - “can I be confident that my codebase is working as intended”) is no. It doesn’t mean the code base doesn’t work, it doesn’t mean that the existing tests are useless, but it means that there can be problems that will go undetected by tests such that an outage is the only way they will surface.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the recommended amount of software/code to be tested for every 1000 lines of code written? What are the industry best practices for testing software/code?
Answer: The best practices assume that: 1) automated testing is important for quality assurance, and that 2) problems should be caught as early as possible. It follows that unit testing is desirable. In order for unit testing to make sense, all the code should be covered by unit tests. In practice this is not always the case, but paradoxically there is also an assumption that the code base is well-tested through automated testing and that there is a total / quasi-total coverage of the code base through unit testing.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some ways to incorporate unit test coverage into code without significantly slowing down development time, such as using Test-driven Development (TDD)?
Answer: The key idea is: If testability is a concern from day one, the system is going to be split into well-delimited components and testing incremental code changes is either going to be naturally easy, or there will be a concerted effort to build some tooling to make testing easy. When writing tests for each code change is effortless/frictionless, and when there is a continuous care / constraint around testing level, test coverage follows. However, if a system is not designed to be testable, or let’s just say it, if it’s not designed, just built as developers go with a vague sense of what it must eventually achieve, then testing is going to be difficult, and adding to this a mandate to keep test coverage high is going to require heavy additional efforts by developers which will shoot down their productivity. The tests that they will write to get the chore off the to-do list are not necessarily going to be useful.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some common mistakes that developers make when unit testing without realizing it?
Answer: I can think of a few. Testing for coverage versus testing for correctness. This is extremely common. I also do that sometimes. Let’s suppose you have a function or method. You write a test that basically exercises the code and write very low-bar assertions - you’re essentially verifying this code runs without crashing whatever it does. This is only marginally useful and this is not what a unit test is supposed to verify. A special case of this is tests that will always be true. Several unit tests test the exact same thing. If there is no actual distinction between 2 test cases then there is one too many. If 2 tests go through the exact same branches and exercise the exact same logic then you are running 2 when you can be running one. As a thought exercise, imagine a unit test that is flaky once every million runs. It runs as part of a suite of 5000. So the suite has 99.5% chances of passing (that’s already an impact). If the suite must run 100 times a day, there’s now 60% chances it will fail at least once. Now if each of these tests were doubled, the chances that you have a day without the test suite failing for no good reason is 36%. So more tests (and especially more not useful tests) is NOT a good thing. Tests that pass because they are actually testing an edge case. One example I use a lot is if we were to write a simple calculator that adds and multiply. Except, the multiply method actually adds. If I assert that “add(2, 2)” must be 4 and that “multiply(2, 2)” must be 4, I am not protecting myself against the eventuality that actually “multiply(2, 2)” is going to add under the hood, but if I tried “multiply(3, 7)” or really anything else I would see the difference. Tests that would be disabled if they fail. This is the opposite to tests which are always true (which are useless). If a test is not going to be acted upon if it fails, it is useless too, and disabling the test is not acting on it, it’s avoiding to deal with it.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How is AI killing software engineers? What can we do to stop it?
Answer: In October of 2021, Github launched Copilot. Dozens of articles were written on how this was going to replace software engineers. I’m sure Microsoft had a version of this technology going on for a while, at Google we had our own copilot-like technology. And yet Microsoft, like Google, never hired more engineers than in 2021–2022. In November of 2022, OpenAI launched ChatGPT. We got to read the same articles all over again, except ChatGPT replaced Copilot. I really get the allure of the narrative. Those who follow me on this platform know that before working at Google, I was at Facebook then Uber, so over the last 10+ years I read my share of articles explaining why Facebook will fail, why Uber will fail, etc. So if you write an article that argues how people who make 6 figures, and that were hoping to make millions like those who came before them, will now find themselves out of a job, you will get readers. These articles will continue to appear. Something that gives a little bit more credence to this new wave of articles is that in 2022 there was the great winter of crypto, followed in late 2022/early 2023 by multiple waves of layoffs. Microsoft, Google (as well as many others) laid off tens of thousands of people, including software engineers, at a time when they signaled how important AI was to their strategy. So what happened to these engineers that were laid off? were they simply replaced by AI? did they have to take jobs outside of tech? Following the tech layoffs, Mary Jantsch made a LinkedIn Post[1] that got a lot of traction where she wrote: “Say hello to Boise’s newest gardener.” and she explained how and why she transitioned out of tech. She wasn’t a software engineer though. In my network I do know certain people who took that opportunity to retire, but this was not a forced decision. Just the little nudge they needed to enjoy their money and time with their family. So while all of this was going on, there are 3 kind of companies who have been on the hunt for developers: In my current company we still have open headcount and we can’t hire good people fast enough. Software engineers are not dead, they are just changing jobs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to perform unit testing on legacy code without making any changes to the code itself? If so, what are the reasons for this?
Answer: it is possible, it’s not necessarily easy because code written without test is usually not written with testability in mind, but if code can be executed in production, then somehow it can be exercised by a test runner. It is also not generally useful. To answer the 2nd part of the question, the general idea is that if you add more unit tests you increase unit test coverage, therefore you make the code base safer and you prevent outages, which is “good”. having unit tests in place also prevents developers from “breaking” other people’s code, another “good” thing. I’m putting quotes because all of this is based on a fallacy. More tests doesn’t mean more safety, especially if these tests are written after the fact. What you are guaranteeing is not that the code base is working as intended, but that the code base is working as it did at time t0, whether that’s right or not (the latter being more likely, if left untested). the benefit of writing tests as you build the code base is not so much to have tests or to prevent outages - that’s a side bonus, but to make the code testable. Keeping the code testable adds constraints but it adds considerable safety and comfort even without tests as that means that there will be separation of concern, clean interface, pure/deterministic code, etc. That effect cannot be obtained by writing code after the fact.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some reasons why a developer may choose not to do unit testing before deploying their code?
Answer: I have answered many variants of this question already. There are 2 assumptions around writing code professionally which constitute some kind of “default setting”. When that’s the case, adding tests is really a negligible amount of extra effort and does add value. It’s so much more comfortable to work in this kind of situation. In my experience, this is not often the case, and a more common situation is that: existing code bases are poorly tested, and unit tests can be difficult to write. In that case, the extra effort to write unit tests is significant. So let’s suppose that you’re an engineering leader and you are squarely in this scenario. You have several courses of action. If you require all code changes to include unit tests, you’re putting the burden of fixing this on individual developers at the time they write their feature code. They are going to treat testing as a check box that must be ticked and write the least useful tests that let them move on. Their productivity will be shot down and the code base will not be significantly safer. Or, you can look at this problem more holistically - has the lack of testing led to poor interfaces between your components? if so, a refactor may be justified, such that the team walks on a stronger foundations, and this will also make testing easier going forward. Is the code difficult to exercise in tests, such that all unit tests include a lot of “boiler plate” code where the developer reinvents the wheel? if so, you need to come up with a testing fixture or a testing framework such that the testing becomes as easy as it should be. Lack of tests is not about an individual developer’s choices, it’s a failure at the organization level. If the org has made the right choices all along, then it’s not going up to the developer to decide that they won’t have unit tests anyway.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: A newly hired senior software developer doesn't write unit tests and he said he has tested the code manually, so he would not waste time to write redundant tests. As the team lead, what should I do?
Answer: This is not something to be solved in a 1:1 setting imo. We’re not talking about a matter of personal preference, but what I refer to as “the contract” which binds all developers in an organization together. These are rules that should be decided at the highest level possible - organization/company, failing that division or team. There are certain choices in development which are a matter of personal preference, like what IDE to use (though - not always). But there are choices which are made as a group so all developers in that group are more effective. When joining a new organization I found that a lot of these rules are implicit - for instance typically people “get” that code must be reviewed, and if somebody offers comment these comments must be addressed, even if another developer approves of the changes. But every now and again there is someone who doesn’t agree with the rules or who finds that the rules doesn’t let them work how they want, and they will violate part of that contract, either an implicit rule or an explicit one which has been clearly communicated to everyone. So when you have a person that thinks: rule X must be enforced, and another person that thinks: I shouldn’t have to abide by rule X, having a confrontation between these 2 people with them either agreeing to stick to rule X or not is usually not desirable. This is highly disruptive for the group. For instance if in a team everybody gets their code reviewed and acts on all comments, and one person bypasses that process to get their changes committed by hook or by crook, this makes the codebase worse and less safe - for everyone. What must be established is, is rule X good for the group? Have we decided as a group to follow rule X? if so, then all developers in the group must follow rule X, and if anyone wants to challenge it, they can write a doc arguing why it should be revisited and support it with data. This can be affirmed through group meetings, or at least through more than 1 interaction with 1 person that would disagree with the dissenter. I haven’t spoken about testing specifically so far. A technical organization that doesn’t have a healthy testing culture is going to have a hard time getting somebody to fall in line and write the expected unit tests, and I tend to think - they would have made their bed. But if people understand the value of QA and testing, and if there are explicit rules in place, then good luck to this developer in arguing that adhoc manual testing is good enough. Beyond changing their mind, which is really the long term goal, as team lead I would make sure that reviewers reject all pull requests / diffs / change lists / code changes by whatever name that do not contained the agreed-upon level of testing.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some ways to determine if a developer's code is good or bad during a job interview?
Answer: Some companies have specific criteria that can be used to evaluate the code beyond a one-dimensional scale. Not everyone agrees though as to what constitutes a good performance. 1) speed. how quickly can a candidate come to a working solution. The idea is that a working code that is written in 5 minutes may be better than production-grade code which the candidate doesn’t quite finish writing by the interview end. 2) legibility. Code which is hard to read often trips candidates that have trouble spotting bugs or off-by-one errors. But even if it’s correct, it’s better to have well-written code, good variable names, code split in sensible functions etc. Everything else being equal concision is good, as long as it’s not obfuscation. 3) modern code patterns. Using recent features of the language when appropriate is good. Conversely sticking to how code was written 10 years ago is typically a bad signal. 4) appropriate data structures. which is similar to the above. 5) no anti-patterns, which demonstrate a shaky understanding of the code. For instance, else after return. 6) performance, if it’s possible to do something in constant time versus o(n2) this is probably what the interviewer expect… in my experience this is usually less important than everything in the above. But some exercises can be squarely about performance. 7) testing. The jury is split on that one, some people consider that adding test cases to an interview is the cherry on the cake and that’s it’s useful to find bugs etc. Some consider it’s sacrificing speed, which is always an important critieria, so it’s net negative. From my POV this is generally useful and a good signal.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Under what circumstances is it acceptable to not use test-driven development (TDD) for unit testing in software projects?
Answer: In my book it’s always acceptable to not use TDD. TDD is a way to get things done. When you use TDD, one thing you can be certain of is that by the time you propose a code change, it has unit tests and these tests pass. These two properties are desirable. If this came for free or for a negligible cost, this would be an incentive to use TDD. Then again, in a world where writing tests is the easiest part of development, and where test coverage is required to commit code, It doesn’t offer a lot of value over writing feature code and then writing tests. It’s really a method, a philosophy, like: should you prep all your ingredients before cooking? you can see how it would make reasoning about your cooking effort easier, but should that be an absolute rule? The assumption that tests are very easy to write, and that test coverage is required for new code, is a common “default setting” for development - I would also consider this as “a good thing” and something an organization should strive towards. In practice though it is less often true than not. When there is a high burden in writing tests, when working from a codebase which is not well tested to begin with, then the added value of providing great testing coverage for any new code change is not apparent, so the return on effort of systematically writing unit tests is less. To be clear that is not a great situation to be in, but when in that scenario this is yet another reason to not use TDD.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do professional developers typically write unit tests?
Answer: Do all kids brush their teeth? in my experience all tech companies understand the value of testing and would agree that “more testing is good” and that “unit tests is good”. The same way that kids would agree that healthy teeth are good and having a dentist drill through your tooth is bad. How this translates in the day to day of developers is really up to the culture of the tech organization. There are places where this is very natural and is not even up for discussion. There are many others where there’s always a good excuse to not write the tests right now. A lot of technology is really holding together by string and duct tape, so there’s definitely fewer well-tested products than one could expect.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the reasons for discouraging the use of Test-driven Development (TDD) in JavaScript projects?
Answer: The general assumption behind TDD is that writing tests is easy and frictionless and that the difference in effort between: writing feature code, and writing feature code and unit tests, is negligible, such that it’s just as easy to write failing tests then making them pass by writing feature code, than writing feature code directly. I think this is generally true when you the testing frameworks get to exercise this code very directly. If I’m writing say python or C++, my testing framework would typically just need to look at the code I just wrote (or that I am going to write, to be very precise, in the case of TDD). But this is not the general case for JavaScript / front-end projects. Typical front-end code will run: 1) in a browser 2) within some kind of web framework like React. So it’s difficult to exercise that code in isolation and in ways which are meaningful. TDD is still possible for front-end work, but it is more laborious because the test setup just represents more work. So the cost/benefit is not as clear cut. For javascript work which is not on the browser, ie node.js etc, there’s really no difference with other languages and no extra arguments against TDD.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why can't Donald Trump pay off the $464 million civil fraud case judgement since he's a billionaire?
Answer: Trump can pay, but he can’t pay without selling assets, which inconveniences him. If you decided to allocate your wealth in a certain way, but then an external factor forces you to change approaches, this is frustrating. He has complained publicly that he would be forced to sell properties for a price which is less than ideal. Be that as it may, the goal of a civil lawsuit is not to cause the least amount of trouble to the person convicted of fraud especially when the fraud was so massive, so egregious and went on for so long. If he didn’t want to have to secure a $464m bond, maybe he shouldn’t have committed fraud?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the purpose of Google asking tricky questions in interviews?
Answer: Google did a complete U turn on their interview philosophy around the early/mid 2010s. My coworkers who started 10+ years ago did have some trick questions in their interviews. Eventually Google decided those didn’t give great signal and removed them, they also famously abandoned the “brain teaser” questions around 2013. Google though asks hard questions, but not trick questions (so that depends what you call tricky) so that you can differentiate the performance of candidates, especially for senior roles. If a coding question is easy for instance, then any developer worth their salt is going to be easily come up with a decent answer and you wouldn’t be able to tell the difference between an ok candidate and an amazing candidate. It’s only when coding questions become harder, when design questions become deeper, when behavioral questions become slightly less of a softball, than the performance of great candidates can be distinguished from those of good but not great ones.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can one cope with rejection from a job interview at top companies like Google, Facebook, or Apple? Is there still potential for success after being rejected?
Answer: I have 5 pieces of advice for that person. Don’t take it personally. I learned from working in big tech that one performance evaluation doesn’t define you. (and interviews are a form of performance evaluation). Yes it is natural to take this personally because it can have such a profound impact. But this is not an accurate and exhaustive measure of you. It is highly situational. Somebody who doesn’t perform well isn’t bad, especially if on paper they could have been expected to perform better. Don’t compare you to people who boast they can ace all FAANG interviews. There are people who base their entire identity on succeeding at tech interviews. First of all, let me tell you that no one is able to predictably ace any tech interview. The best you can hope is to show up prepared and do a good showing. Even if you do amazing at the interview you have 0 control on what happens afterwards, the team you interview for may lose the budget for a new role for instance. As someone who is highly confident in their skillset and knows the interview process very well, I have had offers less than 50% of my interviews. People who got a Facebook or a Google offer have passed the interview once in one specific configuration and have benefitted from a certain alignment of the planets whether they acknowledge it or not. Take pride in having been invited to interview. Arguably the hardest part in getting to big tech is getting to sit at the interview table. This opportunity is only extended to people who have a fair shot at getting a job offer and this is a huge accomplishment in itself. Embrace the new normal. I remember the first time I was rejected from a tech job that I really wanted, I had projected myself in that future role such that I couldn’t imagine any other outcome than starting that job in a few weeks. It was very difficult to adapt to the reality that I wouldn’t get it, but that’s ok. I considered the job I had then which frustrated me for some reasons, and I fell in love again with what I was doing, I found joy in my work even if not in my title, company, etc. and that really lifted me up. There’s more to tech (and work in general) than FAANG. There’s so much innovation and creativity happening in younger and smaller companies. The time where these companies were magical workplaces for a very small number of people is also arguably over.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can personal problems be mentioned as a weakness in an interview?
Answer: why would you do that? you might as well tell your interviewer to not hire you directly. As a candidate your role is to convince your interviewer to extend an offer. Questions about “weaknesses” are insincere and are invitations to candidates to disqualify themselves, because there’s literally no right answer. Just don’t give them material to do that. If I were in an interview where I would be asked about my weaknesses, first of all that would make me question if I want to work there, but I would answer the question as either: do you want me to talk about a project that didn’t succeed and what I learned from that, or about what growth areas have I identified and I am trying to improve on? but not a catalogue of my alleged, inherent flaws.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should I answer the question about my motivation for applying for this software engineering position during an interview?
Answer: In the interview process, we are trying to determine how likely it is that a candidate will perform well in the future. Really we care about 2 things: their skillset and their accomplishments. If a candidate can demonstrate they have the required skillset and that they have achieved a lot, then this is evidence that they will perform well. A candidate that doesn’t have the skills, or that is highly skilled but hasn’t achieved what could be expected of them, doesn’t present evidence that they can do well in the future, regardless of how motivated they are. Specifically: an organization that would hire somebody because they are highly motivated but can’t pass a technical or a behavioral interview, and would reject a candidate that has excellent technical scores and a brilliant track record but doesn’t impress their interviewer with their motivation, is a circus I wouldn’t want to be a clown at. back to the question, I would respond with something vague and non committal that checks the box and move on.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the recommended length for a CV when applying to big tech companies as an entry-level software engineer? Is it acceptable to have a CV longer than two pages?
Answer: I don’t think you should overthink the length but rather try to reason about what is useful/relevant or not to the reader of your resume in deciding whether to bring you in for an interview. There is no such rule as “2 pages maximum or else”, though candidates who send very long resumes...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible for a senior developer to fail an interview?
Answer: No it’s impossible. Upon reaching this grade, they are taught the secret handshake from their peers. And so the next time they find themselves looking for work, all they have to do is perform the secret handshake as they walk into the interview room. At this moment, the interviewer knows, and instead of interviewing, they spend the next 45 minutes trading senior developer stories. For feedback, the interviewer just has to write “one of us”, everyone understands and an offer letter follows a couple of days later.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason behind Google's statement that only 2% of developers are considered good programmers?
Answer: I don’t have the source for that statement, but I think it can be inferred in 2 ways. 1) what is the proportion of Google employees that have the top performance rating? It may or may not be 2%. This is completely arbitrary and the goalpost varies. The 10x engineer may be a myth but there is a reality that two people with the same title and the same amount of experience may differ greatly in their ability to get things done, have impact and create value. That in itself doesn’t make someone a “good programmer” but you already have to be excellent at coding to be hired as a developer by Google. 2) If you look at the total population of people writing code for a living in the world (back of the napkin estimate ~ 30M) and that of software engineers working in reputable tech companies (BOTN estimate of 500k) then the ratio is going to be around 2%. The typical compensation for a developer and a software engineer working in a tech company like Google is very different, but so is what is expected of them.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the benefits of using a unit-testing framework over regular unit tests?
Answer: It should really take as little effort as possible for developers to write unit tests. Unit testing frameworks, when available, take a lot of the toil away from developers so they don’t have to write a lot of “scaffolding” type code in order to write a test case. The trade-off is that testing frameworks take control away from developers, as they make some decisions on their behalf.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do developers test their own code for bugs instead of letting QA Testers do it? Is it a waste of time for developers to test their own work?
Answer: When you start writing code in an organization instead of for your own work, and you’re asked to write tests, you may see that as an extra chore. Tests do help to find or prevent bugs, but that’s not really the point of automated testing or the reason why some organization require a certain degree of code coverage. The point of automated tests is to make the code testable. When developers have to write unit tests on the code they write, this makes them write code in such a way that this code can be tested: there’s well-delimited functions and classes with strong interfaces, the code is deterministic such that the same input always produces the same output, etc. This makes the codebase much more robust and healthy, even if the tests never ran. The fact that automated tests can run and prevent things to accidentally break is a nice bonus. When the people who write the code and the people who write the tests (or who are responsible for QA) are not the same, you don’t get that virtuous cycle. Feature developers can write terrible code that happens to work right now, but which is difficult to read or maintain or troubleshoot when it doesn’t. QA won’t be able to guarantee that all code works as intended because it won’t be able to exercise all of its parts in isolation. Even though writing tests can be seen as a chore, a well-tested codebase actually helps developers go faster. If, as you’re writing code, you work with well-delimited entites, whose role is easy to grasp; if you can have the confidence that the code you just wrote is not going to break anything - and the instant feedback that there is a problem somewhere else in the codebase when you do something risky - this makes you much more productive as a developer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is knowledge of data structures and algorithms necessary for aspiring software engineers? If so, what level or type of understanding is sufficient?
Answer: If you want to be employed as a software engineer, you will need to take a coding interview, and in order to take a coding interview, you will need some knowledge of data structures and algorithms. The scope of what needs to be known to take a coding interview is fairly stable and has been for many years, and is the topic of many books, training programs, websites etc. This is also a subset of the theoretical knowledge that a computer science student will have by the time they graduate. It’s not necessary to have such a degree to get a job as a software engineer (although these days, that caveat is less and less true for entry level jobs) but at the same time, well some theoretical knowledge is required of candidates.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Will Google build their own ERP to compete with SAP S/4 HANA or D365 F&SCM?
Answer: with the caveat that i have 0 insider knowledge on the question, I wouldn’t hold my breath. because: - that would take a significant investment from Google to have a competitive product. Investment here means: taking resources from existing product areas, and throw them on a new initiative. - that is something that Google has done a number of times tbh but in order to move fast on a domain where they had little competition. - there’s one time when Google tried to throw a significant amount of resources to compete against a well-established software leader: Google+. Essentially Google small Google+ division couldn’t keep up with Facebook who were putting everything they had on the line. - it’s extraordinarily difficult to take 100 engineers and build a polished product in a year, versus build a very limited software with a small team, then add features and features over time. Again this is something that Google has done several times, but this just adds to the risk/uncertainty. - assuming that Google could come up with the best product, then they would have to sell it. The customers to an ERP don’t align well with the customers it has for its existing product families, ads and cloud, so there’s no obvious synergy. - Google doesn’t even try to build this kind of software for its own use. When I was an employee, Google would use software from Workday, Oracle, Salesforce etc. rather than develop it inhouse (which is much easier if you only have to worry about your own usecases than if you want to build a commercial product).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it necessary for data scientists and software engineers to go through coding interviews?
Answer: The ability to solve problems with code, which is at the core of what they do, must be evaluated. What we call a coding test has evolved a lot over the past 20 years (especially the last 10). This used to be mostly done on a white board, with trick questions considered a good thing, They are now done over video most of the time, with candidates working in some kind of online collaborative environment, and trick questions are avoided. Because of the relative novelty of remote interviewing which makes very brazen cheating possible, I think the format of the coding test is going to evolve further, and it is possible it will no longer be reduced to having a candidate implement a snippet of code that does certain things in a limited amount of time. That said, individual contributors for technical roles must always be able to demonstrate they can code and code well. Specifically the simple fact of having x years of experience and having worked at such or such prestigious tech company is not enough to establish that the candidate can be successful at the job they apply for. I had some candidates who had a very impressive resume and who couldn’t pass the warmup phase of a coding question.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why does Google auto complete always, and I really do mean always, append some totally unwanted vomit to your search terms, making it functionly useless?
Answer: I know a little bit about how the google autocomplete works under the hood, but that is not going to answer your question. There is a constant trend in consumer tech products (ie - free to use) in which the user demands control. The company which implements these products is looking at a different set of metrics and is trying to make them trend up. They also run (and record) experiments all the time, so they know that: when we do X, the metrics we care about are going down, so there is a high cost of doing X. One good example has been Facebook news feed. In the early 2010s, Facebook had started to heavily transform the content of the news feed based on their “algorithm”. Users complained and said they wanted to see everything in reverse chronological order, nothing less! well, a small group of users were actually seeing everything in reverse chronological order. Their satisfaction, time spent on the site, likeliness to engage with the content, likeliness to come back every day etc. (all things that Facebook very much cared about) was much lower than the people who saw the curated newsfeed. That’s why Facebook never gave in on that. By the mid 2010s, Twitter which had stuck to a reverse chronological order to differentiate themselves from Facebook, followed suit for the same reason, despite very vocal objections from users. In search and especially on the web, Google wants to serve as many searches as possible because every search is an opportunity to display ads, so if you will, every search result display brings a tiny tiny bit of money to Google. Everything that can remove friction to get people to search is good, everything that make them go faster is good. the search autocomplete is very, very successful at this because on average, it makes people submit much more searches. Also, if it were actually helpful to you 99% of the time, but once every 100 searches it would only offer unhelpful suggestions, you may still have a negative impression of the feature, because the 99 successful interactions don’t register.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If an employee is trying to sabotage another employee's work environment, why would they do that? And how should the situation be handled?
Answer: In general, all employees are incentivized to see their company succeed, so their goals are broadly aligned. So by default, you can expect coworkers to cooperate, because if they get to do what they want, this is good for the company and indirectly for you. This is where the “assume good intentions” recommendation is useful. You can see workplace collaboration as a prisoner’s dilemma.
