Question: What is the significance of an interviewer saying, "I hope the rest of your interviews go as well as this"?
Answer: really nothing, because if you’ve actually done terribly, the interviewer could be wishing that you never are considered for an offer while sounding polite.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for writing a unit test for an API that requires login? Can a unit test accept multiple results?
Answer: you can’t write a unit test if there is an actual API call. If there is an API call, then one component is going to interact with another component over the network. There are lots of things that can happen in that scenario that are not captured in the logic of the code of the calling component, there is also inherent flakiness of these tests. You just cannot guarantee that this call will be always successful of the time, because you can’t guarantee that in the physical world. Finally the time that this call will take will have a significant impact on the time of your entire test suite to run. So, if you want to do a unit test around the behavior of the calling component, you have to use a test double for the response. For instance, you can have a mock response - you replace the calls to the API by a static object. You can also regularly record responses to specific queries and serve these results instead of executing the query. Another possibility is to create a fake implementation of the API that has some logic (so it doesn’t always return the same thing) even though it’s not the real thing. The idea though is that if you use a test double, there will not be a call over the network. The response will be in memory or read from a local file. If you want to test the actual call, then you can’t do it though a unit test, you will do it in an integration test. In a lot of languages / frameworks, the infrastructure to write integration tests is the same as the one to write unit tests, but sometimes it is also different. What is probably different is when these tests are going to run. You don’t want to run integration tests all the time. So how would you execute an authenticated call in an automated test? the same way you would do it in production - you have to find a way to pass credentials to a call (whether the call you need or to authenticate). The problem is that you don’t want to store these credentials in your code base. So how you do that depends on your testing environment, it has to be configured such that tests can access “secret” information, that doesn’t have to be committed with the code. For instance, github has the notion of secrets so you can have a github action that can access sensitive information when it runs a process, without that information being visible in the repository.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it acceptable to accept multiple results in a unit test?
Answer: Let’s say your team is building a calculator. You’re reviewing the code. All unit tests have passed. Which would give you better confidence that the calculator is working as intended… Seeing tests of the form expect 1 + 3 to equal 4, or: expect 1 + 3 to equal either 2, 5, 9 or 4 ?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Should a separate plan be created for each type of testing (system, unit, integration, acceptance, and regression)? Why or why not?
Answer: That depends what you mean by plan. In Google’s taxonomy, a test plan is a list of test cases and a testing strategy is a document to explain how a system needs to be tested. But these terms are sometimes used interchangeably. The fact that there is one or two or ten test plans (in the Google sense) doesn’t matter much, there is an arbitrary way to group test cases. The result is going to be the same. There should be one unique testing strategy. Not every system must be unit tested and integration tested etc. The testing pyramid[1] is a useful abstraction to reason about test mix, but again it doesn’t mean that every system gets one type of each. If you can exhaustively test the functionality of your system with unit testing (which is usually a big if and doesn’t happen by accident) then you don’t need higher level testing. The reason why the testing pyramid is useful is to indicate that if your test mix is “top-heavy” (ie mostly relying on large-scale tests) then there is something wrong with your approach. Also, not every system is adequately tested using automated, correctness testing only. Some systems will provide little value without performance guarantees (whether they work correctly or not), or without quality evaluations. All of this is part of the testing strategy, but doesn’t fall into the “unit testing” vs “integration testing” etc. buckets.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the reasons for someone leaving Google to work at Uber? What are the advantages and disadvantages of being a software engineer at these two companies?
Answer: i’ve done the opposite move, but i did go from Facebook to Uber. In the mid 2010s Uber was the hottest startup to work at. The company was still pretty small and a successful IPO seemed to be around the corner. A lot of tech employees dream of a successful “exit” as that can be a life-changing event. In 2014 Facebook bought WhatsApp for around $20b, when the company had fewer than 50 employees. So around 2015 when I joined Uber there were dozens of people joining every week from larger tech companies - Google, Facebook, Amazon etc. and the balance was net positive with every tech companies (meaning: there were more ex-Google people at Uber than ex-Uber people at Google, same for every company). 2015 Uber was seen as the hottest startup because of its growth. This growth didn’t happen out of thin air but because Uber had thousands of “ops” people - boots on the ground - working everywhere Uber operated, recruiting drivers and riders, growing the business through hustle. During my time (2015–2020) Uber engineering grew from a few hundred people who all knew each other by name at least to thousands. The engineering organization became less of a free-for-all zone, it became more structured, acquired experienced leadership (not just people who just happened to be there and be promoted). o Uber in 2017 had a big cultural shift with the ousting of founder Travis Kalanick (TK) and the arrival of now CEO Dara Khosrowshahi. There was a transition which was already under way in the last few years of TK but the idea that the ends justify the means was deeply ingrained in Uber’s culture so every attempt to make the workplace healthier was always going to be half-hearted. The arrival of Dara was an occasion to start off a clean base, but at the expense of moving as fast as before. Over Covid, Uber went through a second big transition, as they abandoned the ambition to be the “OS of transportation” to everyone, including exiting the autonomous car space, and they moved to being a ridesharing company that does food delivery to a food delivery company that does ridesharing. The stock has gone up and down since the IPO but has recently been on a solid up tick. The engineering organization and the rest of the company is more mature, but the nature of the work is more focused. Now Google - what hasn’t been said about the company. Its culture has also evolved tremendously over the years. My take is that the Googler sees themselves as a special snowflake that is entitled to a lot of advantages that their peers inside or outside of the tech industry don’t enjoy, but that is somewhat justified by the fact that every Google employee had an extraordinary journey and is extremely accomplished. As an employee though that entitlement can also wear you down. The seismic shift has been the 2023 layoffs, the months leading to it and the aftermath - before, Googlers were very well taken care of and seen as a treasure. The fact that Google could get rid of engineers and technical roles, even very tenured, very senior was a complete U turn. This has challenged the status of Google as a unique place to work, or one where the employees feel that their needs are put ahead of the business. Another characteristic of Google is that it’s just so damn big. There are (or at least were in my time) over 100k engineers. Quite a lot of these work on things which are not monetized or even, candidly, useful. Google isn’t really focused on solving one problem as a tech company. To Google’s credit though - it has the largest concentration of technical knowledge. The largest code base, so many excellent documents, processes… even code written 10, 20 years ago is amazing to look at. It has many world class experts, in pretty much every domain it operates in, which are many, it has *the* best person in the world. You also have a category of people who have worked there for 20+ years. This is really a privilege to work with this kind of folks. So, I think it makes a ton of sense for people to want to leave Google today to go work at a company which is one or several orders of magnitude smaller: you get more focus, you don’t have the whole Googler folklore weighing you down, you are less constrained by the heavy Google processes, you have opportunities for growth, including maybe a future exit (although that ship has sailed for Uber). Likewise, in the foreseeable future, it’s going to be aspirational to work at Google, i mean, it’s f***ing Google, inventor of many products who are used by several billion people. You work at a scale that is very difficult to see elsewhere, your coworkers are next-level amazing, you get to touch people’s daily lives. And you’re not even forced to use an Android phone or Chromebook (though… definitely nudged to).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How crucial are data structures and algorithms for a software engineer in the real world?
Answer: I’m going to read between the lines and assume that the intention of the question here is to confirm that, well data structures and algorithms (DS&A) may be useful during the interview but not really in the day to day of the engineer. I’ve been a software engineer (in title) for about 9 years. During these 9 years I have spent approx 1 year being open about changing jobs, so I knew I had to get interview-ready. In that year, knowing DS&A is absolutely crucial because if as a candidate you don’t pass a coding test, there’s no job offer, so there’s no engineering. So after having learned DS&A, I need to practice DS&A and be good at DS&A in order to do my job. So again - for every 9 days I spent on the job there is 1 where DS&A are very much top of mind. That’s over 10% (yes engineers need to be good at maths too). As a software engineer, interviews are not something on the margin, to which you dedicate a negligible amount of time. It’s an integral part of your career. It’s the key to secure a job and an indispensable tool in career development. So if DS&A were only useful for interviewing, they would already be very useful skills to have for 10%+ of your career. Now in a world where you never have to interview ever again, two observations. If you don’t have a good command of algorithms, you can’t read or write a design document and this is extremely limiting in your career - this is restricting yourself to the lowest of the low rungs of the ladder. Also, there is a huge difference between implemeting something in code so that it works, and implementing it as it should be. The difference between the two is also, more often than not, DS&A. Everything has to be fast, everything has to consume the least possible amount of resources.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does using an IDE make you a weaker programmer?
Answer: When my parents started their career in science they were at the tail end of the punchcard era. Long after the introduction of magnetic support, punchcards were used - when I would visit IBM for family day in the late 70s/early 80s I remember distinctly engineers (in suits, obviously) feeding punchcards to super computers with the same confidence as Moses holding the Tablets of the Law. Making a typo or really any error while writing code that will go on a punchcard has a high cost because your punchcard is useless, you need to make a new one. So these programmers had to think long and hard in order to write perfect code the first time. Did they write perfect code though… these are the people who thought that 6 digits is enough to represent dates forever. Conceptually programming languages were also so much simpler and more limited in the 80s and before than they are now. Developers of today are not smarter than those of the generation of my parents but they are much, much, MUCH more productive given the tools that they can rely on and they can work on much more scope. In the 80s the most complicated codebase was (allegedly) the space shuttle operating code that was in the order of magnitude of hundreds of thousands of lines of code. Today your typical startup has millions of lines of code, Google has billions.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What steps can one take to transition from being a self-taught programmer to becoming a software engineer at top tech companies like Google, Facebook, or Microsoft?
Answer: They can either: acquire experience in another company for at least 5 years, or find a time machine, set it to 15 or 20 years in the past, and hit go. There was a time when these companies would try to hire every qualified candidate they could. But that policy completely changed in 2022–2023 and these companies all did layoffs - choosing to let go people that they spent a lot of resources acquiring and onboarding and that passed very selective entry tests. Right now, these companies have more candidates than they need to hire coming from campus recruiting, internship programs etc. The era where alternatively educated candidates could apply to entry level roles through other channels is over.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What does it mean to "unit test everything"? Does this mean that every single function in a program must be tested, or can some functions be tested more frequently than others?
Answer: It’s helpful to think about testing as an investment that has to have a return. You have different strategies, and some have a higher track record than others but that doesn’t mean that every single investor follows the same approach. There are some organizations that believe in 100% unit test coverage. That was the approach at Google. It’s IMO a highly rational approach because it’s enforceable. Because it is possible to measure test coverage, it is also possible to verify if a codebase is 100% unit tested or not and therefore it is possible to automatically reject code changes that violate this directive. It’s also worth noting that code can always be 100% covered by tests - if it can be run, it can be exercised by tests, and if it can’t be run, then it can be deleted. The point of 100% unit test coverage is not the tests proper. It’s both the idea that there won’t be outages which could have been caught by a unit test, and the constraint to developers to write testable code, which has many desirable qualities (safer, more maintainable, some best practices by design etc.). But 100% is not 95%. It means everything must be covered by unit tests or be removed. With that said, this approach is more the exception than the rule. The vast majority of codebases have much lower code coverage. When you work with a codebase which is in production and which has low or no coverage, there’s only so much value that writing tests after the fact will bring, then again it is probably useful to add some degree of testing, but the case for 100% is less evident.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you describe the experience of being a software engineer who does not code every day for their job?
Answer: As a software engineer / individual contributor, your career goes (may go) through 2 pivots: in a first phase, you’re assigned well-delimited tasks. You create most value by implementing a solution in code. In a second phase, you’re given problems. You create most value by designing a solution, which you may or may not implement. In a third phase, you’re given nothing. You create most value by determining which problems to take on and why, and getting the planets to align so these problems will be solved, not necessarily by you. As someone who is in the latter bucket, here’s what I do all day: I do write code most days, but I can also go weeks without writing (or at least committing) code. Writing code, or rather having written high quality code / having shipped some valuable piece of code or solved a hard problem through code is essential to building a reputation which is very useful for what is the crux of my job.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why does Google sometimes automatically complete your search query with something else? Is this a coincidence or is there a specific reason for this?
Answer: The why is because Google wants you to use their search service. Each query can be monetized, so Google wants as many queries as possible. As such it’s very important to remove friction. Let’s say I want to know when my local Walgreens closes, I could type “when does the Walgreens at 123 main street, San Francisco close?” and not get an answer unless I typed everything exactly right with no typo, but then many queries will be left unanswered. Instead if I type “w” and “a” I will see “walgreens hours” as a suggested search and get the information that I need, in addition to a map to the closest Walgreens with assorted local business ads. (your mileage may vary on that) The how is that Google doesn’t wait to submit a full query to handle it. They build a database of likely queries based on keystrokes and are able to surface these queries as the user types.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason behind the obsession with achieving 100% branch/line/code/unit testing coverage in software development, particularly for web applications?
Answer: If you start a codebase and you enforce a requirement of 100% unit testing coverage, then the original commit will be tested, and all the commits after that. So, at any given time, if a developer wants to contribute work, they need to make sure the additional work can be exercised by tests. This constraint is actually very powerful - flipping this around, this prevent developers from adding code that cannot possibly be tested. That means that every part of the system is can work independently and has strong, predictable interfaces. that aspect (to simplify: that the system is “testable”) is much more valuable than the actual tests, because this makes things much easier to work with. This effectively prevents parts to be implicitly tightly coupled with each other, to unexpectedly mutate each other, etc. and other dangerous behaviors. But this guarantee can only be had if the maximal testing requirement is held. That’s one aspect. The other aspect is that an outage whose cause is a bug that should have been caught by a unit test is very embarrassing.

Question: Why are Java and Python considered top languages in software development, but not enough to make someone a good programmer?
Answer: I can name on the top of my head several excellent developers who work primarily either with Java or Python.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is test coverage percentage (unit tests) important to developers at their company or do they just say they care to appear more experienced?
Answer: Test coverage as in the intention to have tests that cover the codebase as exhaustively as possible is really important. When you’re a company and you have systems in production, there will be outages. Those outages have a cost - when your systems are offline you don’t make money, you need to take people off other work to fix them etc, and longer term - image of low reliability, loss of customers... When you leave large parts of your code base without tests, virtually all your outages are due to bugs that should have been caught by a test that was never written. So by declining to invest in tests, you are going to face future costs and that’s generally not a good tradeoff. Test coverage as a metric though is often overrated, because most tests are not useful. Put it differently, just adding tests is not enough to guarantee some form of safety unless you have test strategies, test plans etc. As an analogy it’s as if you were equating: “how full is my fridge” and “how many meals can I prep”. I can write a lot of tests (“go to the store a lot”) such that my test coverage metric is very high (“my fridge is almost full”) but if a lot of my tests are flaky (“oops, a lot of my food is past expiration date and should be thrown away”) or exercise things which are always true (“a lot of my food is high calorie, low nutrition content like candy”) or is just one type of tests (“and I guess the rest of my food is only meat”) then you can’t actually do anything useful with all that’s in your fridge. Whereas if you write a testing strategy (“meal planning for the week”) and test plans (“shopping lists for the grocery store”) you end up with a nice mix of tests that are going to address all the scenarios that you want to cover (“there’s a balance of produce, proteins, spices etc so i can cook all the meals that I planned”). When you execute on your testing strategy, test coverage usually follows but it’s a means not an end.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: To what extent does test coverage impact a program's maintainability?
Answer: Test coverage doesn’t, but testing strategy does. High testing coverage means that developers attempt to make it so that a large proportion of the code base is “covered” by a test, or looking at this from the other end: that the existing tests exercise a large proportion of the code base. Testing coverage increases mechanically as tests are added, however, not all tests are useful. If a test that fails doesn’t have consequences other than changing or disabling the test, then that test has no useful value but it has a cost. But when measured by coverage metrics, this test is moving the needle forward and provides a false sense of security. In general, testing added long after the feature code is written has a dubious utility. The role of such tests is to enforce that in the future, the code will work as it does today, but not really that it works as it should. In contrast, a testing strategy is an answer to the question: how can we guarantee that the system works as intended? And this answer is not reducible to: write X automated tests. At a high level, it means we can describe what the system should do / how it’s going to be used, and what are its various parts. When you raise the question of how you’re going to do that for a system which is going to be built, then you’re going to build a testable system. This may be counter intuitive, but a testable system with no tests is safer than one with testability as an afterthought but lots of tests. That’s because a testable system requires parts that can work independently, with strong interfaces between each other. Having a set of independent parts, with a well-defined/stable input and output, not makes this easier to test, but also to maintain and evolve.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can one answer the question "Why are tests difficult to write?" in an interview?
Answer: Tests are not difficult to write. In the general case, writing tests is the easiest part of coding. Tests are difficult to write in the specific cases when developers are working with a system which was not designed with testability in mind and/or an environment which doesn’t have adequate test tooling. This is more the exception than the rule.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is speed important when coding for interviews or pursuing a career in software engineering?
Answer: Speed is very important, because it allows candidates to do more in the allocated amount of time, and because the “output” is always taken into account. It is also important because the other attributes which are evaluated factor in how fast a candidate can go. Bugs or missed edge cases make candidate lose time. Clean code and appropriate algorithms / patterns / data structures make them work faster. Communications and tests is one of these things which are appreciated but the excess of it ends up costing time. The lack of speed is fatal in an interview. If a candidate asks all the good questions and shows they have understood the problem but cannot show functioning code because they run out of time, this is never going to be enough. I add these AI generated images because it’s really fun to me to see what the AI is going to come up with. Next time you interview, make sure you ditch the chair. hands off the keyboard and mouse (is that a game controller?) is some great out of the box thinking. That giant screen on the side with cryptic inscriptions in shades of blue and red? bug plus too.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How much does speed matter in programming interviews and are there scenarios when speed is more important than in others?
Answer: Speed is arguably the most important attribute. Let’s take a step back. In a coding interview, a candidate is going to have to solve a problem. This requires doing several thing: disambiguating the question, identifying the problem category, zeroing on the general idea on how to solve it, possibly sketching a solution first, then starting implementing, re-reading the code, checking for use cases, verifying that the code is correct, and then probably answering follow up questions or taking on a new exercise. And then, they have a fixed amount of time. At the end of the interview, how much has the candidate done is always factored in. The basic split is usually: they finished the problem and ended up with an acceptable solution, or: they didn’t finish the problem. But typically, the appreciation is more granular, from the unfortunate “they were not able to solve the preliminary question” to “I ran out of follow up questions and we still had more time in the interview”. Further, interviewing platforms typically have ways to replay the keyboard interactions and the pace at which a candidate works becomes a demonstrable artifact of the interview. But what about the other attributes? what about communication, what about code style, what about performance, what about bugs and edge cases, what about using the right algorithms and data structure, what about testing? Code style, algorithms / data structure etc. are more a means to an end. Sure they can be evaluated / discussed on their own too. But candidates write good maintainable code and useful variable names and find a sensible way to solve the problem, such that they can work fast and they can be relatively sure that their code works in all cases. Similarly, bugs/edge cases are important because they can cost the candidate a lot of time, that’s why an initial time “investment” in planning how to answer the question can pay dividends. Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you provide an explanation for why certain codes are difficult to test in software engineering interviews?
Answer: to clarify, code written in a software engineer coding interview should be very easy to test. but if I were asked in a software interview why code can be difficult to test in certain situations, the gist of it is that unless code is designed with testability in mind, it soon becomes very difficult to test. Consider a system S which is made of 3 components, A, B and C. S receives an input I, and it will produce an output O. Inside of S, A will take some input and go through 3 branches, A1, A2 and A3, based on that input. It will produce some output which is will pass ot B. Likewise, B and C have 3 branches, B1, … C3. Let’s say you can’t exercise A, B and C independently. So if you want to test S, you’ll have to find at least 27 test cases (3 x 3 x 3) that will go through A1B1C1, A1B1C2, … A3B3C3. And that’s still assuming that A, B and C have clean interfaces, are deterministic and don’t produce side effects, because else that won’t even be enough. Conversely, if you can make it so that A, B and C can be tested independently, then all you need is 3 test cases for each of A, B and C. 3 branches, 3 subcomponents - those are very low numbers. Let’s take a more realistic example of 100 components with 100 branches each, and that’s still a small system. that means that to have full coverage you would need 100^100 tests. That’s one with 200 zeroes. It’s intractable. But if that system was written with testability in mind, all components can work neatly without the other 99 and then that’s just 100*100 tests - 1 with just 4 zeroes. That’s just a very practical, logistical aspect. But beyond that, just having a bunch of unit tests doesn’t mean your system is well tested. What is often missing is a testing strategy, aka some general description of what should be guaranteed to be confident enough that the system is working as intended. From that strategy, you get to test plans, and from there to actual testing. Without having done the “homework” every additional test is just only so useful. In my experience, testing strategy / test plans are more the exception than the rule and poor testing is usually tolerated.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What makes Google's interviews challenging? What is the source of their interview questions?
Answer: I am not sure of the source of the behavioral questions. It is very likely that they are written in-house, but the process as to how a new behavioral question comes to be is not widely known to interviewers. However, technical questions (coding, design, code review when applicable) are definitely written by Google engineers. In my experience what sets Google apart when it comes to questions is that they are very aggressive in banning questions that may have leaked, so there is a constant flow of new questions, given that there’s something like 100,000 engineers. You don’t need many of them to write questions in order to have a huge pipeline of new questions. Interestingly the guidelines for design questions is that every individual interviewer must comes up with their questions. That is different from every other company I’ve been at.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do big tech companies like Google, Apple, Microsoft, etc. care about what university you go to?
Answer: yes and no. If you’re an experienced hire, then where you got your degree from and whether you have a degree to begin with has close to 0 impact. However, as of 2024 my impression is that it’s very difficult to get an entry-level technical position outside of campus recruiting programs, internships etc., which are targeting some specific universities. This wasn’t true a few years ago (ie pre-pandemic) at a time when a self-taught person could get an interview for an entry-level position. Now that self-taught candidate is pretty much expected to acquire experience elsewhere and reach the point where they can apply to slightly more senior jobs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it common for technical questions in software engineering interviews to require writing code on a whiteboard?
Answer: No. The use of white board in interview has been highly divisive. Historically, there was a time where software engineering interviews were very similar in form to an oral exam. Trick questions were generally ok, interviewers wanted to see candidates think on their feet. In the 2010s, an increasingly number of folks, both candidates and employers, started to question that method and felt that it led to rejecting qualified prospective employees. Some went up to banning the coding interview altogether. But, by the end of the 2010s, the typical software interviewing experience was in person, and included coding exercises on a laptop with the candidate code expected to run. White boards were present in interview rooms and candidates would often use them as a brainstorming device. Companies like hackerrank or codepair proposed platforms on which candidates could be evaluated. Some companies, and most significantly Google, were strong proponent of having the candidates write code on an actual whiteboard. They argued that this emphasized reasoning as opposed to syntax - whether the code made sense was more important than whether it ran. This also allowed candidates to write some “pseudo-code” for some less important part of the exercise. The form of the interview changed completely with the COVID pandemic. All coding interviews became remote overnight, which rendered the physical white board impossible to use. Even Google started rolling out its own code interview platform. In the post-pandemic world, the remote interview is still the norm. Tech companies typically allow, but don’t encourage, in-person interviews. As far as I know, no company requires all interviewing to happen in person. Remote interviews being so much cheaper and convenient, I don’t think this trend will revert any time soon. As such, the interview processes are generally standardized around the remote interview, and I don’t know any company that requires writing actual code on an actual whiteboard. As an unfortunate side-effect, candidates often start to code too early and skip the doodling phase on the white board (or on paper) which could really help them.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: When do LeetCode and learning data structures and algorithms take you to the wrong direction?
Answer: Different companies may have different directives on how to evaluate coding interviews, but chances are these criteria are very different than what constitutes success for a LeetCode question. For LeetCode, a good answer: Sometimes these criteria are repetitive, because some test cases are designed to break unless the solution is extremely performant. But are not taken into account: This is very different from how Google (for instance) will evaluate coding interviews. At Google the above is definitely taken into account, and while performance is important, it’s usually not the crux of the question. When I did use LeetCode I found that some of the recommended answers to questions were just a few lines of highly obfuscated code. That approach just won’t fly at most tech companies.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the salary difference for a software engineer at Apple, Google, and Facebook? Is the pay significantly lower for this position in general?
Answer: Every big tech company has a concept of levels for a family of roles. At Meta and Apple, levels are not public but at Google they are opt-out, so they correspond to a title like “senior engineer” or “principal engineer” or my former title, “staff engineer”. In general, for an equivalent level, the salaries are going to be close across Apple, Google and Meta because they have similar compensation strategies. However, salaries are just one part of the compensation, the more significant chunk especially as people become senior is equity - every month, engineers receive shares of the company, in addition to a salary paid in cash. How this works is that when they are hired, engineers receive a grant corresponding to a fix amount in cash. The value of the grant is also going to be pretty close across Apple/Google and Meta. So let’s say I’m given $360k worth of shares over 4 years when I’m hired, that’s going to be around 2400 google shares at $150/share, 800 meta shares at $450/share, and 1800 apple shares at $200/share. so every month, I’d get 50 goog shares, 17.33 meta shares or 37.5 apple shares and when hired that amount will be similar - in our example $7.5k / month. Over the past year, the value of Meta stock has increased by 2.5x. whereas Apple and Google has grown by 20 and 40% respectively. So now our Facebook employee would get more than $10k extra per month compared to their peers at Google and Apple. It’s extremely uncertain how these stocks will evolve over the next year. But this evolution explains a lot of the total compensation (not salary) differences across tech company.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason that recruiters never give feedback on why candidates are rejected, even when requested? How can candidates best respond to this behavior?
Answer: 1) the main reason is legal exposure. Many (most?) candidates belong to one or several protected categories. If a rejected candidate uses the feedback to sue for discrimination, even if they lose, this will cost money for the company, 2) this is no longer the norm afaik. In my last cycle as a candidate, I was regularly offered feedback when not extended an offer. 2 things are being balanced by HR department - the expected cost of a lawsuit, given that such lawsuits are pretty unlikely, and the expected “employer brand” benefits of giving candidates a good experience whether they pass or fail the interview. 3) Yet, I would still argue that feedback after not getting an offer is a complete waste of time and resources. If I work at company A, and I ask for feedback from coworkers a, b and c, and coworker b gives me constructive feedback - what I can improve - I want to take it to heart, because b and I we really share the same goals - the best possible outcome for company A, and I can reasonably assume good intentions from b towards me. So, feedback from b may lead me to work better. Now, if I work on something which is public facing for A, and there’s a person x who says they hate A and they will never buy their products and the product I work on at A is stupid and everybody that works there should quit, then I can safely completely ignore that feedback. I don’t work for x, we have 0 shared interests, they don’t have good intentions towards me. (And as someone who worked at Facebook and Uber, this is not a hypothetical situation). When a recruiter for a company that didn’t hire me shares feedback with me, we are more in the 2nd scenario than the first. They are going to be nice to me but they don’t have a vested interest in my success, more than any other candidate. The feedback I am going to get is not going to help me succeed better at other interviews, because all companies use different criteria and the interviewers are different and the exercises are different.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it true that Google does not hire candidates with low scores on their interviews? Is this a commonly believed myth or a factual policy?
Answer: It’s a total myth. Here’s how it goes. Let’s say every year Google hires 20,000 people. Let’s say they interview 10 candidates per hire, and that every interview cycle takes 20 hours of work, between the interviews, writing excruciatingly detailed feedback and reviewing applications in a hiring committee. That’s about 2000 year/employee cost per year. According to a Google search this morning, the median income of a Google employee is $279k/y. So, the labor cost of the interviews would be around half a billion dollar per year. Another way to look at it is, if Google stopped interviewing, it’s as if they had an organization of 2000 employees that could start a new business line, and generate whatever profit they can. But, yeah. After all is said and done, after candidates are as precisely evaluated as can be, they just put the names of everyone in a propeller hat and draw whoever is getting an offer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Could you be friends with a Trump supporter? If so, why?
Answer: My wife went to law school in what is now a red state. In her class, there were: the only democrat state-wide elected official, and: the chief of staff of the ultra-conservative governor. It’s very likely that one of them (and maybe both) will be governor one day. We are friendly with both. We no longer live in the state but when we did we would see each other (and yes, sometimes: all together). Now, you know… We send each other greeting cards, we check on each other when we visit the other person’s state. To be honest, I don’t know the full extent of the sentiment of the chief of staff (whom we’ll call X) on Trump. The last time I spoke with them in person was in 2021, and at that time X let me know that they felt that Trump was more of a liability than an asset. That was also when Trump was arguably at his weakest. But X is definitely very conservative. Not just simply Republican, but: has been very instrumental in getting some extremely conservative measures into law during their time in DC. And so, I have little doubt they will vote for Trump in November. I am personally strongly opposed to both Trump and this brand of conservatism. And yet, I am glad to be friends with X. This is an actual conversation I had with X in June 2021 when we had them over for brunch. We had tried to not talk politics for almost the entire time and we were doing so good, but my wife and I mentioned that we had just visited California (where we now live, btw). X couldn’t help but say - “yeah, California has been so much more punitive than us during COVID, and at the end of the day, we have the same numbers”. Me: “I can’t let you say that. We’ve had about twice the number of deaths per capita. With their numbers we’d have 1000 fewer deaths across the state” X: “I understand you feel this way, but 1000 is not a lot. We got shots to everyone who wanted them, much faster than California or any other blue state, but we also let people do largely what they wanted and kept the state open as much as we could, and I think in retrospect, people will agree it was the right call.” That statement took me aback because in my circles, lots of people (even after shots) were still acting as if we were going through some kind of plague and as if anything less than a total shutdown was reckless. Even the people I knew in the state were very critical of the governor, who they nicknamed “the reaper” for their laissez-faire COVID policy. Fast forward one year, I’m in San Francisco and I see how the local economy has been devastated by super harsh COVID policies. My office was asking us to wear masks even though we also all had to be vaccinated to be allowed on premises, this really felt performative. In November of 2022, X’s governor was reelected by a landslide. I thought of my conversation with X for a while and I have to admit that they were largely right. X and I disagree on the ideas but speaking with them helps me understand how the other half lives.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the best way to structure a design document for software?
Answer: A design document is not a support to discuss technical aspect of software development in isolation. It is meant to raise a question, provide an answer to that question (and refine that answer through discussion) and eventually build alignment. With that in mind, these are the things I include: The “metadata”: 1) very clear title of what this attempts to solve, 2) name of the author, 3) date of last edit, 4) status of document - draft, in review, approved, rejected/abandoned 5) list of reviewers with approval status (reviewing, approved, rejected) The “substance”: A summary with context, goals and non-goals. The summary is super important, this should help anyone who has some technical skill to form an opinion on the question at hand whether they have knowledge of the document or not. The summary can contain reference to other documents or resources. The goals part is critical. Without a goal, and specifically - something that needs to be approved or rejected, the document is a waste of everyone’s time. The non goal part is optional but can help focus the discussion. The rest - this is a bit more handwavy and subject to context. I usually have a “discussion” section and a “proposal” section. The discussion is where I would list alternatives and the proposal is the one I recommend. I’ve worked at places where there is a fixed outline such that the discussion part will hit on all the aspects a new service/component should cover such as “infrastructure”, “testing”, “costs”, “launch” but I feel this is more contextual. Other considerations: no table of contents. This is a waste of space. It’s no longer going to be distributed as printed copies around the meeting room table. People will see it online and can use find. everything being equal, concision is better and splitting a document into several, more focused documents can be useful. But very long decision documents can still be required. The longest I’ve worked with was well over 100 pages. no jumping the gun. if what you really want to have an opinion on is problem C, but in order to decide on C you have to select an approach for problem A and problem B, do not automatically assume that the way to solve A and B have already been decided. The context of C may impose one solution for A or B, but in general it’s safer to take decisions in the open and step by step.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Should women leaving their state to get abortions be held accountable to the laws in their state of residence when they return home and are found to no longer be pregnant? We prosecute normal murderers across state lines. Why not women?
Answer: Why murderers and not women who have abortions outside of their home state, because abortion is not murder. I’m aware that pro-life activists have pushed the notion that abortion and murder are equivalent, and there are a lot of people who believe that. However, words have meaning, and the definition of murder in English (and in the English / American legal tradition) is very precise - it’s the unlawful killing of a human being. Oftentimes, the focus on the question wether abortion in murder is on whether embryos or fetuses are human beings. There used to be a large consensus that they weren’t, and this consensus is fiercely contested by conservative lawmakers. But let’s forget that idea for a minute and focus on the unlawful part. The lawful killing of a human being is not murder. Military casualties are not murder. The execution of someone convicted to the death penalty is not murder. Self-defense is not murder. - to the extent that these killings are conducted within the legal framework which authorizes them. An abortion in the states where this is legal is by definition not unlawful and is by definition not murder. On another note, the supreme court Dobbs decision overturning Roe v. Wade doesn’t mean that abortion which used to be legal across the land becomes banned across the land. It means that the states have the power to set laws on the matter. But a state doesn’t get to decide how the law of other states work.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can a search engine like Google be built without using their API and data?
Answer: How to build a search engine in 2024 is relatively straightforward, and it can definitely be done without using any piece of Google infrastructure. But it’s also very expensive and difficult to get right. The first step is to build a crawler. This is basically a program that will read a web page, find “tokens” in the page (could be words, phrases etc. ) and then register in a database that such page contains such token. The crawler will also find other pages to look at. Running the crawler consumes a lot of computer resources and the database take a lot of disk space. Then, you need to build a search end point, that takes a query string in, extract tokens and returns a list of web pages. At this stage you’re very close to have a “search engine”. All you need is a web interface, probably some web servers and some application servers that will support the endpoint. All the tasks that this entails are pretty well known/unambiguous so the development can be done with a small team on a short amount of time, even though this will still be an expensive service to operate. In order to have a “search engine like Google”, which if I rephrase would be: “a service like Google search”, you need to do something more. When you type “weather” into the Google search bar, it won’t list all the web pages that contain weather. It will instead give you the weather in the next few days where you live. There are many such interactions (hundreds) such that for vast majority of queries, the user doesn’t get a list of link, but rather a specific card with a specific response to a specific request based on the query. In order to do that you need to build other layers on top of your service. Conceptually you need your service to “understand” the query and to be able to break it down, not in discrete words or phrases but in a sort of formal expression. For instance, “weather”, “weather this week”, “what’s the weather in [my city] this week”, “is it going to rain” and all sorts of equivalent formulations will be evaluated to the same thing. (this is pretty complicated both from a technical and a functional point of view especially when you have to support multiple languages. In addition this operation must be extremely fast). Then you have to fulfill the query. So imagine a world where you can either get a list of links or get the weather. In the first scenario, one service is going to fire a request to the database that holds all the crawling results. In the second, we’re going to fire a request to a weather API somewhere. Now crank up the complexity by a factor of 500. Once you’ve broken down the query into what must be done, how do you get the information that will eventually be displayed to the user? Some will be just getting a result from an external API. But in many cases, you will need to build your own endpoint that will have its own complex logic, which will be connected to other resources. Now, in a world where you’re not Google, it’s quite possible that some of the APIs you need to connect to would be Google owned. (like Google maps). But then again, if you’re reinventing the wheel, you can also go all the way. Finally, you need a way to render everything and to handle user interaction. This is simple on paper but obviously this gets much more complicated as there are more and more scenarios. The rest of these layers require a lot of development resources.

Question: What algorithms and/or data structures would you expect a senior developer to know during a job interview?
Answer: People usually say data structures and algorithms in one same breadth but the coding interview tests slightly different things. Algorithms, the proper use of data structures, some form of pattern recognition / know-how on how to deal with certain forms problems and to some extent domain knowledge. For algorithms proper, the candidate should know: * sorting, especially merge sort, * binary search, tree traversal * graph traversal - DFS, BFS * recursion/backtracking, dynamic programming Candidates should then know when to use / what to do with various data structures like linked lists, arrays, trees, hashes, stacks/queues/heaps and then have some sort of idea of how to use these data structures in an interview. This isn’t really part of the definition of a linked lists but so many linked list problems expect a fast pointer. Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If Mark Zuckerberg came in for an interview in disguise, would he have the skills/education needed to be a programmer at Facebook?
Answer: I answered some variations of this question. My background for answering is that - I have given a ton of software engineering interviews (hundreds), I have worked at Facebook for a bit and during that time I have been in the same room as Mark a number of times, mostly during large meetings but some smaller ones too, and I had some direct interactions with him. So the TL;DR is that I have very high confidence he would pass with flying colors. I’m going to prefix my answer by saying that most people probably have the wrong idea of how a software interview works. A software engineering interview is not: we ask the candidate trick questions and see who sinks or swim. There are 3 parts, coding rounds, design rounds and behavioral rounds. Let’s talk about the behavorial interview for a second. Tech CEOs are extremely well trained to answer questions about work. Most of them hold regular all hands where they present to the company and they take questions too. Zuck has done this hundreds of times, maybe over a thousand by now. He’s also self-reflecting a lot. He also has unique experiences like scaling a company from 1 person to over 60,000, managing organizations and executives, prioritizing, etc. In addition to questions from employees which can be softballs, Zuck has experience facing journalists, investors, lawmakers, many of which have been outright adversarial. So there’s no way he’s not going to have an outstanding performance. Let’s break this down a little bit. There are maybe 500000 software engineers in big tech. You have directors of engineering. Let’s say the top 1% of the lot. Those have very obvious experience solving larger scale problems or complex problems or problems involving many teams or organizations. Your typical engineer sometimes works across teams but your typical director always does. If as an interviewer you sit down with an “undercover” director you can immediately tell they had much superior experience. Next you have tech execs. People who’ve had 1000+ reports, so a little bit less than 0.1% of them. These folks typically have a very long experience, and they’ve solved problems of a different order of magnitude than directors and they’re also involved in the business aspect of things. Everybody knows that when they sat in the same small meeting as an exec, they can feel it. Again, your interviewer would immediately be able to tell the difference. Higher up in rarefied air, you have CEOs of large, public tech companies. There are very few of them, maybe 100 / 200 total depending how you count. So, ~0.03% of the total. They are a little bit like execs but they have dealt with a larger variety of problems, they have to interact with the board, they are somewhat public figures, they routinely engage large groups of people. Again, you reach a new palpable level of experience. Finally, you have the CEOs of big tech which is a very small club. let’s say 0.001%. They each know things that no one else in the world does. And among them, Zuck is the last founder - the only person who took an idea from college dorm to trillion dollar company which he still leads. So, he would just blow the mind of his interviewer. At this stage let’s forget about the other rounds for a second and let’s move to the debrief. The behavioral feedback alone is already going to give the committee pause. Clearly this is not an ordinary candidate, clearly they need to extend an offer and not let him get away. The end. I also think he would have a superb performance for the system design interview, though it’s not really worth getting in the details of why. Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Google lay off hundreds of employees across various functions and warn of more "role eliminations" in the coming months?
Answer: When Google was created it was growing at hyperspeed. It’s pretty incredible that this super scrappy startup born in a literal garage, quickly became better than the big tech companies of the time, backed by billions in funding, on a key aspect of the internet. Hypergrowth means that there’s always tons of very valuable things to do but you don’t have enough resources to do it all. So your projected revenue/metrics/everything you care about becomes a function of your headcount. You hire a ton of people because you need these people to do X which is very valuable for the company. But what happens when X is completed? There’s the assumption that resources would reallocate themselves “organically” to work on what’s the most valuable. The problem is, this is extremely difficult to achieve and it gets more difficult at scale. When I left there were around 10,000 teams at google, each with their roadmap. No one can reason at that scale. On one hand, it’s easy to understand how much the personnel cost and predict the payroll. On the other, it is not clear whether every team, every organization will create value in the short or long term. Or if this will help Google go in the direction it wants to be for the decades to come. Google had 100k employees in 2018. Is it clear to the public what’s the difference between what Google offers now and what it offered in 2018? Where would Google be today if it had stayed at 100k? Where would it be if it had stayed at its 2013 level, 50k? Does Google need to stay at 182k employees or however much they have today? One thing is clear is that they have realized that growing headcount at 20% year over year was no longer desirable. The tech landscape changed drastically over the past 25 years, we’re on the cusp of a major paradigm change - Google knows that they will need to be strong in different things that they used to be. Some efforts will be continued, and some resources can be shifted but there are others which - however skilled, qualified etc. would take too much effort to pivot. This explanation is not unique to Google. Other companies that have reached this level of maturity in this context are doing the same, and shifting to a culture where growing requires hiring and where every employee is a printing press to one where fixed costs matter and prioritization matters.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does Google reject candidates who perform poorly in interviews, even if they have a high score on technical questions?
Answer: A pattern that I’ve observed at Google and elsewhere is that a candidate that does great in technical rounds but not in behavioral interviews will typically be rejected. This is not a 100% rule, this obviously depend on the exact feedback of behavioral interviews and technical rounds, versus just a score. But candidates should appreciate that technical rounds, especially coding rounds, only capture a fraction of the skillset a tech company value in an engineer, even though they tend to be more precise or not overly rely on the skill of the interviewer. Conversely, the behavioral round is usually where candidates can show how they communicate, how they work with others, how they understand organizations, their degree of self-awareness, whether they have internalized bad behaviors etc. which have an outsized importance in the hiring decision. It’s unusal for more junior engineers to do really bad at a behavioral interview but conversely it’s challenging for a senior+ engineer to do well. A very common scenario is that a candidate that has enough years of experience to be a senior engineer isn’t promoted to that level at their company because they don’t have the skills, so they interview to get a role at the level they think they deserve, and the interview is precisely designed to spot a light at these cases and weed out the folks who cannot demonstrate they have acquired these skills. That said again this is not 100% rule, every individual case is different and is discussed as is. Going back to the specific case of Google, they collect more information on each interview than any other company I worked at, and everything is weighted in the final decision.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Tech companies think most senior developers who fail interviews lack problem-solving skills. About 99% of developers are in this category. Why don't these incompetent developers focus on improving their skills instead of blaming the entire system?
Answer: I don’t know what’s the basis for that “Tech companies think … “ statement, but this contradicts my experience. I’ve been an interviewer at Google. At some point, Google received 3 million applications per year. Since that number is public I’m going to use that example to prove my point, but that logic applies to any tech company you could think of, given they they all model their hiring processes after Google. Unsurprisingly, Google only interviewed a fraction of the applicants and only hired a fraction of the interviewees. So here’s Google challenge. Let’s say they have 100 candidates of various levels of skill, so you had a crystal ball, you could give them all a score from 1 to 100. Google wants to hire those will a score above, say, 90. Only it doesn’t have a crystal ball, it has processes and human interviewers, who can guess the score of the candidate 95% of the time within 10 points. Faced with that situation, Google has a choice. Either it tries to make sure to hire every candidate that is likely to be a 90+, but in so doing it will hire some candidates with lower skills (“false positives”). Or it do whatever it takes to not hire anyone under 90, and never wants to hire anyone under 80. But, in so doing, it will reject some candidates that have high skills, but who for some reason were not evaluated great that day. (“false negatives”). On paper these look equivalently bad. But: hiring one bad candidate will cost millions of dollars over time (lack of output compared to a better one, outages, time it costs their organization to get them up to speed or fix their messes…) while not hiring one good candidate has a much smaller cost (just the cost of doing another loop). So, Google has always been very public about their intention to design their processes to avoid false positives. They are very forward about it. Google leaders have also talked a lot about it. A google search on “google hiring false positives” would reveal a deluge of hits. A lot of people don’t believe that the actual google processes actually succeed in avoiding false positive. But no one denies that the intention is to avoid false positives. Generalizing past Google. Tech companies would never say publicly, candidates that don’t get offers lack X or Y skills. Instead they say, we put the hiring bar very high. Companies generally try (again, intentions, regardless of results) that the candidates even those who are rejected have a great experience. They would never call candidates that don’t get an offer incompetent.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for interviewing software engineers at companies that do not require coding in their interviews?
Answer: Coding interviews are extremely common in software engineering interviews, but I can think of a few exceptions. 1) small startup, founder recruits the first engineers, the company doesn’t have the capacity to do regular software engineering interviews, they take a leap of faith instead on a conversation with the founder or on reputation. Somebody referred by a teammate can be hired without a technical check. (note that this is not a rule, some early stage startups outsource interviews) 2) similarly, in small companies, a person can start as vendor / contractor and have some loose connection with the team, and then extended an offer to join as full time employee without any additional process. 3) acquisitions, typically the buyer is going to interview every employee as part of due diligence but sometimes this is just not possible. 4) some companies don’t do coding tests for very senior hires (but some give especially difficult coding tests to their most senior candidates including execs). Some give coding-adjacent exercises. For instance, when I left Google, we would ask engineering manager candidates to do a debugging exercise, where we give them a piece of terrible code and they have to tell us what they feel is off with it. This is code related but doesn’t explicitly require to write code. 5) Somebody may start at a company under role X and transfer to a software engineer, in which case there may or may not be an interview (this is a bit similar to 1/2) but this would still be different from a normal, external candidate’s experience

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can a single person develop a video game by himself?
Answer: Yes, there are many examples. Whether they can develop a successful game is another question. There are 2 obstacles to a solo developer. 1) the sheer amount of work that a game represents and the variety of roles that are involved now. In 2024, a AAA game may have a development budget around $100m. If you assume a (generous) cost of $200k/developer/year, that’s 500 people-year of development. In other words, it would take a single person 500 years. And you need writers, artists, musicians, programmers, level designers, testers, etc. so the solo developer needs to wear all of these hats. Even with much less ambitious projects a game is still a huge amount of work. 2) there’s a ton of competition around games and even in the independent category. Your typical gamer is maybe aware of 5, maybe 10 games which will come out in the next year. But there are thousands and thousands of projects being released each year and it’s very difficult to emerge from the crowd.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the chances of a self-taught web developer getting hired by top companies like Google, Facebook, and Microsoft?
Answer: The chances are low to begin with because Google and Microsoft have scaled down hiring of engineers drastically since their 2023 layoffs. As far as I know Meta is still actively hiring. If the sub-text is that our hypothetical self-taught developer doesn’t have relevant experience, the chances are practically none. The competition for entry-level developer jobs is fierce, and big tech companies have existing recruiting pipelines (ie campus recruiting, internships…) through which they have already get more qualified candidates than they could hire. However for candidates with experience, a degree (or lack thereof) is not going to make a difference. A degree is only useful to get an interview, but big tech companies will treat candidates with comparable experience similarly, regardless of degree.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for becoming an interviewer for Google SWE intern interviews? Is it a competitive process?
Answer: Every engineer is expected to take interview training, though it is not compulsory. Trained interviewers are not forced to participate to interviews and they can choose a maximum amount of interviews per week and per quarter, so many opt out entirely. Who employees get to interview depend on their level. In 100+ interviews I never got to interview entry-level engineers or interns.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is there a pay discrepancy between senior software engineers and new hires at Google? If yes, what is the reason for this?
Answer: Many Google employees opt to share their compensation to a group that publishes aggregate statistics on a dashboard. Based on that dashboard, I could tell that my new hire compensation as a staff engineer, both in terms of salary and stock, was aligned with the median compensation for engineers in my location and my role, which is exactly what my recruiter told me (only I couldn’t verify this). That being said, there is a huge discrepancy between old time employees and new hires. Since the time Google IPOed, the value of the stock increased well over 1000x. So a 100k stock grant back in 2004 is worth over $100m today. When you have that kind of wealth, getting $10k more or less than your peers in yearly salary doesn’t matter much. IMO, an engineer joining Google in the 2000s or the 2010s could expect their stock grant to experience spectacular growth. Those expectations are probably no longer true.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should an interview with a software developer be concluded if it is clear that the candidate will not be hired?
Answer: Let’s step out of the interview room a little bit. Candidate Alice interviews for BigTech co. The next day, she meets Bob for coffee. How are you, asks Bob. Well, I interviewed for BigTech co yesterday, says Alice. So, how was it? wonders Bob. The interview experience is designed, so that we can influence what Alice will say next. “Oh, they were really super nice, but I don’t think I am going to pass. Too bad, because it looked really cool. “ Or “I don’t care, they’re pompous assholes, I won’t take an offer no matter with how many 0s. “ Candidates talk far and wide about their interviewing experience, so a positive or negative experience can have a profound impact on the employer brand. This should inform how to talk to candidates, regardless of their performance.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you think Trump supporters are intellectually challenged, i.e. dumb?
Answer: No. I think the divide between MAGA people and never-Trumpers/liberals/others is more a matter of philosophical positioning. German philosopher Kant has introduced the idea of categorical absolutes. To simplify, this is the notion that there are certain principles or beliefs which take precedence over everything else. You can oppose Kant’s “universalist” view to utilitarianism, a view according to which something is good if it is useful. So let’s say that you’re the CEO of a company that is going to launch a widget, for which you would make 1 billion dollars in profit. But you’re also made aware that now and again it’s going to blow up and kill its user - then again, you can write checks to their survivors for a few million dollars total. If you are a universalist CEO, you will not launch the widget, because you can’t in good conscience take a decision that will result in the loss of human life. If you are a utilitarian CEO, you feel that all things considered, launching the widget is a good thing. Both philosophies had tremendous impact on American thought and politics, but as a nation we lean on the utilitarian side. I’m going to say that you can believe in either, or maybe a mix of both, but there’s not one which is inherently superior to the other: it’s a matter of moral preference rather than correctness. Back to politics. If you just look at our lawmakers and political leaders, some are very much guided by principle and values, for instance they may believe in the separation of powers, in the constitution, in liberty and justice for all, the greater good, etc. It doesn’t mean that they all agree, there are people with a strong ideological compass among both conservatives and liberals. And then, you have some who are motivated by a drive to win and who believe that the ends justify the means. Again - you will find them on both sides of the conservative/liberal divide. Now, Trump and the MAGA clique sit squarely on the utilitarian side. Taking a step back and considering the population in general - Most Americans are motivated by their own interest and not by principle. There is a large group of Americans who think they would benefit from a Trump presidency, and who don’t see why they should make sacrifices for climate change, world peace, advancement of minorities. This is not an irrational or “dumb” choice. But there are also many Americans who think they will not benefit from a Trump presidency, not even in the short term, and many Americans who put certain principles over their immediate self-interest.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to get hired by Google without a degree but with self-taught coding skills and projects? How difficult is it to get hired by Google under these circumstances?
Answer: Possible yes, common no, and very difficult. I’m reading between the lines and I’m assuming that “without a degree but with self-taught projects” infers “with no relevant experience”. That means, for an entry level role. Bad news: an entry-level applicant is going to compete with pretty much every CS grad on the planet, for a limited number of roles, for which there are already existing recruiting pipelines. In addition, Google has still drastically reduced its hiring. In theory, Google does not require a CS degree of its engineers. But it doesn’t make it easy for anyone to apply for an entry level job. With relevant experience, this is a completely different story, and candidates actual degrees (or whether they have degrees at all) matter much less.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you think Google's layoffs will impact employee morale?
Answer: I don’t think it’s going to make a big difference honestly. The huge difference is going from working in a company that has never done large layoffs, to a company that has done large layoffs. Google pre-2023 layoffs: So morale was fairly gloom. But on the plus side, So the days before the announcement, everyone was aware that: All the lunches I had this week, and during most of the social interactions, people had brought it up. “Do you think we’re going to do layoffs?” Then the announcement came between Thursday and Friday. Friday was a huge shockwave to everyone, those who stayed and those who left, because it was as if all the reasons not to do layoffs, some of which were very much baked in people’s identity, just disappeared. As if they never existed. Google went from being that special place, to being just another public company. This has been hard to accept for a lot of people, though many others had already shifted their mindset. Since January 2023, there have been a number of smaller-scale layoffs. January 2024 is the biggest since January 2023. But people now no longer see Google as a company that would never do layoffs. So this is not a big change in perception anymore.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why are companies like Google or Microsoft removing useful features from their software?
Answer: Let’s say you bought a car. That’s cool: you can go from A to B without walking or taking the bus. But then, you have to pay for gas, you have to pay for insurance, you have to pay for service, you have to pay for new tires, you have to pay each time some other idiot dings your car on a parking lot (or keep your car dinged). And maybe you don’t drive your car that much. There comes a time where your car is no longer an asset, but it’s a liability. It’s a money pit that doesn’t provide that much given how much it cost. And maybe you love your car, may because it’s the first “nice” car that you ever owned, and you never want to give it away, and you took such good care of it. But also maybe it comes a time when you feel that the only reasonable thing to do to sell it or scrap it. The reasoning is pretty much identical with any product. The second you release a product, then the headaches begin. You collect the metrics, and you iterate on the metrics, and you release updates, and you collect more metrics, and you receive bug reports, and you fix bug reports, and you get feature requests from partner teams, and you prioritize them, and you sink ever so much resources in the product, and every new feature is like a new mini product with its metrics and its bugs and its roadmap. Eventually this costs so much for declining value, and so deprecating becomes the rational course of action. In addition, as the owner of the product a company has more insight as to what is useful than a user would. One of the most talked about product deprecations by Google was Google Reader. So many people were upset about it. And now the way people consume information is the radical opposite of how Google Reader used to work.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why does Google show Quora answers when you search a question, as if those hold any validity? So many people dont realize how incorrect most answers are. Am I the only one who thinks they should be excluded?
Answer: As someone who has spent a lot of time using Quora and understanding Google Search, I believe I can give a decent answer to this question. When you think of search engines of the 90s, you have that search box where a user is going to enter text, and then after they submit the search, they are going to get a series of links that contain the text searched. This is not how modern search engines work (Google or otherwise). Today, what people enter in the search box is less a phrase to look for in a vast pile of documents, and more a command. Users expect to get something relevant in response to that command. Technically, what people put in the search box is called a query. The first thing the search engine is going to do, “understanding”, is to extract an intent from the query. An intent is a formal representation of what the user wants. To take the quintessential example of Google if a user types “obama height” they do not want to find all the documents that contain the phrase obama height, but most likely want to know how tall Barack Obama is. Extracting an intent is not enough. There are hundreds of servlets which are treating a query and which are either detecting an intent in a query or assigning metadata to the query, such as: how polite is the tone, as this yields different results. So typically, many intents are extracted. Next the search engine is going to rank these intents. Sometimes one intent is overwhelmingly likely, and it’s very unlikely that the user actually meant something else. Sometimes, it’s not as clear cut. So in our example, maybe the user wanted the height of Michelle Obama. Maybe by some logic they wanted to know Trump’s or Biden’s. And maybe, you know what, they wanted to see webpages that talk about “height” and “obama”. OK, so now Google has several intents ranked. What to do next is fulfillment and execution. Fulfillment means that it’s going to prepare answers corresponding to all the intents. Execution means it’s going to actually get those answers from the servers and render them on screen, and is not super relevant for this question. In the case of “obama height”, in google’s parliance there are a couple of intents which are going to be fulfilled, one is “knowledge base lookup” and one is “web search”. Knowledge base lookup means that the user is looking for a well-known facet (“height”) of an well-known entity (“former US president Barack Obama”) is Google’s representation of the world, its knowledge base. BTW the answer is 6′2″, a fact which is drilled into the mind of anyone who works or has worked in Google Search. When there is a “hit” for knowledge base, or really for any of the intents it understands, then Google is going to answer to the intent with a special card. That’s the happy path because if Google actually guessed the intent of the user, then the special card is going to do a much better job at responding to it than expecting them to click on one of 10 blue links. But web search is almost always fired as well, which is the list of blue links with a blurb. So on to Quora content. Quora is used by Google’s knowledge base as one of many trusted sources of information. This doesn’t mean that Google feels that whatever is in a Quora answer is absolute truth. But there is some curation, there is some validation by other users through upvotes and downvotes, so it’s much better than an arbitrary piece of web content. That is not foolproof. A notorious example is when some folks decided to update the height of cartoon character Caillou on the Fandom wiki (another trusted source, due to its human curation). Caillou, a toddler, still comes up as being 5′11″ if you google “caillou height”. Google is well aware that “it happens” and generally doesn’t care as long as directionally, content from trusted sources is more reliable on average. It also has mechanisms to address poor results. As a user you can report an answer as poor (and as a human you can also try to tweak the source of the knowledge base which I suspect is still going on with Caillou). So the answer of your question is that for the queries for which there are Quora answer, Google doesn’t have more authoritative content and it believes it is more useful to the user than just sending them to a list of links. Google also found that more often than not, when displayed, Quora content is actually helpful.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How likely is it that Google's laid-off employees will be able to find open positions elsewhere within the company?
