Answer: Very unlikely. Pre 2023 layoffs, Alphabet had roughly 190000 employees. They cut 12000, to ~178000. So to the 12000 that were laid off, let’s add 10% of natural attrition (Alphabet is supposed to be a little less than that but let’s give them 10%). Let’s round up to 18000, and say that employees that left Alphabet willingly or not since the last layoff round is 30000. That gives us 160000 employees who started before January 2023. Pre 2024 layoffs, Alphabet had 182000 employees. So, over 2023–2024, Alphabet would have hired 22000 people. If that seems like a lot, we can remove former interns and other new grad hires (let’s say 3000) - any one who’s worked is not going to be able to enter the company through these channels. Alphabet didn’t increase its employee count much through acquisitions in 2023 (less than 100 people) so we can ignore that. So we have 19000 people hired by Google over last year. If applications have gone at the same pace as before, which is likely, then that’s 3000000 per year. That means that 0.06% of applicants will get a job. If all people who were laid off were to apply, statistically less than 1 would be re-hired. Traditionally former google employees had an advantage when applying but I don’t think that’s the case of laid off employees.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the benefits of working in product management for a large company like Google or Facebook, as opposed to a start-up?
Answer: Google, Facebook etc. have been historically very selective when it comes to hiring product managers. The easiest way to become a product manager was to found a company that would be acquired by Google or Facebook. The founder could then work as a product manager. Google and Facebook also had a program where they recruited a handful of students which could become some kind of “assistant product managers” and later, “graduate” into full-fledged product managers. This program was extremely selective, it was much harder to get in than to be hired as an engineer or designer. The flip side is that having been hired as a product manager at a large tech company means something. These folks can go apply to work in product anywhere, and they sometimes pivot to venture capital, to being an executive out of tech, etc. Conversely anyone can take an online class on product and call themselves a product manager. It just doesn’t describe the same reality.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the reasons for people preferring to work at Google over Facebook, despite Google offering lower pay and fewer benefits?
Answer: I’m not sure if either part of your question is true, but looking at the history of Alphabet and Meta stock, Meta is more volatile. There’s been several occasions where Meta stock dropped brutally. I feel in general working at Meta is a bit riskier than working at Google. That said, there are many people that switch from one to the other. Having worked at both, my personal perception is that Google benefits are better but Facebook may have caught up since then (I left Facebook about 10 years ago) Google offers a unique benefit which was much discussed and envied when I was at Facebook - if you die while employed, then Google would vest all your stock and pay half your salary over 10 years to your survivors. Knowing that this safety net existed provided me with really valuable peace of mind.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: I feel like JavaScript is easier to learn than CSS. Am I wrong?
Answer: yes. it’s a completely arbitrary distinction. JavaScript, CSS and HTML are three facets of the same entity, the web API. So in a way CSS would be included in JavaScript, but JavaScript would also be included in CSS.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you view the calls for Defense Secretary Austin to resign?
Answer: There was no legal requirement for Lloyd Austin to disclose his medical condition to anyone. With that out of the way, let’s step back a little bit. Should anyone that has to undergo a medical procedure be forced to resign? How absurd is that?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it common for people who work at Google to have been rejected by other top tech companies such as Facebook, Amazon, and Microsoft?
Answer: It’s not something that we discuss much. The “canon” career for software engineers at Google is get an internship in college, start working there right after school, and spend many years there. Most of the people I worked with had followed that pattern. That’s anecdotal evidence though. I can tell you with very high confidence that the vast majority of engineers at Google, if asked to interview for a similar position at Facebook, Amazon and Microsoft, or reinterview for their current role, would fail at least once. That doesn’t mean they’re bad, but the interviews are designed to filter out false positives, and besides the behavioral interviews for these companies value different traits.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: I went for an interview today, and I was asked how much is your salary expectation, I told them whatever the company is willing to offer for the position, that I just want to work with the company. Do I sound desperate?
Answer: The company has a salary range in mind for the position. By saying that, you are inviting them to offer you the lowest compensation of that range. It’s totally fine to not be aware of your “market value” or the range offered. There is great information asymmetry in salary negotiations and companies take advantage of that. So what to do. In some jurisdictions, employers have to disclose what is the compensation range for different roles. You can also base yourself on your current compensation. But saying “whatever you want” is not a great negotiation tactic.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What makes being interviewed by a Googler challenging? Why are Google interviews known to be difficult compared to other companies and industries?
Answer: I don’t think the Google engineering interview is necessarily difficult to a qualified candidate, but it definitely has a special status compared to other tech companies, which says something because joining the tech industry as an engineer is arguably harder to join most industries as a professional. When I interviewed for Google, I definitely felt the significance of the moment, and when I was an interviewer at Google, I was also trying to be very mindful of what that day meant to my candidates. There are a few reasons for that. Ever since Google went public / became the undisputed leader in search engines, so circa 2004, it’s been the poster child for silicon valley companies - it took that role from Microsoft. Tech companies today model their HR practice after Google’s, they either copy its approach on such or such aspect or they consciously decide to diverge from Google on highly specific points. The process for the software engineering interview is one such practice. Google didn’t really invent the modern software engineering interview, the way Microsoft conducted it in the 90s was pretty similar but it was Google that made it the golden standard in the early 2000s, other big tech companies copied Google’s format and after that pretty much all of Silicon Valley. In the aughts, joining google meant you were 100% going to become wealthy. Every $1000 of Google stock in 2004 is worth well over $1m today, and engineers back then were offered tens, hundreds of thousands of dollars of stock as part of their compensation. As a result Google could afford to be very selective, only picking the very best off the very best schools, and the interviews were known to be brutally difficult with trick questions and brain teasers. The Google interview is arguably less brutal than it was at some time but the process is still highly selective as they get millions of applications a year. Life as a Googler was also given a special treatment in pop culture, with extravagant perks communicated to the outside world, movies like the Internship, etc. Finally, when you interview for Google chances are your interviewers are going to be very accomplished people. Several of my interviewers had their Wikipedia page - same when I interviewed at Facebook, but unlike any other tech companies I interviewed at. All of this compounds to make this a very special moment.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What methods can be used to test code quality? Why is it important to write clean and efficient code?
Answer: It’s generally not possible to have an automated, pre-commit check that guarantees that new code is of high quality before it’s being merged to a code base. It’s possible though to have a number of such checks even earlier as developers type in their code - you can come up with rules that code have to comply to and have the IDE exercise these rules through automated linting - but while this guarantees that some problems won’t occur, it is not enough to guarantee that the code is good. However, it’s possible to evaluate the health of a code base, but not in a timely fashion. For instance, one can count all outages that relate to a specific part of the code, the testing coverage and whether tests were able to catch bugs as expected, performance issues (speed), resources cost (RAM/CPU usage), etc. On top of that engineers can also look at a codebase and highlight issues like poor interfaces, subpar architecture etc. Could this be done automatically at the time of commit through AI, possibly in the future but this is also the kind of task where AI is not great. You would really want a strong guarantee - if this code commit going to move things in the right or the wrong direction, and it’s really tricky to avoid false positives / false negatives here. Besides, for most codebases, the problem is not going to be, how to make sure that every new code change is going to be “healthy” but, knowing that I have a number of issues in my codebase, what can be done to address that and what changes would have a positive ROI.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you explain the purpose of the math.floor() method in JavaScript for different data types such as objects, arrays, strings, etc.?
Answer: Math.floor, like most of the other methods of the Math object, takes a number as argument and returns a number. In practice, Math.floor(x) will try to convert x to number before returning anything. This is not explicitly covered by the specifications. This is similar to doing Math.floor(Number(x)) first, with a couple of exceptions, for instance Math.floor(BigInt(123)) will throw an error but Math.floor(Number(BigInt(123))) will not. This is a pretty convoluted example as BigInt are integers so floor is not super useful. I would not consider this good practice to rely on this implicit conversion. Either you should be sure that the argument to Math.floor is a number, or you should convert that argument to a number first.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you determine which part of your application is not covered by unit tests and what steps can you take to address this issue?
Answer: The way you do that is by writing a testing strategy and a testing plan. The general idea is that you need to define what does “working as intended” means. The ultimate goal is to guarantee that your application will work as intended. Concretely, this can be done by listing user journeys. This is where product and engineering responsibilities touch. But a product manager should be able to determine a concrete list of things that users should be able to do with the application. Ideally, this list can also be ranked with priorities. The next step is to determine how each user journey can be tested. The goal here is to have a set of tests which, if they all pass, indicate that the user journey is covered, and if there’s an issue on any of the tests, then there is a problem in the feature code that needs to be fixed. Once you have that, you still need to figure out a way to collect the results of the tests and to compute what’s the percentage of your user journeys which are covered, and based on that, whether the application is working as intended.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does forgetting some commands or codes as a software engineer make you less smart? E.g to always turn to Google or ChatGPT when you can't remember them.
Answer: let’s say for the sake of discussion that a “smart engineer” is one that can write high quality code in a short amount of time. There’s obviously more to it. so let’s turn to fictional engineers Alice and Bob. They both have an assignment where they have to write code to fix a specific problem. Let’s say that Alice forms an idea of how she wants to do it, then writes code in her language of expertise, checks if the code is correct, may find a couple of ways the code can be improved, and when it’s good enough she sends it for review. And let’s say that Bob’s mental model is to ask google or chatGPT how to do this. Then copy whatever code they find, see that it doesn’t exactly do what they wanted, then search/ask again why there is a discrepancy, edit the code, and so on and so forth until this is close enough from the desired result. Alice is going to be much, much faster than Bob. It’s totally fine to look up the syntax of commands or to ask an LLM to synthesize very boring code for a highly specialized task. The problem is overrelying on this as a way to solve all problems.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do I need to learn JavaScript graphics as a front-end developer?
Answer: No. In general you don’t need to learn anything besides fundamentally how interfaces and browsers work. I’ve been a front-end developer for many years, and I’ve seen many resumes. You may be surprised the number of entry-level resumes with people claiming that they “master” x, y and z technologies. On one hand I get it, this is how you get found by bots. But on the other, just because you used such or such technology at a time T doesn’t mean you’re going to be as good at it at time T+1 let alone at time T+n. Really the only thing that people are going to be competent with are things they have used in the last few months, with a specific objective, having their code peer reviewed. The rest doesn’t matter. Nobody is going to hire someone on their ability to draw a circle in canvas without looking it up. Beyond that there’s a world of very specialized knowledge when it comes to web graphics, that a tiny fraction of web developers know and that very low percentage of all developers use on a regular basis. If this is something that interests you, by all means knock yourself out, there is demand for such specialists. But this is not a prerequisite to work in front-end.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible to be a successful frontend web designer/developer without any knowledge of coding languages such as HTML, CSS, and Javascript?
Answer: Is it possible to be a successful surgeon if the only medical training you got is from playing operation? Is it possible to be a professional athlete if you haven’t played sport since going down the slide in kindergarten? Is it possible to fly a commercial plane by looking at “the handbook” 30 minutes before takeoff? let’s be serious for 2 seconds.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How difficult is it for senior software engineers to get an interview at Google?
Answer: Google’s “senior software engineer” / L5 is probably in the upper range of what’s understood by “senior software engineer” in terms of work experience. It is quite an achievement to be promoted to that level, and that’s something that happens usually between 5 to 8 years after being hired. By the way, there are people who elect to never go for that level and stay 15 years at L4. There are a lot of places in tech where you can become “senior software engineer” after 2 or 3 years of experience. It’s really up to any organization to determine where to draw the line between junior and senior and what level of experience represents the pivot. The TL;DR is that in order to be invited to interview as a senior engineer, a candidate must have experience comparable to what a “homegrown” senior engineer at Google would have.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why is bonjour said as "bonjooor" instead of just "Bonjour"?
Answer: the [u] sound (the “ou” part of bonjour) doesn’t have a direct equivalent in most pronunciations of English (Wikipedia describes the “oo” sound of “boot” as “typically more front than cardinal [u].“). As a result English speakers have a hard time to “nail” the end of bonjour and let it drag a little bit longer (and slide towards a [w] sound). Add to it that the final r, which doesn’t exist in English, is also really difficult for native English speakers.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How important are algorithms and data structures in the interview process? Will not knowing them be looked down upon?
Answer: it may come as a shock, but if you go through an interview on data structures and algorithms, with an interviewer who is a professional engineer, who passed that test themselves and who is tasked to evaluate you on data structures and algorithms, and you don’t know the first thing about data structures and algorithms, then you will fail the interview. It’s like trying to get your drivers license without knowing how to drive. Many have tried. Still doesn’t work.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can you describe the interview process at Google and provide tips for preparing, particularly for those without a background in algorithms or data structures?
Answer: If you don’t have a background in algorithms or data structures, and don’t interview for a coding role, then you have nothing to worry about. If you do interview for a coding role, then my tip is: decline to interview. You’re losing your time, you’re wasting your interviewers and recruiter’s time, you will not get the job. And that’s ok. A Google (/big tech, meta, amazon, microsoft etc. ) role as a software engineer is not the only fulfilling job where you get to write code, nor is it the best paid. But Google (and again big tech) notoriously expects their engineers to be good at computer science, and they don’t owe a role to candidates who are not. There are tons of resources to learn computer science on your own, but the time to do that is not between the moment you get an opportunity to interview and the interview proper. “but algorithms and data structures have nothing to do with the role”. let me dispel that notion. At Google, engineers (including entry level) spend a good portion of their time reading and commenting working papers. They also have to wrap their head around why things are implemented a certain way, why libraries work like this or like that, etc. All of this requires formal CS knowledge. This is not true all across tech, there are lots of places where engineers mostly implement and have to do very little research. But Google is different.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is learning Git necessary for any beginner programmers who want to work in web development?
Answer: I don’t think so, it is arguably the most common source control tool today but there are lots of organizations that do not use it. Also, it’s technically possible to do web development without source control. Understanding how source control work is certainly useful, but for instance it can be argued that understanding databases and/or SQL is also useful given how ubiquitous databases are in software development, and yet I wouldn’t say that it is necessary to become a web developer. Same goes for git.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can anyone with no experience get hired by Google (as an engineer) if they impress the interviewers enough?
Answer: No professional experience with a software engineer title but the equivalent skillset and a resume that would get them an interview: possibly, no experience writing code: absolutely 0 chance. The entry-level applicants are competing with graduates from top CS programs around the world, many of which have already gotten an internship at Google.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can an HR ask why you left your last job during the interview process? If yes, what is a proper response to this question?
Answer: Yes. An interviewer can ask you that. This is not a question that is going to lead to discrimination. Whether they should ask this question is a different matter, as the answer is probably not going to be useful for their decision to hire or not. The mental model of interviewers who think this question is useful (of which there are many) is that this helps raise a “red flag” which otherwise would have gone undetected, for instance, a candidate can volunteer that they have done something really reprehensible in their last job and you would dodge a bullet by not hiring the...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is your opinion on the Bay Area's ability to keep its tech workers now that they can work remotely permanently?
Answer: The problem is different in San Francisco and in the rest of the Bay Area. Looking at the Bay Area (minus San Francisco), I don’t think the situation is that bad. First, tech employees haven’t exactly conquered the right to work from home indefinitely. Most (though notoriously not all) tech cos are bringing people back to the office. The power dynamics are a bit different too compared to pre-pandemic. In 2019 or even in 2021, anyone could walk out of Google and get a better job elsewhere. Now, with wave after wave of layoffs, employees don’t exactly have the upper hand and can’t dictate their terms. Many employers that offer remote work will adjust compensation. This means that for the highest paid employees, from a purely monetary point of view it is more interesting to work in a high cost of living area with a full comp than take a 20 or 25% discount on compensation, which represents more money than what they’d save on cheaper cost of life. From a non-monetary point of view the region has a lot to offer, weather, healthcare, well-connected airport, dynamic job market. At the end of the day, Apple, Google and Meta are not going to leave the region (mostly because they don’t want to) and that represents not just hundreds of thousands of high-paid workers but cores of a larger ecosystem. However the situation in San Francisco is a bit different. The City expected everyone (tech and non-tech) to diligently return working downtown in 2021. That hasn’t materialized, plus the generalization of the hybrid week (ie employees working 2+ days a week at home) makes downtown much emptier than it used to be, which makes it less attractive for businesses that cater to these professionals, many of which have closed shop, which makes this less attractive for people to come work downtown, etc. Additionally, SalesForce who used to be the biggest tech e...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do people want to work at Microsoft, Facebook, and Google so badly?
Answer: According to Comparably, the median annual salary at Microsoft is $162,818 per year. The median salary at Meta is $149,718. The median salary at Google is $135,386. (Those figures are for all employees, not just software engineers. Median means, a value such as 50% of employees make more and 50% make less. It is a better representation of a “typical” salary than an average, because averages tend to be skewed up by people having very high compensations. There are definitely employees making 7 figures at these companies, and not only in top leadership). According to the BLS, the median salary in the US was $54,132 in 2022. It’s not just about the money, but the money already explains a lot.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you think that interviewers should ask what a person's biggest weakness is, or should they ask something else like "what makes you tick"?
Answer: Let’s say that you have 45 minutes (or 30, or an hour - a limited amount of time) to decide whether you want to recommend that your company hire a candidate, or not hire this candidate. You have two approaches. One is to say, I’m a good judge of character, I can instantly tell if somebody can be a star even though they don’t have much of a track record, and I can also tell phonies that may have a stellar resume but which won’t deliver. The other approach is to rely on facts. You would gather evidence that the candidate will do well or will not do well. The amount of time (again: fixed, limited) makes this difficult, because you must bet the value on years of possible contributions on a couple of hours of probing. But there can be a method: you have a role definition, there’s probably performance evaluations and somewhere your company documents the attributes of a good professional for that role, and you can come up with questions that give you a sense of how good the candidate will be according to these attributes. It’s hard to defend the first approach. Many people still think like that, and many companies get away with this. It’s just not rational. Don’t you want to make the best hiring decisions? Don’t you want to be able to say that you’re confident you hired predictably good candidates, versus than followed your hunch? So closing this parenthesis. If you believe in fact-based hiring, neither quest...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How would you tell an interviewer that you can't answer a question? For instance, a hypothetical situation where the answer would depend on too many variables and you need more information that they refuse to provide?
Answer: I’ve only ever refused to answer an interview question with an hypothetical once, because I found it completely inappropriate. Other than that, I guess it’s part of the exercise to see the candidate make assumptions and trade offs. for the record, the question was, if my son were abducted and I had to come up with $30k overnight without asking friends or families for a direct handout, how would I do it. I refused to operate under the assumption that my children would be victims of a crime. My interviewer insisted, I asked whether they had children (since we already had crossed the red line), they did not. I really was that close to tell them to F off and get up and leave, which I should probably have done in retrospect since I knew right then I would not work there.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do people who have worked at Google and Facebook regret leaving their former employer (or vice versa)?
Answer: I worked at both Facebook and Google. If you ask me, rationally, whether I miss working at Facebook or Google my answer is a definite no. I don’t miss the perks, which I once enjoyed. I don’t miss early access to the products. I don’t miss feeling in “team Facebook” or “team Google” when either of these companies were having a bad PR moment. I definitely do not miss the work. I have no shares of either companies. At a micro level I do miss the people, as the people who end up in these companies have had a very interesting journey and I also miss the camaraderie. But over the past 10 years, I sometimes dreamt of being back on the facebook bus (which was not the most fun part) or back on either campus. I guess there’s always going to be a tiny part of me that’s going to always be jckr@google.com or jckr@facebook.com. At the same time, I’m well aware that the organizations i worked for are gone forever. I joined Facebook when it had just a couple of thousand employees, and Google when it was still pre-pandemic with people coming 5 days a week to a busting campus. Unless someone invents a time machine, there’s no way to ever experience that again.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is your opinion on not having any questions to ask an interviewer after the interview is over?
Answer: it’s the candidate’s privilege, but it’s a lost opportunity. If extended an offer, the candidate is asked to make a life-changing decision, and that’s the best time to get the most unbiased information to support that decision one way or another.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If you are rejected by Google, Apple or Facebook, is there any point in interviewing with them again?
Answer: When I was at Google and interviewing candidates, we could see all of their previous applications and all the questions they were asked. It was very frequent for candidates to have applied previously. I can’t give a percentage because even though I did a ton of interviews, it was still a tiny sample. So let’s just say it was relatively common. Same for when I was at Facebook. It’s definitely easier the 2nd time. It’s not for everyone, but to some people, this will be a great opportunity, so there’s no less reason to interview the 2nd time than the first.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does Google use any programming language other than Java and Python?
Answer: does google have iOS apps? can an iOS app be written using only Java and/or Python? does google have open source projects not written in Java and/or Python?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason that tech companies are so desperate for software engineers yet they make them take whiteboard coding interviews?
Answer: I don’t think the premise is true. 10–15 years ago, Facebook, Google and Amazon couldn’t get the features they needed out the door soon enough, and they invented the modern tech hiring pipeline - professionals in technical roles are showered with perks and paid “market rates” but at the same time the interview is highly selective. Many many tech companies copied that playbook. In 2023, the consensus is - maybe they overhired and maybe there is no short term return on investment on every single hire. Maybe big tech companies could do just fine with 20%, 30%, 50% less headcount. But even then. Let’s go back in time 5 years. The point was never to make it easy for anyone to get a software engineering job and make 200k+ per year. Specifically, interviews were never optimized such that people who can’t pass a whiteboarding test would have an easier time getting a job.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the best way to convince your boss that you need time to write automated tests (unit/acceptance) before starting on new features or bug fixes?
Answer: you shouldn’t ever be in a situation where you need to convince your boss to take time to write tests. If your organization shipped features which are poorly tested, this is what it is. There are going to be incidents and outages which are going to take a tax on the engineering productivity. After the feature code is written though is not the right time to consider writing tests. A testing strategy should be written at the time the feature is designed. The point of the testing strategy is not to catch bugs after the feature code is shipped, but mostly to help developers work faster as they write code (along with testing the code they wrtie) knowing that each time somebody commits code, they do not break the system. As an added benefit, once the code is shipped, it has decent code coverage and is less likely to have outages. Once code is implemented/shipped, advocating to refactor the code to improve engineering metrics, reduce tech debt etc. is very unconvincing. If I were “the boss” I would be displeased that resources that could be allocated to creating value are wasted on scratching the “best practices” itch. The best practices including testing are not an end in itself, they are an investment that if done right is expected to yield a return. Another thing to keep in mind is that code naturally deprecates. A lot of code is just going to be replaced organically within one or two years. So putting resources in writing tests after the fact is usually the wrong call. There are times when it does make sense to refactor or to add a layer of tests but only with an ulterior motive in mind. Doing this for the sake of refactoring/for the sake of there being tests is just not a great use of resources.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How many lines of code should be in a pull request/code review?
Answer: Everything else being equal, larger PRs are harder to review, however, there are some very simple changes that can only be committed through a very large PR. So a maximum number of lines of code changed is not a good heuristic.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If Taylor Swift joined Quora, what topics would she follow other than "Dating and Relationships?"
Answer: When I first started using Quora, I was amazed that the service could connect people asking vague questions with the undisputed expert on the topic. For instance, somebody would ask a question on something only insiders of a company would know, and it would be none other than the CEO of that company that would answer. I don’t think Taylor Swift is the undisputed expert on dating and relationships. She certainly has her view on this topic but she expresses it with the caveat that it’s highly personal and subjective. Also, her audience seems to prefer to hear her stance on the topic in music form, preferably live or with videos, over miniature essays. That said, I can think of a number of topics on which she has superlative expertise, that is, no one can contest she’s the most accomplished in the world or among a small group of the very best people in the world. The music industry. Pop culture. Songwriting. Mainstream influence. Image management. Personal branding. Community building. The actual day-to-day of an A list celebrity. Career and personal growth. Entrepreneurship. Negotiation/deal making. Doing business as a young woman. Really the list goes on and on.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: As a senior developer what do you wish you knew as a junior dev?
Answer: There’s a huge difference between impact and effort. Around the time I started my professional life, which is before I was a software engineer, the phrase “exceeds expectations” started to become a gimmick, as in: “we at company xyz strive to not just meet but always exceed expectations”. I notice that there is a trend among well-meaning junior tech professionals to focus on the “exceed” part, as in: I know I’m supposed to do X, but if I do Y which I think is good and no one asked me to do, everyone will see me as the superstar I am. The problem is that as an individual and especially in a junior position, it’s very difficult to come up with a good way to evaluate the value of your work. So you can easily end up in a situation where you spend countless hours on something you think is important but which no one really cares about, and because your time is limited, you get less time to spend on something you can perceive as boring but which yields tangible benefits. This leads to a frustrating situation where you work a lot and assume that you are doing very well, when in fact your contribution is not valued. I have found myself in that situation several times even after I thought I understood what “impact” is. We tend to post-rationalize what we want to work on. This problem is exciting, therefore people will appriciate my work. The problem is large, therefore it’s important. The problem is something I’m good at, therefore it’s valuable to solve. But all of these are fallacies. On top of that, individuals run the risk of doubling down and persisting on a dead end, and further drifting away from what would make a good performance. There’s 2 solutions for that. First, devs should balance their curiosity with their time. If you have an assignment: do the assignment, but if they have free time and not a very obviously valuable way to leverage that time, then they can do some research and exploration. Not the other way around. Second, they should lean on their organization to figure out if they’re on the right track and never on their own intuition.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Did Google ever use TDD (test driven development)?
Answer: At Google, some developers are devout followers of TDD, but there is no company-wide mandate to use it. Parts of the code base have to adhere to certain rules, so owners of a project can enforce some checks that all changelists (the Google equivalent of a pull request) for that project must comply with. As a result, in general, Google code has great unit test coverage but there is no distinction between a changelist when tests have been written before the feature code, and one where feature code has been written before the tests.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How does it feel to get rejected from Google after passing all of their interviews, including the final one with a hiring manager?
Answer: Early in my tech career I interviewed at a company that I really wanted to work at. I had some experience at Facebook where I was some kind of jack of all trades, my role was somewhat in between designer, engineer and data scientist but I wasn’t really either of these things. When I interviewed for that company, I actually never knew the actual role I was interviewing for. I was also completely unprepared, how could I not be. In retrospect, there was no way this could have worked, and yet I was highly confident and thought I had done great. Of course I didn’t get the job and that hit me really really hard. Since that interview, I have done about a dozen interviews - I got some offers, and also got rejected some times. But now that I understand the tech interview exercise much better, well, I can’t say it ever feels great to be rejected but it never upset me as much as it did then. But being unprepared (and btw, most of my candidates as an interviewer came out as unprepared) meant I was a very poor judge of my performance and that my expectations were way off, which set me up for a huge disappointment.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How common is it to get rejected by Facebook during the interview process for a software engineer position?
Answer: I haven’t interviewed for Facebook (or I guess, Meta) in a really long time so this is not backed by actual data, but I would say a ballpark figure would be 90% of the time. When I worked at Facebook, for 250 candidates that were considered in our group, we would extend an offer to 1. These were different times and I was in product design, so not directly applicable. Virtually all candidates were referred or scouted by a Facebook product designer, and there were several steps before an actual interview and offer, the face to face interview being the last one. The 90% figure comes from my more recent experience at Google where I worked for 3 years and interviewed about 120 engineers. We received the outcome of the interviews and on that sample, the success rate was around 10%. Those numbers are highly dependent on circumstances and are pretty meaningless in absolute. The fact that somebody unprepared is invited to interview and doesn’t get an offer has no bearing on the chances of someone for a totally different role in a totally different team at a totally different level. From the point of view of a candidate, these numbers shouldn’t mean: if I reach the last stage of the hiring process, I have 10% chances of getting an offer. Really the only thing that can be inferred for that candidate is that they now have a shot at getting an offer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Aren’t the unit tests written after the fact usually not as effective as unit tests created via the TDD process?
Answer: This depends on what you call after the fact. IMO, writing a unit test before writing feature code or immediately after is largely equivalent. That means that the same person is going to describe their intent in feature code and in test. TDD makes a lot of sense on paper, but is also pretty ideological, and I personally don’t think that it’s required to adhere to TDD tenets to have a well-tested, safe code base. Writing tests years after the feature code has been written, however, is not as useful. The best the test author c...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the purpose of writing unit tests for private functions?
Answer: There are two opposite forces at play. One school of thought considers that you need to test interfaces not internals or implementations. The idea here is that other components, or end users, will only ever interact with the public interface of a class/component - by definition. Therefore, we should only guarantee that these function as expected. The public interfaces (methods, functions etc.) will in turn call all the private code that they need, so this private code will be exercised. As for the private code which is not needed by a public interface, and the branches never travelled - that should be removed. With that in mind it makes sense to advocate against even attempting to test internal methods. These internal tests will try to verify that the sausage is made in a very specific way, which doesn’t matter, as the only thing which does is whether we get the same sausage. Such tests would be brittle - changes which should be acceptable would make them fail, causing overwork - and not verify ultimately that the component works as intended. But a somewhat conflicting tenet is to shift left, that is: have tests so that they can detect problems as early as possible. That means, privileging smaller, atomic unit tests which are very fast and very cheap. So the question becomes, when do private methods are internal implementation details (which should not be tested, and should be “swept under the rug”) and when are they a key part of the business logic, and really should be tested. consider this pseudo code: assuming that _a, _b and _c are private methods and getResult is a public one. I would argue that it would be more useful to test _a, _b and _c (possibly by refactoring them as standalone functions, that the class can call) than to just test getResult, because one step logically follows another and having smaller-scoped tests would help us isolate the problematic code in case of bug. But this determination cannot always been made. My views on this is that there is no one size fits all answer. The view that whatever logic is behind private functions should never be tested is wrong, as is the one that nothing should be private and everything should be exposed and tested.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If the Petty family sues Lara Trump for covering "I Won't Back Down," do you think they have a strong case?
Answer: They may sue, but they’ve also already lost. Lara Trump has been able to perform, record and broadcast the song, the song has already “reached the charts” - probably using the same techniques as other right-wing influencers this year - and this moment has already been commented. The Petty estate may get damages, they may get an injunction to stop Mrs Trump...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does Google ask programmers to write code on paper during interviews instead of doing it on their computer systems? If so, why?
Answer: I haven’t done interviews for Google in a while now, but the start of Covid marked the end of the onsite interview as a norm. There was a short transitional period when interviews where carried over Google docs but soon enough Google had their own interview platform, which is a low-feature code editor that has some syntax highlighting, but no code autocomplete and significantly, doesn’t run code. So on one hand, there hasn’t been paper or white boards in a while. My understanding is that in person interviewing resumed but is more the exception than the rule. As someone who went to the office every day and interviewed twice a week I was never once asked to interview in person in the ~8 months I spent at Google after RTO. On the other, Google definitely doesn’t use HackerRank or equivalent, which is the norm anywhere else. This year, I have done a few interviews as a candidate, and everyone was either using hackerrank or asking me to code on my laptop (which was also “the norm” pre-pandemic, but not at google). Why is that, well - the goal of a coding interview is to determine if a candidate has the skillset. A live coding environment is optimized to check if code runs. A candidate’s own environment can also come with a lot of bells and whistles (like AI assisted coding) that may get them to a result quicker but doesn’t help determine if they think like a software engineer. 2 candidates can write a very similar piece of code, using a similar logic but one could contain an unfortunate typo and not run. The question is, do we consider that these two interview performances are similar, or that one is very superior to the other? Google is in the first group.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it beneficial to add projects on GitHub when applying for your first job as a software/web developer?
Answer: To take a couple of steps back, the goal of a software engineering interview is to determine if a candidate has the skillset to be a productive software engineer. This determination is usually done in two steps: first, a sourcer will identify potential candidates, and then, these candidates can enter the recruiting pipeline and go through interviews proper. A lot of discussion about tech recruiting focuses on the 2nd phase - how to be “good” at interviews - but the real difficulty is the first one and it’s something candidates have less control about. In order to be considered by sourcers, a candidate must demonstrate that they probably have the skillset. If the next Alan Turing has always worked by themselves and has no public presence and doesn’t have any artefacts that can show how great they are at computer science and/or building software, they would not make the cut no matter how good they are. This is kind of a catch 22 situation because you need experience to get a job and you need a job to get experience. That’s where degrees and internships help. It’s easier to get an internship (especially when studying at a reputable university which has established relationships with businesses) than a first job and they are as good as employment when it comes to demonstrate skillset. Same goes for degrees. But, how do you get in when you have no degree, no relevant experience, etc. Personal projects and personal brands help, with the caveat that this candidate competes for entry level jobs with people who have CS degrees, have done internships etc. So yes these are helpful but in the grand scheme of things, a personal project (esp. one that didn’t get traction) is a rounding error compared to work experience. Personal projects are better than nothing but using the same amount of time to work on issues on open-source projects is a better use of one’s time.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can we contact our interviewer at Google interviews directly and ask him/her about our status (after the interview)?
Answer: You can try, but your interviewers are told not to respond to limit legal exposure, and most significantly: they don’t know. They don’t participate to the hiring discussion beyond writing a report on their own interview. They don’t have access to other interviewer’s feedback until the decision is announced, at which point the recruiter knows and tries to tell the candidate asap.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you respond to an interview question about how you would handle working with a senior developer who doesn't like to explain things?
Answer: Let’s make this question a little bit more generic. A candidate has to explain how they have worked / would work with someone their senior, who doesn’t do what they’re supposed to. This is a delicate inter-personal situation because the candidate can’t just demand that the other person change their ways. There are a number of ways to approach that. Direct feedback can work. It’s the simplest way and is worth trying first (unless there’s a strong reason to think it will not work). Describe the situation, tell the person how that makes you feel, what are the consequences and propose a solution. In our case: something like: “Hey, last week, you asked me to work on task 123. I asked you questions and you said you would get back to me but you never did. I’ve just been here 3 months and I felt a bit overwhelmed, but I tried. I spent three days reading the codebase in order to form an idea of what to do, and when I wrote my code change, when you reviewed it you pointed out in 5 minutes all I had done wrong. From there I was able to come up with a better change within an hour, but if you had taken these 5 minutes for me at the beginning of the week, I could have accomplished so much more.” This rests on the assumption that most people in an organization have the shared goal of having everything work better. However this doesn’t always work, and more often than not the person experiencing that issue is going to have to use a third party - either peers (the 2nd or 3rd time the senior person hears the feedback may have more impact), a peer to the senior person, or the manager. The person that feels that their senior is not collaborating the way they want can also figure out tactics to not “trigger” the undesirable behavior. That’s managing up. For instance, ask the questions in public in an open chat channel or by mail with people on copy.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do I deal with a senior developer who expects the junior developer to not ask stupid questions, which for the junior would be not that stupid?
Answer: As a software engineer advances in seniority, the expectations on their roles and responsibilities change. It’s generally easy for engineers of all levels to keep up with the technical aspects of what’s expected of them. But the non-technical aspect is not trivial. Those are skills which are difficult to acquire - no one is born overnight a senior software engineer. It’s also difficult for a “new” senior software engineer to internalize that they are going to be evaluated not just on their code. Helping others is a key part of this new set of expectations. Ideally helping others is a very good way to use your time as an engineer - something you know well takes you little time to explain but can help someone else save considerable amounts of time. Experienced engineers seek opportunities to help others - they may not necessarily go out of their way and try to spend as much time not doing their main project but instead helping others, but they will more often than not seize that opportunity if that’s immediately available to them. When an engineer that has the opportunity to help someone else learn or grow forfeits it, this is good feedback for them. They may not be open to feedback from someone junior if they consider their questions stupid, but that junior engineer can talk about it to their manager, a peer of the senior engineer etc. Senior engineers must understand that this is a part of their job and responsibility and also an occasion to demonstrate they do well.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do Facebook software engineers get paid less than software engineers at other companies like Microsoft, Amazon and Google? If so, why is this the case?
Answer: This is highly dependent on how the stock is doing. That’s the stock of these companies over the last 5 years. Let’s suppose that you get a job offer with either of them in 2018. They offer you 200k a year and 1m in stock over 4 years. Actually let’s pretend the stock vests over 5 years to make this chart more relevant. Let’s also pretend you never get raises or bonuses or equity refresh just to make our maths simpler and that you never sell your stock until it vests in full. So 5 years later: With Google, you’ll have received 3,194,700 over 5 years. (5 * 200000 + 1m * (1 + 119.47%)) With Amazon: 2,256,900. With Microsoft: 3,729,800. With Meta: 2,805,100. So there’s a difference of 65% between Microsoft and Amazon. Candidates have 0 clue how the stock of their companies will evolve over the next 5 years. To make things more complicated, they grow at a different pace. There are definitely been periods where each of these companies offered the highest compensation. Over the past year, Meta stock has been growing much faster than any of the other 3 (which you can see at the end of the graph).

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How difficult is it to obtain an entry-level software engineering position at Facebook?
Answer: The typical compensation for a new grad software engineer at Meta is about $250k per year. Compare this to the typical compensation for a new grad in the US which is below $60k, or the average compensation for a software engineer (all levels of experience combined) which is around $120k. in other words: for a typical software engineer, an entry-level software engineer job at Meta will pay 2x more. For a typical new grad, it will pay 4x+ more. So it’s difficult and selective, as it’s difficult to get paid multiple of what you’re making overnight.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If you had the choice between being given 100,000 dollars today or 2 million dollars in one year, what would be the better choice?
Answer: To answer a slightly different question: if I had a choice between having 100,000 dollars right now and 2 million dollars in a year, I would very confidently choose 100,000 dollars right now. Let me rephrase the question. If I’m offered an investment opportunity that offers a 19x return in a year with no additional information, this is a hard pass. I have every reason to believe there will never be a 2 million dollars payout.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What does a programmer actually have to do at his/her job? What is the day-to-day work of a programmer like? Does a programmer just sit down and type away on code all day long, or is there more to it than that?
Answer: Software engineers who work in an organization do not write code all day long. The key difference between writing code as an independent developer or as a side project, and within an organization, is that your code is going to be reviewed. This has very significant implications on how you spend their time. First, this means that in addition to writing code, you need to spend time reviewing other people’s code. This is not as easy as looking for typos. Now, let’s go back to you writing code. In order for your code to be committed to the code base, it need to be reviewed and approved. So how do you do that? You’re going to describe your changes, why you do them and what they do. That’s typically not enough for somebody to feel confident that bringing this change on board is the right thing to do. So, your code change is probably going to be linked to an “issue” or a “ticket” or a “bug” or any unit of work, that’s been decided by another group that this is something that needs to be done. As an engineer, you get to decide and influence what you work on, so you will also spend your time planning your work and breaking your workload into manageable chunks, and making sure these chunks are traceable. This is usually done in recurrent meetings. Then, you have other meetings with your team to make sure things are moving along and that no one is stuck. You have more recurrent meetings without going too much into detail. There is some aspect of research that goes into your work - after all, it’s not called computer science for no reason. Given a problem, how to solve it? what are the steps? A lot of this is driven through documents. You write documents, read other people’s documents, comment, respond to comments, have meeting to talk about documents, etc. You also spend time speaking with people from other teams. Many engineers are able to focus solely on an assignment and can pretend that the world outside their project doesn’t exist. That luxury is lost to more senior engineers who need to figure out how to connect the dots and how their work will serve the need of other teams. Some engineers also participate in user research or design review and work with people outside of engineering, including clients. The more senior you get, the more you are detached from day to day coding. In my previous job at Google I didn’t write code most days, but I spent most of my days reading and writing documents and a few hours in meetings. In my current job I code about 10 hours per week by choice.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the working hours for a software engineer at Google/Facebook/Microsoft? Are you required to stay back late at night if there are any urgent work requests from your manager?
Answer: I worked at Facebook and Google. My days in big tech are over so I’ll probably never know what it is at Microsoft. At Facebook, working long hours was not frowned upon. But I was there at the time when the company was still pretty small and individuals had a very large responsibility. Nobody is going to make you stay late and the manager is not bossing you around, but instead you understand that there are certain expectations for somebody of your caliber and the financial incentive for meeting and exceeding these expectations is a lot. On a typical year, my annual “bonus” was more than what I would make in a year before I worked in tech, on top of a salary that was already multiple of that. And you also know that if you are one of the chosen few with stellar performance, the reward can be life changing. One of my buddy got a discretionary award worth several million dollars. Conversely you know that if you’re not delivering you can be cast away from heaven, and bye bye cold pressed juices in the morning, bye bye ice cream parlor, bye bye heavily discounted personal trainers, bye bye free laundry and dry cleaning. (And bye bye, potentially earning millions of dollars). When I was at Facebook, I worked a lot, often taking the first shuttle leaving at 6am and taking the last one back leaving at 10pm. Then again, I had 3 (free) good meals, my gym etc. Conversely, by the time I was at Google it was a very large company (well over 100k employees). The typical age was much older than anywhere I’ve been in tech, people had families, lived far from the office. I was given the impression that the company cared a lot about work life balance and they would rather go slow and by the book to develop products than at break-necking speeds. When the pandemic started, staff was encouraged to “prioritize self-care” and was given extra days off. There was of course a course correction when people didn’t go back to the office as diligently as they could have. By the time I left google I was definitely working a lot of hours, but this was by choice.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you end an engineering / computer science interview with a candidate who is not performing well, but also has not failed outright?
Answer: There are two possible scenarios here. One, the most likely, is that the candidate hasn’t come up with a good solution in the allocated amount of time. Two, the candidate has a solution which they feel happy about but which actually doesn’t work. But let’s imagine the opposite scenario. The candidate has actually done a good job. Maybe the problem is so hard that getting things mostly done is good enough. So, if a candidate doesn’t finish an exercise, this doesn’t mean that they failed the interview (especially if they’ve just done “not amazing”). If the candidate feels that they bombed the interview, this really affects their morale and this can impact their other interviews. This happened to me many times as an interviewer to have a candidate seriously underperform at the end of their cycle, because they perceived that they’ve already blew it. This is a problem because it prevents us from evaluating them objectively. So I try to make my candidates end on a win. I try to help them find a natural stopping point. There is some tension here because it’s important to end on time (as to let the following interview start on time, too, and because it’s unfair to give a candidate too much time). If my candidate has completely missed the interview, we would have switched modes earlier, and instead of continuing the exercise I would have walked them through the solution (this applies for coding or system design) But unless we are in that scenario, I would let them continue and end the interview such that the candidate can reasonably believe that they have either done well, or that if they haven’t, they haven’t failed bad enough to completely destroy their chances of passing (which is the truth). My main care is to avoid that their morale be broken.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If a program and its code from 2023 were sent back in time by 10, 20, and 30 years, during which of those times could a programmer still have a good chance of understanding how the program works?
Answer: I’ve experienced something close to that hypothetical. When I started at Google, I was very much a front-end programmer, mostly comfortable with JavaScript. My first assignment was in C++. Let’s just say the last time I worked with C++, I had to install a compiler with floppy disks. This was somewhere in the 90s. Now, JavaScript is one of many C-style languages. It uses code blocks with curly braces, loops, if statements, functions etc. as they all do. So that core part of the language is something that everyone who’s been working with computers in the last 50 years will get. Not a problem. I also feel that even though I hadn’t touched C or C++ in 20+ years, I could write a decent C program, especially if I can look up things online. maybe not with the best practices. I still remembered the syntax. And, I mean, I was hired by Google as a staff engineer. It’s a selective test. I’m a good developer. All right. So here I am trying to figure out, with my 20+ years old understanding of C, what the F is going on in Google’s codebase. And the answer is not a lot. So much of the syntax is very specific to C++ and to modern C++ (and then, there’s a layer which was specific to Google, and their own style guide, their own libraries etc.). C++ has changed a lot especially after C++ 11. The subtleties of writing things in a way which look almost identical to a developer looking for familiar features would be completely lost to someone who isn’t proficient in them. So I think this would be extremely difficult, especially before a time when valuable information started to be available on the web. There are certain concepts and certain innovations in our languages which would be extremely difficult to wrap one’s head around. Like, in 1993, most computer users spent the vast majority of their time on applications that were a stand-alone binary file on their computer (think Microsoft Word. woohoo, word 6.0 just came out!). The amount of abstraction needed to envision how a very simple consumer app works in 2023 is mind boggling: the simplest way is to literally serve it across the web, with one part of the code being executed by inside a web browser (!!!!), after being downloaded from a CDN on the Edge (!!!!!!!) and working in near real time in sync wit...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How useful is Cracking the Coding interview in preparing for a programming interview?
Answer: I still feel it is the most useful resource, bar none, for a coding test. While it touches on other aspects of the software engineering interview there are better resources to address other tests (ie Alex Xu books on the system design interview). To be very explicit, I am highly confident that a candidate that spends 100 hours reading the book and doing all the exercises, and spends 0 hours on leetcode or an equivalent platform, will be much better equipped to pass an interview than a candidate that spends 100 hours on an online platform and 0 reading the book.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the responsibilities and differences between a senior staff vs. a principal software engineer?
Answer: Those differences are fairly arbitrary and company specific. When I was at Google, L7 and L8 represented around 3% and 1% of engineer headcount respectively. L7 were senior staff engineers and senior managers, and L8 were principal engineers and directors. Companies can move that cursor any way they want, and decide where the cliff is. In my current company the staff, senior staff and principal represent 5%, 0.5% and 0.05% of all ICs. By the way, this doesn’t have to correspond to how managers are ranked and titled. I think there are 2 ways to look at senior staff vs staff / principal vs senior staff. One is: they are manifestly working on things which are one level of magnitude harder than what staff engineers / senior staff engineers are working on. By the way, identifying what one should be working on is a key part of the staff+ IC role. I said harder and not more impact intentionally. Working on low hanging fruits and unlocking lots of revenue is not how one is promoted, although that will translate into great performance evaluation, bonuses and other rewards. Difficulty of a problem is a key aspect there. Back to figuring out what should a staff+ IC work on: discovering what is the key problem an organization should tackle, when that’s not obvious to anyone, is a key part of the difficulty. At Google, principal engineers would be behind paradigm shifts that could affect an entire org. They could be like: hey, thousands of youses, instead of working like this, you should all be doing that, and drive a project that will make that seismic shift a reality. There’s a technical aspect to this (if you’re going to make thousands of people change the way they approach a problem you better be right) but there’s also a huge organizational challenge - you need to build alignment with other teams, with other organizations, which means interfacing with other super senior ICs, with execs, etc. But back to the difference between senior staff and principal, a senior staff would work on something obviously too big for one staff, an a principal would work on something obviously too big for one senior staff. A second way to look at this is organizationally. A principal engineer is usually paired with a director, not formally but typically the ratio of principal eng to director is around 1, so the principal does to an org what the director can’t and goes deep into problems rather than go wide or across. As such a principal is expected to know everything about the problem space of a ~100 people organization (at least that’s my experience). Using the same analogy, the senior staff is the peer of a senior manager, and is supposed to know beyond what’s just in front of them but don’t have to be familiar with every nook and cranny of a large organization.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you interview for software engineering positions when the candidate has no prior experience in the field?
Answer: How would I interview a candidate who has no industry experience, exactly like a candidate who does. They would get the same coding tests and the same behavioral interviews. A lot of the professional experience of a candidate can be used for these behavioral interviews regardless of their actual role. How would I prepare as a candidate had I no experience as a software engineer, well, how I’ve done it when I interviewed as a software engineer from another career. I prepared for the coding test until I felt I was ready. There’s ample material available, much more than when I made that career change. Candidates won’t get a pass just because they had a different job title before, but they also get a shot at it even though they don’t necessarily come from a software engineering background.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What do software engineers do who can't keep up in their field of software development as years pass by?
Answer: Let’s take this question and reverse and see what would happen if they don’t do anything and their performance degrades so much that they have to be let go. What next? If they need another software engineering job, they’re going to interview, and if so they need to prepare for interviewing. Preparing for interviewing means catching up with the state of the art. There’s more to it, but if somebody doesn’t have the skills, they are going to use that time for learning. For someone who had expertise in one domain, it is not going to take a huge amount of time to do that catch up exercise, especially if you have full control of your time. One month of learning full time is probably enough. A lot of folks just save themselves the pain by factoring some time for learning during the year. Even reading an article that gives a retrospective of all that happened during the year in such or such domain goes a long way. For people who can’t do that, it’s probably time to just hang up the gloves.
