Question: Why is software testing more difficult than other fields like web designing or development?
Answer: It is not more difficult, as all software engineering fields include testing. You do front-end development? Guess what, your job also includes testing your front-end.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why is there no feedback after an interview with Google, Facebook and other big companies?
Answer: The technical reason is because sharing feedback after rejecting a candidate exposes a company to legal risk. But really, the feedback from interviewers is completely useless whether a candidate passes or not. Treating feedback as useless may come as a shock in tech, where feedback from users, from from coworkers or even the general population is highly regarded. Because in these case, the people giving feedback have some interests that align with those of people receiving it. In the interview case, the interests of the candidate are completely orthogonal to that of the interviewers (by design). The interviewers don’t have skin in the game. When they write an evaluation, they’re not trying to help the candidate get better. Don’t think for one minute that having access to the evaluation would help the candidate do better at other interviews. When it comes to coding, for instance, there are many ways to evaluate an interview. One specific interviewer, for instance, can care a lot about whether a candidate writes error-free code even if this takes a bit longer. Another will be impressed by a candidate moving very fast, and able to spot their mistakes and fix them. Even within the same company, the very same performance will not be evaluated the same way by two different interviewers. I’ve received feedback from companies after being extended an offer or rejected because not everyone shares that policy and it’s been a complete waste of time.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: I am currently working as software engineer II. I had an interview with a reputed company and they offered me software engineer I position. So, does that mean my salary range will be less? Also, should I settle for less salary?
Answer: This really depends on how far your company, and the company you are interviewing for, are from the big tech market rate when it comes to specific titles. A junior engineer at Google in Mountain View or New York makes about 180k USD/year in total compensation. I know people with the title (and the skills) of a senior software engineer who make 50k USD or less. And that’s only short term. Let’s look at this over 10 years. Let’s assume somebody who will start as a software engineer I at a big tech company for 180k/y, which will be promoted 3 years later to software engineer II for 270k/y, then 3 years later to senior engineer for 350k/y. That’s 275k/y on average, or 2.75m over 10 years, and that’s without raises, without “accelerating” promotion by switching companies, etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the best way to switch careers into software engineering if you have no experience in it?
Answer: You don’t need work experience as a software engineer to become a software engineer. I’ve had many titles before I became one. However you absolutely need the skillset of a software engineer before you get the title of software engineer. There are many skills which are transferable from other professions like problem-solving, communications, people relations etc. Software engineers though are expected to have some domain knowledge in one or more specialties, a more global level of understanding of what’s going on when code runs, and be competent code developers. How much is expected of a prospective software engineer depends on their level, but even junior engineers are expected to be good developers. Anyone who wants to switch to a career in software engineer should first learn the skillset, and more specifically look for demonstrable ways that they have these skills. For instance it doesn’t matter that you know Swift or that you’ve made a to-do app which I can download and build from your github page. Have you made meaningful contributions to a useful open source project? Have you built an app that got some tractions? Those are visible ways that would show a developer, even though this candidate doesn’t have years of experience they have the skills we need.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you have any tips or tricks that helped you get through a Google interview? How did you pass your interviews with them (SWE)?
Answer: Yeah, prepare. I’ve been an interviewer more often than a candidate. Candidates fall into 3 buckets: In an ideal world, all candidates would be in the first bucket, alas most of my google candidates were in the 2nd with some in the 1st and some in the 3rd. If you are very underskilled for a role, there’s really nothing you can do. The system is designed to reject you. There’s no crash course that will make you likely to pass, and do not give money to anyone who pretends otherwise. You really need the experience expected for the role. If you feel you’ve adequately prepared, there’s nothing much you can do besides resting well, being present and engaged during the interview and hope that you “see” the problem quickly. If that helps, be assured that your interviewers would much rather pass you than fail you. But if you are in the larger group that has a lot of relevant experience and feel you can just wing it, consider spending a serious amount of time preparing. It’s just one of those situations. If you’re going to do a presentation in front of 500 people you do slides and rehearse. Yeah you may know what you’re talking about, but will it be better if you rehearse or not? If you’re going to run for a marathon, you run every week to build the capacity. Yeah you have run one 10 years ago, and you’re still in shape, but aren’t you maximizing your chances of finishing (and minimizing risks of injury) if you prep? If you have an exam coming up, you read the textbook, even though you paid attention in class. Etc, etc. Do yourself a service and prepare.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Google create a new framework called Angular instead of simply updating AngularJS?
Answer: Once the abstractions of React were known to the world, the cat was out of the bag. React has made a lot of choices, some of which were controversial and got a lot of pushback, but overall, React code was both much clearer to follow and much more concise than AngularJS code. So Angular took a leaf from React playbook but by so doing, also introduced a number of breaking changes. Even though React introduced itself as a “dissenter” and ran against established conventions by both AngularJS and other frameworks like Ember, Backbone etc. I’ve always seen Angular as a more opinionated framework with a clear best way (which I see as a good thing), while React, Vue, Svelte etc. are more “do whatever works”. With that in mind I feel breaking changes were to be expected in the Angular ecosystem. The goal is not to ensure continuity but to maintain a “well-lit path” to writing robust apps.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you prepare for an interview at a tech company when you have never worked in the tech industry before and don't know much about coding?
Answer: This is completely hypothetical. People don’t get invited to interview for a technical role in a tech company because they found a golden ticket in the packaging of their new laptop. Candidates reach the interview stage because they have been selected, and they are selected because they are expected to have the skillset. If you don’t have the skillset - this is a going to be a miserable moment for everyone involved. If you manage to pass, as the proverbial gaggle of monkeys that could theoretically type the works of Shakespeare on a typewriter, then every day is going to be very unpleasant. My advice for anyone who is in that situation is just to remove themselves from it.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: In spite of Ron DeSantis being an intelligent person, why is he coming over as a stumbling incompetent presidential candidate who is losing funding and support?
Answer: M. DeSantis’s strategy was twofold: to position himself as the best substitute to Trump if the latter wouldn’t or couldn’t run, and failing that: to come up as a better candidate than Trump to the conservative voters and ultimately in the general election. There was a time when there was a legitimate doubt on whether M. Trump would run or could run. As of today, M. Trump is definitely running and campaigning. His multiple indictments have not hurt his considerable lead in the Republican primary, and further, virtually all Republican candidates have pledged to support him if he were the nominee even if he were convicted. So it’s extremely unlikely that M. Trump would need a substitute. So with M. Trump running, where does that leave M. DeSantis? The two are very aligned on the issues. What could a voter get with M. DeSantis that he wouldn’t get with M. Trump ? So, it seems very unlikely that M. DeSantis can execute on his strategy. If someone were to unseat M. Trump as the front leader for the primary (which is quite unlikely as of now), it would be someone who could propose a different profile to the conservative voter.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: When did NPR become so left-wing?
Answer: In public accounting, there’s a notion called Government expenditure by function or COFOG which can be used to compare how different countries spend their budget. One of these functions is labeled “Recreation, culture and religion”. OECD countries spend 0.7% of their GDP on that, EU countries, 1.2%. The US spends 0.3%. A lot of the expenditure on culture proper actually goes to the CPB, corporation for public broadcasting. They get roughly $500m a year, which is a tiny part of the 0.3% (which is already less than half of what most countries spend on culture). $500m is about 0.01% of our federal budget of 5.3 trillion dollars, and that’s about 0.002% of our GDP. Again - some developed countries spend approximately 1% of their budget on culture alone. And yet, conservatives regularly call to defund CPB and/or to reduce funding from CPB to NPR or PBS. Because 0.002% is still too much. So maybe NPR is not super conservative, though it’s not like it’s blatantly partisan either. But conservatives have been actively trying to kill the concept of public-funded media for decades, when this is the only way that our federal government invests in culture.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: My manager says I will be put on PIP, should I quit now or wait for the process to end?
Answer: These are not your two only options. Quitting is lose/lose - you no longer have a job with all the attached perks (such as but not limited to getting paid), and the company is missing a worker. That said, if your situation is so bad that you prefer not having a job to going to work every day, this is not off the table. If you try to work within the plan and see what happens, this is 100% in the interest of your employer. They get: better output from their worker. You get: nothing more than you have, and definitely not the certainty that you won’t be let go at the end of the period. You have no control in how you will be evaluated. You have no guarantee that the process will be fair, or that what’s expected of you is even possible. Some people managers can be like, I’ve done all I could with this employee, I know I can’t just fire them outright because they haven’t done anything wrong, but they just don’t deliver and it would take too much effort to get them back to being productive, so we can just gently start the uncoupling and at least they’ll have enough time to decide what to do. If you try to wait it out and just check out, this is kind of in your interest but on a very short term. You get a mini vacation, you know you have nothing more to expect, but you’ll be out of a job soon. Of course this is not great for the company, but what did they expect. You could still get fired during that time (though this is exposes the employer to legal risks that most of them would rather avoid) but you’d have the satisfaction to not put any extra effort, or not effort at all really, in a process that may end up poorly for you. What a lot of people end up doing is looking for a new job, then move on. While looking for a new job, because this is time consuming, it’s hard to give the same level of efforts so some people’s performance degrade, because their priority is the job search. So, that puts them at an increased risk of failing the PIP, but it’s a calculated risk. The last option is do regular checkins with your manager to make sure you’re on track, course correct if you don’t and don’t just wait for them to decide. Just give yourself as much chances as possible to land on your feet. Whatever you decide will depend on what you want to do and what are your preferences and goals for the future.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do most of the software engineers shy away from becoming an engineering manager?
Answer: I don’t know if that’s the case. For people who have that opportunity, moving on to people management is a popular choice. I personally prefered staying as a senior IC - I feel that the nature of my work is similar, i influence the technical choices of my org, I charter the path to go with key stakeholders, I get projects started, I mentor more junior engineers and advice them on their career but I don’t have to do the HR part of the job - I’m not on the hook for having the difficult conversations, I have less work around performance review time etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for getting a job at Google or another big tech company if you didn't go through the campus recruiting process?
Answer: It would start either from you or from someone in the company. Either you apply to a job in the career websites, or a sourcer identifies you as a potential candidate and sets you up to talk to a recruiter. Alternatively to that, you can use your network to reach through the hiring manager, or get referred by an existing employee.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What has been the first hand experience of very senior software engineers using software CoPilot tools and generative AI like ChatGPT, to write sophisticated custom software with complex business logic?
Answer: In terms of developer experience, I think Copilot and ChatGPT are extremely different. I see Copilot as a part of my toolbox now the same way that modern IDEs include a lot of niceties that developers don’t have to think about. 10 years ago, if I didn’t have the agreed upon number of spaces in front of each line of code, I wouldn’t have been able to submit a code change, and I would have needed some level of manual verification to make sure that everything was in order. Today, this is one of the many auto-fixable problems that I know my editor will take care for me without thinking. This is a tedious task which I could always accomplish, but I also don’t really want to. Copilot is exactly in that category. I start writing code, some extra content pops up, it may be good or bad but the extra effort of reading the generated content is, in general, negligible compared to how much time it saves me to type it if it’s good. One analogy is what it felt to have auto-spellcheck on when it was introduced by word processor software in the 90s, versus having to check the spelling of any questionable word in a paper dictionary, which was my experience prior to that. ChatGPT though is a different animal. I very routinely ask chatGPT questions on what I’m doing, and I take its answers with a massive grain of salt, but some of the answers are pretty good and save me time. What I like are answers on things which are low-value code that I don’t want to overthink, like a proof of concept. I know that code isn’t going to win me the ACM Turing Award, but I don’t want to spend more time than strictly necessary. A side effect is having to pause and formalize what I want to see in plain English. Having used ChatGPT-4 almost daily with coding tasks ever since it came out, my overall experience is that I can’t rely on code generated by it, however that code is going to be ok for very well-delimited, easy to describe tasks. The main issue I’ve had with ChatGPT-generated code is the model’s propensity to be “confidently wrong”, ie to generate code that is not going to answer the problem as described but present it as if it might. This trait, if present in a human coworker, would be unbearable, but with ChatGPT it’s just a known fact. This is made more acute by the fact that if you ask ChatGPT to generate code outside of your area of expert...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some reasons why Facebook might be using React instead of developing their own JavaScript framework?
Answer: The 2 reasons are that it was born at Facebook, and every major design decision was motivated to support the facebook.com use case, which has different constraints than pretty much every other website / web application out there.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What does it mean when a Google interviewer says, “There is no feedback on this one” after an interview question?
Answer: After an interview, interviewers are required to give detailed feedback according to several criteria. However, over all the time that the interviewer and candidate interact, there are periods when candidates are not judged, roughly the first 5 minutes and the last 5. It can be difficult to detect when the interview time proper actually starts, versus when the interviewer is still trying to build rapport. Likewise, candidates can feel that they are being evaluated as they ask questions, and feel forced to pick questions as a last opportunity to score points versus as a chance to get a candid answer on something they want to know. So, some interviewers like to signal when the candidate is “off the hook”. If a candidate says or does something completely outrageous during that time, the interviewer will still have to report it, but the bar for outrageous is pretty high, like: personal attacks.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for negotiating salaries at Google, Facebook and other tech giants? Are there any tips or advice for negotiating salaries at these companies?
Answer: I’ve negotiated my compensation for both Google and Facebook. Facebook was a very long time ago so I don’t think my experience is relevant any more, but all my discussion was with my recruiter who had full authority to tell me yes or no (she said yes). I also got to change the wording of my employment contract, though this was on Facebook’s initiative as a courtesy to me, not an actual demand (basically they put in writing that they will never refuse me taking time off or requesting remote work to visit my family). For Google it was a bit different, as the hiring process goes through several formal checks, hiring committee, VP approval etc. so my recruiter didn’t have the final say. I don’t think I got every penny I could have had from Google and what I got was something of a pyrrhic victory, though on paper it looked much better than my original offer. I got an offer to start in December 2019, with X salary, Y equity and 0 starting bonus. X and Y were pretty decent numbers and well within my expectations. My recruiter explained I would be in the middle of the band for my hiring level (which was staff engineer / L6), and once I joined I verified this was the case as many employees share their salaries internally. I thought it would be hard to ask for a higher salary or a higher equity but I felt that there was no harm in asking for a starting bonus. After all, if I started then I was not going to forgo my bonus at my current employer. So, I asked for a 50k starting bonus. My recruiter couldn’t give me 50k herself, so she had to send back my offer and wait for an answer. It came within a week or so and it was granted. That’s the least I’ve ever worked for 50,000 dollars. But then, the time was a ticking and did I really want to start in the 2nd half of December 2019, while presumably everyone would be away? It didn’t make a ton of sense, plus, I had a big deadline for the first week of January so was already thinking of starting mid January, after taking a little bit of time off. I told my recruiter as well, so she could finish my offer letter. Good news, she told me, X USD was if you started in 2019, but since you’re starting in 2020, we’re revising our scales and you’re getting like a 3% raise. Great - I still haven’t done any type of work for Google, and I already got 50k and a 3% bump. So I signed and started to work and off I was for my first year, then pandemic happened as we all know which just made my ramping up more difficult. Tech companies in general are better at onboarding remote folks but Google, which was very much an everybody must come to the office every day type of company, had a rough start. I was doing ok but not great, and I was thinking that if I had another 6 weeks at the office - starting early December with everyone versus mid January, it would have made a pretty big difference. Comes the time for my first performance review, and I fall in the middle bucket, which I was pretty proud of actually. So I get a little raise but unlike virtually everyone, I don’t get a bonus because… I’m evaluated on a partial year, having started during the year. Yeah, partial is 50 weeks out of 52. Only very strong performers can get a bonus in their first year, and I was not that. The bonus I would have had was 100–200k. Also, I would have had it had I started in December 2019. That could explain why I got 0 pushback when I asked for 50k. They were more than happy to give me 50k now, vs 150k in a year, AND i got a few extra thousand dollars in salary to make me feel great. So what did I learn.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the reasons why it is not possible to reach 100% test or code coverage?
Answer: It is always possible to reach 100% testing coverage for working code. If the code can run in production, then bring up a test environment that is similar enough to the production environment (up to the production environment) and run it automatically. Every branch which is reachable in the real world can be run for automated testing, and branches which are not reachable can be cut (getting you closer to 100%). The question is whether it is practical or economical to do so, and whether there is a return on the investment given the effort to write certain tests and the extra level of confidence they bring.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it possible for an older programmer with no experience to get a job at Google or Facebook?
Answer: What exactly has an older programmer with no experience been doing with their career so far?

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do most candidates who have accepted offers from Google regret their decision after working there for some time?
Answer: I’ve worked at Google 2020–2023. I haven’t been very happy at Google, though I don’t think i ever regretted my decision to join. This seemed like a very rational decision when I took it, and I’ve learned so much while there. I understand why it is such a special employer for many people, why it means so much to them. At the same time, it can be incredibly frustrating to work at Google, both as an employee who cares about their career and as a member of an organization. Regarding my career at Google, I mostly didn’t get to work on the problems I was very interested in when I joined. There was no good fit between my skills and my role, and I never was able to transfer for various reasons. On the plus side, I did learn a lot, but my career didn’t progress how I expected and so much of my energy was wasted on things I didn’t want to care about. But also, as somebody who attached their name to Google, it’s been frustrating to see positions that the company took, for instance regarding the departure of Timnit Gebru, or which products were just killed, and which products received investment. As a person you don’t necessarily align with how your employer behaves and their decisions have a tremendous impact on the world. Despite these frustrations, I think regretting joining Google would be a huge overstatement. In my experience, the vast majority of Google employees are very proud to be employees and of what they can accomplish within the company.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do companies like Google care about your algorithm solving skills if you have zero experience building an app or working as software engineer before going through their interviews?
Answer: It’s very difficult to get an interview with Google. There are different ways (all selective) to enter the pipeline but if a person doesn’t have a way to demonstrate they have the skillset prior to interviewing, usually through their experience, they will simply not have a chance to interview.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do startups pay more than large corporations such as Facebook and Google for software engineers?
Answer: 10 years ago the consensus was that “FANG” companies offered the best risk-adjusted compensation for tech employees. That’s no longer true. On one hand you have mid-sized companies like OpenAI, Roblox or Cruise that offer better packages, sometimes through different compensation model, than big tech (see 2023 Mid-Year Compensation Report ) On the other some start-ups are willing to pay top dollar for the talent which is critical to their success. As a rule, working in a startup is riskier than in a large company, but in some specific cases hiring the right person for the role is so important that compensations at startups can go through the roof.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the process for someone with no college education to work as a software engineer at Google or Facebook? How long does this take?
Answer: Education gives a leg up for candidates because Google and Meta are actively recruiting in certain campuses. The easiest way is to get an internship and convert it into an offer. But in the general case, you get hired by passing an interview, which takes 2 steps: being invited to interview, and performing well at the interview. Anyone can succeed in step 2 regardless of education as long as they have the skills, and anyone who has the disposition can learn the skills. When you don’t have a degree, it is step 1 which is harder. When I was working at Facebook, I had 2 teammates that didn’t have a college degree. Prior to Facebook, one was a key contributor to an influential open source library, and the other had already a resume more impressive than most people twice his age, having started a sold a business. In my personal case, I had a degree, just not in computer science. But what I had was a well-read blog. This helped enter the hiring pipeline.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: When a senior developer doesn’t know something basic that all developers should know, is it okay for the tech lead to tell him/her that even a junior developer in the team would know this and that they are surprised that the senior dev doesn’t?
Answer: No this is completely backwards. Engineers are experts at learning. They are not walking encyclopedias. During most of my career I felt that virtually all technical decisions I make are based on what I learned in the previous 6 months. This very morning, I was in a meeting where a senior engineer thanked a junior engineer for teaching him something he didn’t know. That is the way it should go. When people don’t know something they should know, this is a learning opportunity. That should be celebrated not shunned.
