Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How difficult is it to get into Google or Facebook as a software engineer with no CS degree?
Answer: As someone who was hired by both and who doesn’t have a CS degree, it is more difficult but not substantially more difficult. The prerequisite, anyway, is regardless of degree, to have the required skillset for the job. You’re not going to be hired knowing nothing of coding or algorithms. The difficulty is really to get an interview. If you’re a CS major from a good school, you have opportunities for internships, that help you pad your resume and also gives you a good chance of a return offer, with which you can start your career. If you’re not, you need a way to enter the pipeline. If you can get an interview, and you already have the skillset for the job, it’s then possible to learn the specific skillset for the interview. ie: you may know how to code in such or such language, but you can learn how to code for the coding interview, you may understand architecture at a high level, but you can learn about the system design interview, etc. That has nothing to do with a degree.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How can you show off your work experience and projects on GitHub while interviewing with big companies like Facebook or Google?
Answer: Those two things are different. Work experience definitely helps a candidate get an interview at the right level. Side projects help to some extent, but these are usually a rounding error compared to work experience - unless a candidate has created a truly ground breaking technical solution on their own time. Once you are interviewing, side projects are mostly irrelevant (with the same caveat). This is all about how well a candidate does in the interviews. The behavioral interviews lean heavily on the work experience though, it is not possible for someone to do well without the relevant experience. No hiring committee is going to say, well the candidate completely bombed the coding interview, but they have a to-do app on github, so…

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do companies like Apple stay in California (8.8% corporate tax) instead of moving their HQ to a state with 0% tax (S. Dakota)? Couldn't they just move their HQ in a low-tax state and have R&D offices in Silicon Valley?
Answer: Tech companies don’t see every decision only through accounting lens, but even if they did - if they asked tens of thousands of employees to relocate to South Dakota, first this would cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and second many of these employees would quit, and now Apple would have to operate with many key roles left unfilled and will have to spend tens of millions hiring for these roles, then hundreds of millions relocating new hires to South Dakota, and this would push back the release of time-sensitive products (that’s billions, possibly tens of billions of dollars). So that would be a very big flex just to “own the libs”. Besides, being in California whatever the price is very important to Apple, it’s something they showcase in their products and which is important to their brand. Last point, Apple already does significant tax optimization as it is, so the benefits of moving their HQ would not be as clear cut.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Are there any advantages to having fewer lines of code than more when coding/programming?
Answer: Everything else being equal, brevity implies legibility and clarity. but also, a codebase that has reuses components rather than reimplementing similar functions everywhere, or which uses strong interfaces between components rather than loose and vague interfaces, is going to be shorter. Also, a shorter code (usually) means a shorter compiled code which has a number of benefits. That said, concision is not a goal in itself, and more obfuscated code for the sake of having fewer lines of code is not a good thing.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some signs that your interview went well at Google (especially for software engineering and research)?
Answer: When I had my onsite at Google, right after I left, my recruiter called me and told me that the early feedback was positive, so I guess that’s a datapoint. She also made clear that there were a number of further steps like reference check including full feedback, hiring committee, internal references, team match, VP approval etc. so I didn’t feel I was out of the woods.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What do you think about the cognitive assessment test before software developer interviews? Are they an adequate tool to screen candidates?
Answer: The point of an interview should be to answer the following question in confidence: can this candidate perform well as a software engineer of a given rank ? Which we often simplify as, does this candidate have the skillset expected of an engineer of that rank? Lots of people, even today, assume that character or attitude is just as important as skill to performance. But attitude can easily be coached and character is not deterministic, whereas skills have to be acquired. So, there is a general consensus in the engineering interview that questions around attitude do more harm than good. This leaves questions around the innate capacities of candidates, specifically: do you need to be smart to be a good software engineer, and if so, why not assess this independently of anything connected to software engineering to filter out candidates? IMO, the assumption that you have to be smart to be a good engineer can sound reasonable, but I’ve met many very intelligent people who were poor performers, so I don’t think this is a very useful criteria. At Google, up to a point the word “smart” was in some of the criteria, one engineer questioned that and this was reworded. At the time I left Google, officially, interviewers don’t try to assess the cognitive capacities of candidates and that’s not used to make a determination. As a candidate, I have never taken such a test as a condition to interviews, but I did have to go through a cognitive interview once as part of an onsite round. All questions were asked in a specific context, so this was really an assessment of whether the candidate (me) had preexisting knowledge on a variety of topics, more so than how they could think about an abstract problem. Think of the questions I was asked as variations of “why are manholes round”. Somebody who’s never thought about it could come up with the actual reason, but most likely, people will know because they were once told, this is why manholes are round. So, I didn’t feel it was a great experience or very useful. So after all is said and told, I don’t think such tests are useful, and interviewers should stick closer to evaluating the skillset.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If someone feels stuck in their career as a software Test engineer, how can they make the transition to full development?
Answer: Different people understand different things by testing engineer. At Google there were various technical people who were 100% focused on testing and who had different titles, and which may be called “test engineers” in other organizations. People who did manual QA were contractors, and it would be extraordinarily difficult for them to become full-time employee, software engineers, though if they have the skillset, they would still have a leg up compared to other candidates. It would also be difficult for people who coordinate these tests (who are full-time employees, and who have a role similar to program managers) to transfer to an engineering role, but still possible and at any rate, they could pick up software engineering tasks and become an engineer in anything but by name. On the other hand, the Googlers whose title was test engineer are peers to software engineers. An analogy would be dentists to other medical doctors. It’s just another specialty. Test engineers focus on coming up with testing strategies and solving some technical problems around testing. There is a regular flow of people who transfer from test engineer to software engineers, and in the other direction.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is wrong with W3Schools that it is often referred to as a bad resource for learning?
Answer: I don’t think there’s anything wrong with w3schools per se. However, it overlaps with MDN Web Docs . MDN is an open-source reference documentation for the web. w3schools is really good at SEO. So, when you’re looking for some information about some web API, let’s say flex layout, you can get: Among other things. In my google query, these 3 links appear in order: w3schools, then MDN, then W3C spec, which is my typical experience. They will also rank from the least exhaustive to the most exhaustive, and the least authoritative to the most authoritative. For people who know nothing about a topic and want a bite-size nugget of information, w3schools is fine and possibly best. For people who want to verify how a given property or method works, which browsers support it or not, and best practice recommendations, MDN is the best resource. This is the most frequent use case for professional web developers or software engineers. For web nerds that want to dive into the internals of the implementation and exactly what the standards say, neither is enough and nothing short of the specs will do. Personally, my use case most frequently calls for the MDN level of detail, w3schools is typically not adequate. But it does fill a purpose and it can be more helpful than a more dense piece of information.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How much time would you allocate for yourself to read through and make sense of a large enough (let's say anything between 50k to 200k lines) codebase for a Software?
Answer: I have started in a new company a couple of months ago. My scope is about 100k lines of code. One of my first priorities was to get acquainted with the code base. It’s difficult to give an answer as a direction function of time, but if I were to I would say ~5k loc per day. So, in my case, 20 work days. In yours, 10 to 40. One reason it’s difficult is that you don’t read a codebase like a novel from start to finish. Even as a domain expert there is a time when fatigue sets in and you have to switch to do something else. Comments, documentations, tests can also make this work much easier. In my case, I didn’t spend the 20 days. I’m reasonably familiar with some parts of the code base that need my attention now (or that exhibit some interesting characteristics, such that I feel I should know about them). I also know some metadata about the code base, such as code coverage. Where some unsavory patterns are used. Which parts have the most dependencies, which parts of the most dependents. Which have been involved in outages, which seem to trigger the most support requests.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the reason for the high number of failures in technical interviews at Google and Facebook? Is it due to lack of preparation from candidates, or is there another reason?
Answer: Google gets about 3 million applications per year. There are very few open positions. That’s all you need to know. During a big part of the 2010s, the reasoning behind tech hiring is that someone who is good enough should get a job. This may still be true in some companies that are in very fast growth. In most of the tech world though, candidates are applying for a specific role in a specific team, so there will be a limited number of candidates who will get an offer. This allows employers to move the bar up. So sure, there is a lot of advice out there for candidates, and a lot of it makes sense. But there is no such thing as “the most common mistake” which if addressed will guarantee a spot. At the end of the day, interviews are complex human interactions with a lot of variables in play, evaluations are subjective to some extent, hiring committee is also composed of humans and there are lots of factors that contribute to a decision.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If front-end development is more complex than backend development, why are new developers continuously encouraged to pick a career in front end development?
Answer: In my experience, neither part of this proposition is true. Specifically, front-end work is neither simpler nor more complicated than any other specialty.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the fundamental test design mistake of testing too much in a unit test and how can it be avoided?
Answer: Too many unit tests is usually not a problem, because the costs of having one or thousands of extra unit test is not high, so the extra safety brought by more unit tests is worth it. Conversely, leaving large swaths of code uncovered and vulnerable to preventable outages is expensive. On a side note, many tests including unit tests are useless. They exercise parts of the code base and they can “cover” it but they may always pass, or they don’t really test scenarios that people can ever care about etc. But that doesn’t challenge the fact that unit tests as a concept are useful and are the most important line of defense against regressions and potential outages.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Are testing components on the front-end a unit test or an integration test?
Answer: The distinction is not necessarily useful. Regardless of the front-end context, component testing is a concept that is different from unit tests and integration tests, whereby you divide your system in components and you test the system at the component boundary, ignoring internals. The division between components doesn’t have to follow files or classes, but it’s usually on the same executable program, so there’s no network calls between parts of the component. Integration testing is tests among 2 different components, which may call each other, possibly over network. In front-end, components are usually one class or class-like function, and testing one class in isolation can be considered unit testing. In the React world specifically, there has been several trends which make the distinction between unit testing and component testing blurry. First, functional components is the new normal. These components may have functions defined within the function....

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Would you rather have $10 million dollars right now or $10 bucks per second for the rest of your life?
Answer: I’ll save you the math. 1 million seconds is 11 days and a half, give or take. But: there’s a huge difference between money now, and the promise of money in the future. It’s extremely unlikely that someone who promises you $10/s in perpetuity will make good on their commitment, especially over a long period of time. So between the certainty of getting $10m today and the virtual impossibility to get billions over my lifetime, I will definitely choose the former. Put it differently, if I’m asked to invest $10m and in return I would be promised an income of $10/s, without any form of guarantee, I would definitely pass.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What would happen if Facebook bought Amazon and Google?
Answer: To put things in perspective, both Amazon and Alphabet are valued well over a trillion dollars each. Meta has maybe 40 billion dollars in cash, which is a ton of money and enough to buy smaller companies, but a tiny fraction of what it would take to acquire another big tech company.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Will Blizzard ever remaster Warcraft 1 and 2? Are there any chances for these to happen?
Answer: I’m not betting on it. Warcraft 1 was an genre-defining game but it sold about 300,000 copies, which was a huge lot in 1994. 30 years later, the video game industry is about 10 times larger than it was then, and successful games sell tens of millions of units. Even if the development cost of a Warcraft 1 or 2 remaster would be fairly low, that would be developers that would not work on existing franchises with a near-certain business impact.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Facebook choose to make React out of PHP instead of JavaScript (like JQuery)?
Answer: React is almost entirely written in JavaScript (GitHub - facebook/react: The library for web and native user interfaces ). There’s 0 PHP in it. When React was created, Facebook the web site had a PHP web server layer. This was a fairly common setup (and still is, given that WordPress which represents a significant part of the web, also uses PHP). PHP would generate html and javascript files, that referenced to React, and could create interactive web sites. A lot of websites that use jQuery have the same approach. A server generates HTML loaded in web browsers that use jQuery for interaction and animation. In a way, React and jQuery are both JavaScript libraries. What they do and their scope is a bit different though.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do companies like Google, Facebook, etc. ask candidates to write code on a whiteboard during interviews? How can one be expected to remember algorithms from college after so much time has elapsed?
Answer: Let’s say hypothetically, you get a phone call. Somebody has a strange proposition for you. “In a month, we’ll put you in a room for a few hours. It will be an exam of sorts, nothing you’ve never learned though and actually the scope of what we’ll ask is very limited. If you pass the exam, we’ll give you a new job, with hundreds of thousands of dollars more than what you make in your current job, with a good chance to make millions. How does that sound?” If after you hang up, you decide to do nothing to prepare, then don’t be surprised if you don’t get the job.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Are CEOs required to act in favor of the company or the shareholders?
Answer: CEOs have a fiduciary duty to the shareholders. Typically shareholders, or the directors who are supposed to represent them, give some latitude to the CEO to act in the best interests of the company and its stakeholders (employees, customers/vendors, government, citizens at large / environment) but the CEO has an obligation towards the shareholders. It is assumed that the interests of the company are aligned with those of the shareholders as the shareholders own the company.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Is it ethical for interviewers to ask to see your previous company's report (similar job scope) during an interview (these 2 companies are not in the same industry and are definitely not competitors)? I didn't but I was surprised at the question.
Answer: All legal considerations set aside, if we just focus on whether this is ethical - This defeats the point of the interview. The moral contract of the interview is: One big difference between say reference checks and reviewing performance evaluations is that the performance reports could be written in a very adversarial way and that the candidate had no input on that. After all, employees frequently leave because of a conflict with their manager. So, those documents shouldn’t be construed as a source of truth. Conversely, there can be some objectivity in the interview - or at least, the candidate is going to jump through the hoops that the employer sets u and demonstrate the skill they care about. So undermining a formal evaluation from interviewers that the employer trusts with a document which is not written by someone who has the interests of the candidate or the future employer in mind, and without any guarantee of objectivity or truth, just doesn’t seem the right thing to do.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can a bad personality result in a rejection after the coding round of interviews at Google, Amazon, and Facebook? If so, how can one avoid this situation?
Answer: I’ve never interviewed at Amazon, but I’ve spent about 5 years at Google and Facebook combined. Not all of my coworkers could be described as fun or the life of the party or even likable (me included). If a candidate is rejected, it’s definitely not because of their “bad personality” - it’s because they didn’t do great at one of the tests, or when trying to fill a specific position, because another candidate was an objectively better fit. Some candidates can be rejected based on something very offensive they say or do during the interview. But that’s not their personality, it’s skills that are learned or not. For instance, it’s not a personality to be racist or to yell at people. You just learn to be respectful of others in the workplace, and you develop some common sense / self-awareness.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why did Google choose Angular over ReactJS or Vue.js?
Answer: AngularJS, then Angular were born at Google and given a dedicated team at Google. What you will not find a big tech company doing, Google least of all, is say hey, we spent 10+ years developing something and going in a direction we thought the right one, but you know what? let’s scrap it, use something developed by one of our competitors that were optimizing for a slightly different problem, and do a massive migration. And yet it’s not really accurate that Google “chose” Angular. There is some React in the code base, a very tiny amount of Vue, but most of Google’s big web properties (gmail, google search, google maps…) don’t use Angular, but use an in-house framework which is not open source.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How much time does it takes to learn & master HTML + CSS + Javascript?
Answer: 10 years as a ballpark figure. That’s approximately the number of years of practice is takes to make senior software engineer at Google, that is education + professional experience. Roughly put, senior front-end software engineers at Google are good enough to work on any front-end problem, short of completely reinventing large paradigms of the web. The majority of technical decisions are made by senior software engineers, which in turn have a big impact on the way the web works. (Same goes for Meta or Microsoft, even if their titles are different - the experience to impact relationship is the same). But even they don’t know everything there is to know on HTML, CSS or Javascript. One thing that many people don’t realize is how wide the scope of HTML is. There are well over 1000 propositions in flight, dozens and dozens of existing web APIs that most people never heard of let alone used, and several possible “futures” of the web. CSS and HTML are pretty much conjoined at the hip, so advanced knowledge of one presupposes knowledge of the other. The coding part of web is a different animal because it’s not “just” JavaScript (which is also very much a living language with a rapidly changing syntax) but also type management, frameworks like React/Angular, the web server layer, modules/bundlers, performance tuning, testing, browser internals, back end integration etc.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are the best ways of getting a better loading speed on a website?
Answer: There are lots of possible causes for delay in a web application. When a user visits a web site, there are a number of tasks that happen, some in succession, meaning one must be complete before moving on to the next one, like resolving the IP address for a given domain name, some happening in parallel, such as loading the various assets of the web page. So, there’s a critical path of all the tasks that must be completed before the page is available, and any extra millisecond on any of them pushes the time when the page is ready. Fortunately web developers also have tools at their disposal to get a good sense of where that time is spent and what can be faster. Lighthouse (or https://pagespeed.web.dev/, same thing different package ) is a good place to start. The usual suspects are: * too much javascript. When a web page is generated through code, it must download a javascript script, then decompress it, then parse it, then execute it. All of this takes time. This is often negligible if the code is fairly small and the network conditions are great. But the code can become bloated and the amount of javascript to download can be unreasonable, and because of all of these operations, this holds everything up. * big assets. A web page can load an uncompressed, 2mb image when a 10kb version would look identical. Same goes with videos, fonts, stylesheets etc. * optimize for bandwidth vs optimize for computing power. In general, modern web sites assume that users have a high quality internet connection, so the user can fire many requests and download a lot of data and the result is faster than fewer requests / less data and let the client device do the heavy lifting. But that’s not always the case, sometimes it can be expected that many users will have a terrible connection and if the web application doesn’t take that into account, this will result in massive slow downs.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: As a software engineer and US citizen, if my US-based company hires me as an independent contractor, could I move to Europe?
Answer: The main question there is whether you are authorized to work in Europe. Even then, this also raises taxes questions. If a US company doesn’t do any business in a given country, and then have people who start working in that country, then they can be liable to pay tax, not just on the payroll of these employee but on the basis of their entire revenue. Different countries have different rules but this is no trivial matter. At any rate, it would be up to them to figure out how to report this to the various interested parties and it will probably not be their preferred scenario.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How isn’t it sexist to expect men to open doors for women? The last time I checked everyone should open doors for everyone regardless of gender.
Answer: Good manners are about acting in a way which is consistent with what others expect. There isn’t a universal rule around doors. The etiquette around holding doors is quite subtle. I remember as a young man that one of my women coworkers resented that I didn’t open the door for her and let her exit a building first in winter, when this is one of the textbook cases when a man is supposed to go first. But going by the etiquette is not always the right call. Some people expect the person in front of them to hold the door for them, some resent that. Some women expect a man to let them through first, some don’t. There are some times when how people will react and what they expect can be anticipated, but in all other cases, there’s really no obligation prevent the door from hitting the person behind you. And yes, etiquette perpetuates conservative gender roles, so it’s fair to call it sexist, but that doesn’t mean it’s always wrong.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: In React.js, what is the usage of setState (useState() [1]) and passing a function instead of a value?
Answer: This is very hacky. Normally you would write something like const [state, setState] = useState(). One side effect of calling setState is that it will trigger a rerender. Let’s say you don’t really care about keeping state, so you don’t really need to keep the value of the state anywhere. useState()[1] would just be a function that, sure, would update a state somewhere but will also trigger a rerender. in Reacf with hooks, there is no way to for e a rerender without updating a state - forceUpdate() is no more. But even then, you can be clearer in your intentions. For instance: const [_, rerender] = useState(); then as needed: rerender();

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How should you answer an interviewer when they ask, "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?"
Answer: Let’s pause on that question for a bit and what would be a “perfect answer”. A candidate is a professional, so they have a career. I think it’s a reasonable expectation that this professional takes some time to think of their career and develop a certain degree of self-awareness. So, it follows that they can be expected to set goals - what do they want to accomplish in the next few months, in the next years or longer, what do they not like about their situation they want to avoid, what do they miss, etc. If a candidate periodically reflects on their career, they should have clear answers to these questions, and from then give an eloquent answer to that question. There’s no such thing as a formula that works every time.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you persuade an engineer from Google or Facebook to join your startup?
Answer: As a former Facebook and Google employee and recipient of hundreds of recruiters cold emails, I see about 3 strategies.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is your opinion on using Google during an online coding test or whiteboard interview?
Answer: When I interviewed for Google (so, 2019) I also interviewed for Stripe. Google, like most tech companies afaik, has a policy to not let people use google (somewhat ironically) during the interview, but candidates can ask questions to their interviewer. During my Google interviews I was never blocked or stumped so it was irrelevant. Stripe had the opposite policy. Back in 2019, the idea was that the interview had to reflect the daily work of an engineer, and so candidates were not just authorized, but encouraged to use Google if stuck. In 2019, I had spent the past few years as a front-end engineer writing JavaScript code that ran in browsers. Browsers, then, had very restricted access to local files, and so reading and writing to files was not something I was doing regularly. So, for my coding interview, I’m asked what language I want to use, I say JavaScript, my interviewer is not a front-end engineer and gives me a “language agnostic” problem which, as you could have guessed, revolves around reading and writing files. It would be possible to do this with node.js, so not the end of the world, but because it’s not something I do on a regular basis, I’m just not sure of the syntax to use. Naturally, I’m asking my interviewer, who gives me something like: in a real life situation, you would google it, so go ahead and google it (in a real life situation I would ask somebody who I am confident know the answer, but I digress). So I comply and google it, and the first hit is a medium article that describes exactly the task I have at hand, as far as reading multiple files are concerned - not the crux of the interview. So, I follow the article, and then do what I have to do to solve the problem. It doesn’t work. I’m very sure of the code I wrote, except for the file handling part but this comes from that article. My interviewer just watches and doesn’t offer feedback, until I run out of time without having a working solution to the problem. Once back home, I try to do the exercise again, and this time because I’m not time constrained I open the official node.js documentation and I’m ready to go down the rabbit hole if needed. I instantly see a glaring error in the article I followed. I feel in this interview, my coding skills were not tested as much as my luck. Luck is always a factor in interviews, tbh, but usually this is by circumstances, here it was by design. It’s only a matter of time before asking a technical question in a search engine will get the user an LLM generated answer, like a snippet of code that implements exactly what the user wanted. At that stage using a search engine is going to be completely off the table because then what are we testing? In the meantime I don’t think it’s a good service to candidates to allow them to use a search engine. Rather, they should be in a situation where all technical questions about the interview can be answered by the interviewer.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why do tech companies spend so much time testing software engineering candidates on algorithms, at the expense of equally important topics such as design patterns, OOP/SOLID principles, database design, debugging, and unit/integration testing?
Answer: In my experience people have a somewhat outdated impression of what the engineering interview entails. The Google interview is probably the most classic, and is comprised of coding tests, a system design interview and behavioral interviews. That said the nature of the coding tests has evolved significantly, and is neither trick questions or remembering hundreds of leetcode-type questions as it once was. There are also a lot of possible variations. The system design interview as Google does it is also very different from the system design interview as presented in Alex Xu’s System Design Interview: an Insider’s Guide or Educative.io’s Grokking the System Design Interview. It is more a domain specific technical discussion than a completely abstract high-level problem. I left Google earlier this year and interviewed in a number of companies. None of the companies that I interviewed for - not. one. - had coding, system design and behavioral interviews. Each and every one had a different type of interview not listed above, or had a significant variation of one of these interviews. Here are some of the interviews I had to do: refactoring a piece of code (that’s a few hundred lines). Fixing broken tests. Math test. Presentation of a past project (this one, which I had never done before this interview cycle, I had to do several times and the employer expected such different things under the same label that I ended up presenting a different project each time). Coding in pseudo-code. Likewise, everyone’s behavioral interviews format was completely different - some included technical discussions, some did not. Now back to the coding tests. I have been more often in the interviewer seat than in the candidate’s. But going recently through coding interviews made me realize how many different ways there are to evaluate an interview. Depending on the individual interviewer or employer guidelines, the same performance can be amazing in one context and bad in another. Let me clarify: Maybe performance is very important. Or code style. Or communication. Or using modern code features. Or handling edge cases, including writing test cases. Time/pace is almost universally important, but some people may think whether the candidate finishes is critical and others won’t. Making code that works the f...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is a code review? What kind of questions would be asked during a code review for a dev job with Google, Facebook, etc.?
Answer: A code review interview is an interview where the candidate is shown a piece of problematic code and they have to discuss what’s wrong with it. At Google, It is given to engineering managers, on the assumption that it gives similar signal to a coding interview, but is more fair to EMs who haven’t been coding regularly.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: If you had the power to transform or create a new interview system, what changes would you make? Please provide a rationale for your answer.
Answer: For the software engineer interview process, the start of the funnel is completely broken (that is, the part up to the actual interview). Candidates that show up to an interview may not be qualified. Most qualified candidates are not in the pipeline. They are either not on the radar of companies, or are rejected for irrational reasons such as their application is never taken into account. With AI we have an historic opportunity to challenge the way that applications are reviewed which is very labor intensive, i.e. : it takes several hours of calls with recruiters and technical interviewers to determine if a candidate is qualified to go further in the pipeline, it also take a lot of time to the candidate when they don’t have a take home assignment on top of it all. But, AI can do a good job at generating unique problems, and evaluating candidate performance on these well delimited tasks. That can go beyond writing code, it could be more general problem solving, code reviewing, document writing / reviewing, etc. So instead of sharing the workload of the first segment of the funnel between employer and candidate, a machine could take the brunt of it, which would allow employers to scale up, while having a well-rounded assessment.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some good reasons to write a unit test first when starting an application from scratch in Python or JavaScript (especially with React)?
Answer: As somebody who cares a lot about testing, and who uses a lot of React, I have never started a React application with a unit test. React is notoriously hard to unit test. A lot of the code in React applications only exist for the sake of React, so a lot of tests effectively test the framework not the business logic. Those tests are largely useless. The tooling around React testing, although it has progressed significantly, is still not great. It’s still difficult to test individual things that React components should do. It is now easy to test that a React component renders correctly given the right props, which is very useful and very good. But it is hard to test the actual business logic of the components, and that is really what unit tests should be about. The world of React testing is very opinionated and dominated by react testing library, and a gaggle of end-to-end testing solutions like Cypress. The natural evolution of the testing landscape is that end-to-end tests, and simulation of user inputs do most of the testing, but this leaves some code, which is relevant and useful in production scenarios, in hard to reach places for such tests. So. while starting with unit tests is a sensible strategy for a lot of environment, I really can’t recommend it for React, this is really a huge overhead of work.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How does Google review code submitted during interviews?
Answer: it’s not Google who reviews, but the individual interviewer, and later the hiring committee also has access to that code. There are 8 metrics by which a coding interview is evaluated, and it’s not strictly the code which is analyzed but the interview as a whole. For instance, you can’t tell how well a candidate has communicated with their interviewer just by looking at their code, but that’s one of the things which is taken into account.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why are senior software developers speaking out against using AI platforms to write code, when some of the largest tech companies are developing the tools to do exactly that?
Answer: When copilot was introduced, it came with the commentary that it was going to replace software developers. This comes in a larger context where it’s becoming possible to prototype or even launch full-scale commercial services using no-code or low-code platforms. I have in my network a few founders of tech startups that have paying customers and 0 engineers. All of this contributes to a narrative that software engineers are going to be replaced by AI. This is a story which, whether true or not, generates engagement and one which we start hearing over and over. This is like - whenever there was a story announcing the downfall of Facebook or Uber, it always gained traction because the founders were seen as so arrogant. The rest of the world can’t wait to see them trip and fall. Likewise, the world is waiting with bated breath for something bad to happen to “tech bros” what with their teslas and their stock options. I’ve now spent 10+ years in silicon valley and the typical software engineer is so different from the stereotype. Needless to say, software engineers are not thrilled with this vision of the future. What’s exactly happening is more complex than that. The nature of the job of software engineers (among other professions) is evolving, a little bit like the role of accountants changed with the availability of calculators and personal computers and many generations of software, though the accounting expertise remains relevant. That’s why it still makes sense to push back on one hand against the story that all developers are becoming obsolete, while on the other actually helping build the very tools these stories are about.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Does Google hire anyone who doesn't pass its coding test called 'Google interview'?
Answer: it’s a bit more complex than that, for software engineers there are multiple interviews and they each need detailed, formal feedback. Then that feedback is sent to a hiring committee who doesn’t know anything about the identity of the candidate, in order to make objective decisions. On top of that, there are other processes like checking references, including internal references (i.e. people at Google that may have worked with the person) and that can impact a hiring decision. So, more generally, have people been hired which have not done well on one coding interview, yes. Thousands. As long as the interview as a whole is successful and that there’s enough signal in other interviews to advocate for hiring the candidate. In my own experience as an interviewer, and I was a very prolific interviewer while at Google, hired candidates never have a perfect scorecard.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Why are unit tests more frequent than e2e tests on the front end? In that case, isn't it better to test whether the site is working in a browser than to test an isolated component?
Answer: There are problems that unit tests cannot prevent and that larger tests could cover. As a result, there is a narrative in favor of larger tests as a safer approach than unit tests. That’s misguided for at least three reasons. (As an aside, end-to-end test is always a misnomer. Both “ends” of an “end-to-end” test are arbitrary and leave part of the system uncovered. So let’s talk about “large tests” instead. ) So, three reasons: 1) you need much more large tests to have the same guarantees as few unit tests. With unit tests, you can cover every branch of a function. When you do, you have complete confidence on what this function do - you literally have tests for any possibility. Let’s say your function has 3 branches, 3 test cases are all you need. Let’s say that you have a system with 3 components A, B and C, each have 3 branches. The system will use component A, then B, then C. How many unit tests do you need? 3 for each component, so 9. Now let’s say you don’t want to test components, and instead only at the system boundary. To have the same confidence, you’d have to write 3x3x3 = 27 test cases. That is a super simple example, and in practice, the combinatorial explosion is such that you just never can have enough large tests to cover the entire system, if large tests it all you have in your toolbox. 2) large tests are flakier, and there’s nothing worse than a flaky test. The larger a system, the higher the chances there’s something non deterministic in it, like dates, random functions, dependencies on live data, etc. The simple fact that a system involves network calls already introduces some uncertainty. Flaky tests are tests that may fail even when the code under test is valid. If a test can be flaky, then developers will stop relying on its result - even when it repeatedly fails, they are likely to just disable it rather than act on it. So the test just acts as a speed bump, it’s never actually useful. By contrast, unit tests on deterministic functions with no side effects are highly reliable. 3) large tests run late and are expensive. You can normally run unit tests in seconds and any time. The entire system doesn’t have to function in order to run some unit tests, and some may fail sure, but some may pass and give some useful signal about code as it’s being built. By contrast, developers need to be at a stopping point before it makes any sense to run a large test. These never run in seconds (unless you have a toy application). Also remember that without reliable unit tests, you need a ton of large tests, so when these tests run is when you see the difference. That can also have a non negligible impact on your server costs. Now, everything else being equal, you want to catch potential bugs as early as possible. Having unit tests isn’t incompatible with testing the code that actual users will interact with. It’s perfectly fine to not test every method of every class (or equivalent, not everything in front-end world is a class but in practice a lot of code works like classes) and only test the public interfaces to components, with the assumption that this will naturally exercise all internals. But only test by simulating user sessions, in other words, test the entire web app as a block is just very inefficient and unsafe.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the importance of unit testing for front-end developers?
Answer: The vast majority of front-end developers do not care about unit testing, and for three reasons. 1, it’s very easy to see what front-end code does in a browser or to debug front-end code. So, it’s naturally tempting to forego automated testing in favor of manually checking that the things work. By contrast, it will take extra effort to see what server code does manually, you need logs, or some kind of user interface that isn’t part of the system under test. For this type of code, it is typically much easier to run automated tests than it is to do manual QA. 2, setting up a testing environment for modern front-end code is too hard. A reasonable expectation for a developer is that they can just write a little test script that exercises the feature code they just wrote. But that’s very insufficient for front-end code, which typically runs in a browser. Now, you don’t want to run your tests in an actual browser (or if you do, you’re bringing up a 1.5gb application on top of your 1kb code), so you have to simulate the browser environment on a server. And some parts won’t be exactly the same, but on top of that you have to bring up all the dependencies. That’s where the real fun begins, because “your code” is much more than the code you write, it’s also made up of a very heterogenous set of “modules” written in very different flavors of javascript, some use typescript, some don’t, some use common modules, some use ESM modules, some expect their code to be transpiled specifically with babel, some don’t, some can be run on a browser or node, some only on clients and some only on server, etc. So the testing environment has to rebuild an application but not exactly has the main application does, and most of the difficulty lies in code that developers that have to write tests have never seen. To be fair, the tooling for unit testing has become much better over the past 10 years but the complexity of front-end environments has grown even faster. 2b, further on that note, modern front-end code is also hard to test because it’s usually written in a very specific context, ie as “react components” or “angular modules” or tightly coupled with Svelte, Vue etc. There are typically few completely agnostic, standalone functions with just business logic that can be tested. Most of the logic lives in these components/modules and so it’s difficult to test smaller parts of the system, without testing big chunks of the system as the smallest possible unit. 3, the testing narrative around front end testing is just poor. For a mix of reason 1 and 2, front-end developers don’t love testing and tool vendors try to woo them by pushing the narrative that there are better ways to keep a codebase safe. There is a lot of activity, for instance, around end-to-end tests and some tools, like storybook, are also used as an alternative to automated tests - when it’s really just a fancier way to do manual QA. And now with AI, there are several solutions around automating test generation which is the topic for another question. As a result, I assume that most of front-end code in production today has little or no unit tests. I’ve spent the past 10 years in large tech companies and in my experience, well-tested front-end code is more the exception than the rule. Many popular open source front-end libraries come with absolutely no test. This doesn’t mean that unit testing shouldn’t be important in front-end. But until it’s very easy for front-end developers to write tests, the situation won’t change.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What is the correct order of software testing: unit testing or integration testing?
Answer: Integration tests, or other large scale tests, exercise a large portion of the code in one go. So in order to gain “testing coverage” quickly, just one test can cover 30, 50% or more of a system. The main problem with integration tests though is that it is typically difficult to come up with all the scenarios you should care about and for which you should write tests. I’ve read many incident reports where the conclusion was that an integration test could have caught the bug, sure, but then again the right test would have to be written to begin with and it was not trivial to come up with the idea of exactly what to test. With unit tests though, it’s easier to go through every possibility and make sure that a function, a class, a file etc. is properly tested - not that just every line of code is covered, which should be a by-product of good testing, but that every which way we’re going to use that code is addressed by a test. If a bug could have been caught by a unit test, then it absolutely should have been caught by a unit...

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: How do you write unit tests for private methods?
Answer: You don’t. If there’s a piece of code that has some logic you want to test independently of the class - you can put it in a separate function, that has a very clear interface and no side effects. That function can be tested independently. If all the code doesn’t really make sense outside of the context of the class, you just test the public methods. And then:

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: What are some reasons why you left Accenture or Deloitte after being there for one year or more? What were your plans when you left them, and what do you do now?
Answer: Deloitte was my first job after school. I left it about a year later and the triggering factor was reading the book, The Power of Corporate Kinetics which had been written by 2 partners and distributed to the consulting staff. The TL;DR of that book is that companies can become very performant if they adopt a certain number of best practices. Not super surprising from a consulting firm. What caused me to leave was that I was seeing some of these recommendations in action in other (non-consulting) companies I interacted with, but none of them at Deloitte. I realized we were in the business of getting paid to go tell clients, do as I say not as I do. That didn’t sit well with me. Another factor that was bothering me was that my cohort of junior consultants had a general disdain for deontology and would just do whatever it takes to be promoted, putting their self interest above that of their clients, their coworkers, the firm and sometimes the law. I didn’t want to become like that. I left over 20 years ago and I’ve done a number of things since then. Even though I was a business grad, eventually I pivoted to be a software engineer in the tech industry.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Do you agree with Mark Zuckerberg that making a company "more technical" is a good strategy?
Answer: No. When Facebook was created the vision was clear and the problem was essentially technical. How do you make a website that scales to 100s of million of users with petabytes of data changing in real time? How on top of that do you make this experience the state of the art for web sites? How do you make an app expected to be on nearly every one’s phone in the planet, from the latest iPhone to devices that can barely to connect to low-speed internet? In the last ~10 years, the focus has shifted to a feature explosion. The Facebook and Instagram app do tons of things no one ever asked, most of which do more harm than good. And then there’s Messenger, WhatsApp, Oculus and what not on top of it. All these apps come with tons of technical challenges and opportunities. But Meta is turning into what Google is which is an R&D lab funded by ads with no vision. Today, Meta’s core problems are not technical in nature and won’t be solved by a product team launching the billion-th new feature. How to stay relevant, how to provide a positive experience to end users (not just advertisers), how to fight harmful content. Those are mostly “how” questions not “what code to implement this already known solution” problems. Meta leadership’s job is to provide a vision. I think it’s no exaggeration to say that few people were energized and inspired by the metaverse (or at least Meta’s spin on it). But the problems are essentially non technical now, more in strategy and ops.

Name: Jérôme Cukier
Question: Can AI help software developers to write more robust code?
Answer: AI can help software developers write more code. This can free up time to make the code base more secure. But code generated by AI come with its own issues. The AI is good at executing a very specific task fast and gives the impression that it understands the larger context. But it doesn’t, it doesn’t write code to be legible or maintainable, it doesn’t write code that will work with the code base or not break things - just code that will impl...
